(1964) | | _**Out to Lunch!**_ is a 1964 album by the American jazz multi-instrumentalist [Eric Dolphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy "Eric Dolphy"). His only recording on [Blue Note Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records "Blue Note Records") as a leader, it was issued posthumously as BLP 4163 and BST 84163. Featuring Dolphy in a quintet with trumpeter [Freddie Hubbard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freddie_Hubbard "Freddie Hubbard"), vibraphonist [Bobby Hutcherson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Hutcherson "Bobby Hutcherson"), bassist [Richard Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Davis_(bassist) "Richard Davis (bassist)"), and drummer [Tony Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Williams_(drummer) "Tony Williams (drummer)"), it is considered by critics as one of the finest albums issued on Blue Note and one of the high points of 1960s [avant-garde jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde_jazz "Avant-garde jazz").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_to_Lunch!#cite_note-aaj-2) [Reid Miles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reid_Miles "Reid Miles")' cover artwork features a photo of a "Will Be Back" sign displayed in a shop window showing a seven-handed clock. ## Background \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Out_to_Lunch!&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Background")\] Dolphy declared in the album's liner notes that "Everyone's a leader in this session",[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_to_Lunch!#cite_note-liner-3) and he was fortunate to be joined by four sympathetic musicians, three of whom had previously performed and recorded with him. [Freddie Hubbard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freddie_Hubbard "Freddie Hubbard") had roomed with Dolphy when they both first arrived in New York,[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_to_Lunch!#cite_note-4) and was featured on _[Outward Bound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outward_Bound_(Eric_Dolphy_album) "Outward Bound (Eric Dolphy album)")_ (1960), Dolphy's debut as a leader. Dolphy and Hubbard had also appeared together on [Ornette Coleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman "Ornette Coleman")'s 1961 album _[Free Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Jazz:_A_Collective_Improvisation "Free Jazz: A Collective Improvisation")_. [Bobby Hutcherson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Hutcherson "Bobby Hutcherson") had participated in the July 1963 recording sessions that produced Dolphy's albums _[Iron Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_Man_(Eric_Dolphy_album) "Iron Man (Eric Dolphy album)")_ and _[Conversations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conversations_(Eric_Dolphy_album) "Conversations (Eric Dolphy album)")_. Dolphy expressed his excitement regarding the opportunity to work with Hutcherson again: "Bobby's vibes have a freer, more open sound than a piano. Pianos seem to control you, Bobby's vibes seems to open you up."[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_to_Lunch!#cite_note-liner-3) Bassist [Richard Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Davis_(bassist) "Richard Davis (bassist)") had also participated in the July 1963 sessions, during which he recorded three duets with Dolphy ("Come Sunday", "Ode to Charlie Parker", and "Alone Together"). Davis was also the bassist on Dolphy and [Booker Little](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Booker_Little "Booker Little")’s dates [at the Five Spot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/At_the_Five_Spot "At the Five Spot") in 1961. One reviewer stated that the pair "had one of the more meaningful connections in jazz; they communicated almost telepathically, as if completing each other's thoughts."[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_to_Lunch!#cite_note-5) Dolphy commented that "Richard doesn't play the usual bass lines. He plays rhythm with his lines. He leads you somewhere else."[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_to_Lunch!#cite_note-liner-3) Drummer [Tony Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Williams_(drummer) "Tony Williams (drummer)"), credited as "Anthony Williams" on the album, had joined [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis")' " [second great quintet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#1963%E2%80%931968:_Second_quintet "Miles Davis")" in May 1963, and turned eighteen only in December of that year. Regarding Williams, Dolphy stated that he "doesn't play time, he plays pulse."[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_to_Lunch!#cite_note-liner-3) Dolphy biographers Vladimir Simosko and Barry Tepperman praised the musical chemistry of this group, observing that "the other musicians match and support \[Dolphy's\] conception with a truly fantastic sense of freedom and interplay."[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_to_Lunch!#cite_note-bio80-6)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_to_Lunch!#cite_note-bio81-7) Roughly a month after the _Out to Lunch!_ session, Dolphy, Davis, and Williams participated in the recording of [Andrew Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Hill_(jazz_musician) "Andrew Hill (jazz musician)")'s _[Point of Departure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_of_Departure_(Andrew_Hill_album) "Point of Departure (Andrew Hill album)")_. Shortly afterwards, he moved to Europe following the completion of a European tour with [Charles Mingus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus "Charles Mingus"): "Why? Because I can get more work there playing my own music, and because if you try to do anything different in this country, people put you down for it."[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_to_Lunch!#cite_note-liner-3) Dolphy died from a [diabetic coma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diabetic_coma "Diabetic coma") in [West Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Berlin "West Berlin") on June 29, 1964, at the age of 36.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_to_Lunch!#cite_note-8) ## Music \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Out_to_Lunch!&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Music")\] The title of the album's first track, "Hat and Beard", refers to [Thelonious Monk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thelonious_Monk "Thelonious Monk"), about whom Dolphy stated: "He's so musical no matter what he's doing, even if he's just walking around."[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_to_Lunch!#cite_note-liner-3) The piece features wild bass clarinet playing, and contains a percussive interlude featuring Williams and Hutcherson. "Something Sweet, Something Tender" also features Dolphy on bass clarinet, and includes a scored duet between Dolphy and Davis on bowed bass.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_to_Lunch!#cite_note-bio81-7) Dolphy commented that "The group got just the lyrical feeling that I wanted, and, taking it out, Richard and I really got together in the unison duet."[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_to_Lunch!#cite_note-liner-3) The third composition, "Gazzelloni", which showcases some of Dolphy's most advanced flute work,[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_to_Lunch!#cite_note-bio81-7) is named for classical flautist [Severino Gazzelloni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Severino_Gazzelloni "Severino Gazzelloni"), under whom Dolphy had studied the instrument.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_to_Lunch!#cite_note-liner-3) This track features the album's most conventional [bebop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bebop "Bebop")-based theme; Dolphy noted that "Everybody holds to the construction for the first 13 bars, then - freedom."[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_to_Lunch!#cite_note-liner-3) The second side features two long pieces with Dolphy on alto saxophone. On the title track, the pulse is implied rather than being stated explicitly, which lends a sense of freedom.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_to_Lunch!#cite_note-bio80-6) Dolphy commented: "Even though the rhythm section breaks the time up, there's a basic pulse coming from inside the tune. That's the pulse the musicians have to play."[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_to_Lunch!#cite_note-liner-3) The final track, "Straight Up and Down", was intended to evoke a drunken stagger.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_to_Lunch!#cite_note-liner-3) Dolphy's solo contains swaggering, voice-like lines on which he employs [multiphonics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiphonic "Multiphonic") and smears.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_to_Lunch!#cite_note-bio81-7) Regarding the group's contribution, he stated: "It gasses me that everyone was so free. I wanted a free date to begin with. All rhythm sections are different, but this one was really open..."[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_to_Lunch!#cite_note-liner-3) In late 2013, previously unissued alternate takes of the first two tracks were released on Toshiba EMI TYCJ-81013 in Japan. ## Critical reception \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Out_to_Lunch!&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: Critical | Professional ratings _[The Penguin Guide to Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Penguin_Guide_to_Jazz "The Penguin Guide to Jazz")_ selected _Out to Lunch!_ as part of its suggested "Core Collection" and awarded it a perfect score and "crown", deeming it "a slightly tentative masterpiece."[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_to_Lunch!#cite_note-Penguin-11) The album was identified by [Chris Kelsey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Kelsey "Chris Kelsey") in his [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic") essay "Free Jazz: A Subjective History" as one of the "20 Essential [Free Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz") Albums".[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_to_Lunch!#cite_note-13) Writer [Martin Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Williams_(writer) "Martin Williams (writer)") stated that on _Out to Lunch!_, "we hear a full development of \[Dolphy's\] talent, in its five, finely crafted compositions, and in his equally well-conceived solos."[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_to_Lunch!#cite_note-14) In a review for AllMusic, Steve Huey described the album as Dolphy's "magnum opus, an absolute pinnacle of avant-garde jazz in any form or era. Its rhythmic complexity was perhaps unrivaled since [Dave Brubeck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Brubeck "Dave Brubeck")'s _[Time Out](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_Out_(album) "Time Out (album)")_, and its five Dolphy originals...were a perfect balance of structured frameworks, carefully calibrated timbres, and generous individual freedom."[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_to_Lunch!#cite_note-allmusic-9) Writing for _[The Wire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wire_(magazine) "The Wire (magazine)")_, [Brian Morton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Morton_(Scottish_writer) "Brian Morton (Scottish writer)") described _Out to Lunch!_ as "Dolphy's most adventurous album and his most self consistent attempt at freedom within some, at least of the confines established by bop writing." Morton deemed the bandleader "an instant composer rather than a strict improviser."[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_to_Lunch!#cite_note-15) [Kevin Whitehead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Whitehead "Kevin Whitehead"), writing for [NPR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NPR "NPR"), referred to _Out to Lunch!_ as Dolphy's "masterpiece", stating: "Half a century later it still sounds crazy in a good way. The organized mayhem starts with Dolphy's tunes, often featuring wide, wide leaps in the melody and ratchet-gear rhythms...in time you could hear its influence in [Anthony Braxton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Braxton "Anthony Braxton")'s or [Roscoe Mitchell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roscoe_Mitchell "Roscoe Mitchell")'s zigzag solos and odd timbres, in [David Murray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Murray_(saxophonist) "David Murray (saxophonist)")'s yawping bass clarinet and [Jason Adasiewicz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Adasiewicz "Jason Adasiewicz")'s clanking vibes. You can also hear it in ambitious music by all sorts of modern composers who grapple with the same kind of contradictions Dolphy did."[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_to_Lunch!#cite_note-16) In an essay for Jazz History Online, Thomas Cunniffe wrote that _Out to Lunch!_ "was an effort to break our expectations about the very nature of jazz", and stated that "In addition to dispelling the notion that improvised solos should maintain the mood of the melody, Dolphy called for his sidemen to rethink their preconceived notions about improvisation", noting that "Dolphy and company re-examined the very framework of this music."[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_to_Lunch!#cite_note-17) Trevor Maclaren described _Out to Lunch!_ as "one of the finest records of its kind" and "easily at the caliber of _[A Love Supreme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme "A Love Supreme")_ and _[The Shape of Jazz to Come](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Shape_of_Jazz_to_Come "The Shape of Jazz to Come")_". He stated that "Dolphy shows himself as solid bandleader and arranger who opens up plenty of room for his players. Much in the ideology of his fellow avant-garde players, the solos exude experiment. Yet Dolphy's control is masterful and no matter how far out he gets, you can feel his passion and know his path has been well articulated."[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_to_Lunch!#cite_note-aaj-2) Greg Simmons of _[All About Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_About_Jazz "All About Jazz")_ called the album "undeniably brilliant" and "an essential watershed in the jazz canon, representing a creative peak for the soon-to-be-gone Dolphy". He praised Dolphy's bass clarinet playing on the opening track as "as complete a statement of musical independence—from fashion, commercial concerns, and tradition—as is likely to be found."[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_to_Lunch!#cite_note-18) ## Track listing \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Out_to_Lunch!&action=edit§ion=4 "Edit section: Track listing")\] All compositions by Eric Dolphy. 1. Primarily an [alto saxophonist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alto_saxophone "Alto saxophone"), [bass clarinetist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bass_clarinet "Bass clarinet"), and [flautist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flute "Flute"),[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-baker-1) Dolphy was one of several multi-instrumentalists to gain prominence during the same era. His use of the bass clarinet helped to establish the unconventional instrument within jazz.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-2)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-am_guide-3) Dolphy extended the vocabulary and boundaries of the alto saxophone, and was among the earliest significant jazz flute soloists.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-4)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-am_guide-3) His [improvisational](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_improvisation "Musical improvisation") style was characterized by the use of wide [intervals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interval_(music) "Interval (music)"), in addition to employing an array of [extended techniques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extended_techniques "Extended techniques") to emulate the sounds of human voices and animals.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-5)[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-gioiahist-6)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-feather-7) He used melodic lines that were "angular, zigzagging from interval to interval, taking hairpin turns at unexpected junctures, making dramatic leaps from the lower to the upper register."[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-gioiahist-6) Although Dolphy's work is sometimes classified as [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz"), his compositions and solos were often rooted in conventional (if highly abstracted) tonal [bebop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bebop "Bebop") harmony.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-8)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-9)[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-10) ## Early life, family and education [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/56/Eric_Dolphy_-_Dorsey_-_1947.jpg/250px-Eric_Dolphy_-_Dorsey_-_1947.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Eric_Dolphy_-_Dorsey_-_1947.jpg) Dolphy's senior high school class portrait (1947) Eric Allan Dolphy Jr. was born on June 20, 1928, in [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles"), [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California"), where he was raised.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-sparked-11)[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-Ratliff-12) His parents, Sadie and Eric Sr.,[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-13) had immigrated to the United States from [Panama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panama "Panama").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-baker-1) He began music lessons at the age of six, studying clarinet and saxophone privately.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-thomas_76-14) While still in junior high school, he began to study the oboe, aspiring to a professional symphonic career,[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-thomas_76-14) and received a two-year scholarship to study at the music school of the [University of Southern California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Southern_California "University of Southern California").[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-Ratliff-12) When aged 13, he received a "Superior" award on clarinet from the California School Band and Orchestra festival.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-thomas_76-14) He attended [Susan Miller Dorsey High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susan_Miller_Dorsey_High_School "Susan Miller Dorsey High School") in Los Angeles, where he continued his musical studies and learned additional instruments.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-thomas_76-14) By 1946, he was co-director of the Youth Choir at the Westminster Presbyterian Church run by Reverend Hampton B. Hawes, father of the [jazz pianist of the same name.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hampton_Hawes "Hampton Hawes")[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-thomas_76-14) He graduated from high school in 1947 and attended [Los Angeles City College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_City_College "Los Angeles City College"), during which time he played contemporary classical works such as [Stravinsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stravinsky "Stravinsky")'s _[L'Histoire du soldat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L'Histoire_du_soldat "L'Histoire du soldat")_ and, along with [Jimmy Knepper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Knepper "Jimmy Knepper") and [Art Farmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Farmer "Art Farmer"), performed with [Roy Porter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_Porter_(drummer) "Roy Porter (drummer)")'s _17 Beboppers_.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-thomas_76-14) He went on to make eight recordings with Porter by 1949.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-baker-1) On these early sessions, Dolphy occasionally played [baritone saxophone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baritone_saxophone "Baritone saxophone"), as well as [alto saxophone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alto_saxophone "Alto saxophone"), flute, and [soprano clarinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soprano_clarinet "Soprano clarinet"). Dolphy entered the U.S. Army in 1950 and was stationed at [Fort Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Lewis_(Washington) "Fort Lewis (Washington)") in Washington.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-15) Beginning in 1952, he attended the [Navy School of Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Armed_Forces_School_of_Music "United States Armed Forces School of Music").[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-feather-7) Following his discharge in 1953, he returned to Los Angeles, where he worked with jazz musicians including [Buddy Collette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddy_Collette "Buddy Collette"), [Eddie Beal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddie_Beal "Eddie Beal"), [Clifford Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifford_Brown "Clifford Brown"),[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-16) and [Gerald Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerald_Wilson "Gerald Wilson")[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-feather-7) (to whom he later dedicated the composition "G.W.", recorded on _[Outward Bound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outward_Bound_(Eric_Dolphy_album) "Outward Bound (Eric Dolphy album)")_).[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-17) Dolphy often had friends come by to jam, enabled by the studio that his father had built for him in the family's backyard.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-Ratliff-12) ## Career Dolphy had his big break when he was invited to join [Chico Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chico_Hamilton "Chico Hamilton")'s quintet in 1958.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-sparked-11) With the group he became known to a wider audience and was able to tour extensively through 1958–59, when he left Hamilton's group and moved to New York City.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-feather-7) Dolphy appears on flute with Hamilton's band in the concert film _[Jazz on a Summer's Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_on_a_Summer's_Day "Jazz on a Summer's Day")_, documenting a performance at the 1958 [Newport Jazz Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newport_Jazz_Festival "Newport Jazz Festival"). ### Partnerships #### Charles Mingus [Charles Mingus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus "Charles Mingus") had known Dolphy from growing up in Los Angeles,[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-18) and Dolphy joined Mingus' Jazz Workshop in 1960, shortly after arriving in New York.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-19) He took part in Mingus' big band recording _[Pre-Bird](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pre-Bird "Pre-Bird")_ and is featured on "Bemoanable Lady".[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-20) He joined Mingus' working band at the Showplace during 1960 (memorialized in the poem "Mingus at the Showplace" by [William Matthews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Matthews_(poet) "William Matthews (poet)")),[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-21) and appeared on the leader's two Candid label albums, _[Charles Mingus Presents Charles Mingus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus_Presents_Charles_Mingus "Charles Mingus Presents Charles Mingus")_ and _[Mingus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mingus_(Charles_Mingus_album) "Mingus (Charles Mingus album)")_. Mingus considered Dolphy "a complete musician. He could fit anywhere. He was a fine lead alto in a big band. He could make it in a classical group. And, of course, he was entirely his own man when he soloed.... He had mastered jazz. And he had mastered all the instruments he played. In fact, he knew more than was supposed to be possible to do on them."[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-limelight-22) In the same year, Dolphy took part in the Mingus-led Jazz Artist Guild project and its [Newport Rebels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newport_Rebels "Newport Rebels") recording session.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-23) While touring Europe with Mingus in 1961, Dolphy continued performing as a solo artist, and he was recorded in Scandinavia and Berlin. Recordings from this period are collected on the albums _[The Berlin Concerts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Berlin_Concerts "The Berlin Concerts")_, _[The Complete Uppsala Concert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Complete_Uppsala_Concert "The Complete Uppsala Concert")_, _[Eric Dolphy in Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy_in_Europe "Eric Dolphy in Europe")_, and _[Stockholm Sessions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stockholm_Sessions "Stockholm Sessions")_.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-24) He was later among the musicians who worked on Mingus' album _[Mingus Mingus Mingus Mingus Mingus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mingus_Mingus_Mingus_Mingus_Mingus "Mingus Mingus Mingus Mingus Mingus")_ in 1963, where he is featured on the track "Hora Decubitus". In early 1964, Dolphy returned to Mingus' working band,[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-feather-7) now including [Jaki Byard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaki_Byard "Jaki Byard"), [Johnny Coles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnny_Coles "Johnny Coles"), and [Clifford Jordan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifford_Jordan "Clifford Jordan"). This sextet worked at the [Five Spot Café](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Five_Spot_Caf%C3%A9 "Five Spot Café") in Manhattan before playing at [Cornell University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornell_University "Cornell University") and [Town Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Town_Hall_(New_York_City) "The Town Hall (New York City)") (both were recorded: _[Cornell 1964](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornell_1964 "Cornell 1964")_ and _[Town Hall Concert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Town_Hall_Concert "Town Hall Concert")_) and subsequently touring Europe. The short tour is well-documented on _[Revenge!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revenge!_(Charles_Mingus_album) "Revenge! (Charles Mingus album)")_, _[The Great Concert of Charles Mingus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Great_Concert_of_Charles_Mingus "The Great Concert of Charles Mingus")_, _[Mingus in Europe Volume I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mingus_in_Europe_Volume_I "Mingus in Europe Volume I")_, and _[Mingus in Europe Volume II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mingus_in_Europe_Volume_II "Mingus in Europe Volume II")_. #### John Coltrane Dolphy and [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane") knew each other long before they formally played together, having met when Coltrane was in Los Angeles with [Johnny Hodges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnny_Hodges "Johnny Hodges") in 1954.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-25)[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-Ratliff_2007_68-26) They would often exchange ideas and learn from each other,[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-thomas_80-27) and eventually, after many nights sitting in with Coltrane's band, Dolphy was asked to become a full member in early 1961.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-28)[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-29) Coltrane had gained an audience and critical notice with [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis")'s quintet, but alienated some leading jazz critics when he began to move away from [hard bop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop "Hard bop"). Although Coltrane's quintets with Dolphy (including the _[Village Vanguard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Complete_1961_Village_Vanguard_Recordings "The Complete 1961 Village Vanguard Recordings")_ and _[Africa/Brass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africa/Brass "Africa/Brass")_ sessions) are now accepted, they originally provoked _[DownBeat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DownBeat "DownBeat")_ magazine to brand Coltrane and Dolphy's music as 'anti-jazz'. Coltrane later said of this criticism: "they made it appear that we didn't even know the first thing about music (...) it hurt me to see \[Dolphy\] get hurt in this thing."[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-Kofsky-30) The initial release of Coltrane's residency at the Vanguard selected [three tracks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coltrane_%22Live%22_at_the_Village_Vanguard "Coltrane \"Live\" at the Village Vanguard"), only one of which featured Dolphy. After being issued haphazardly over the next 30 years, a comprehensive [box-set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Box-set "Box-set") featuring the music recorded at the Vanguard was released on _[Impulse!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impulse!_Records "Impulse! Records")_ in 1997, called _[The Complete 1961 Village Vanguard Recordings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Complete_1961_Village_Vanguard_Recordings "The Complete 1961 Village Vanguard Recordings")_. The set features Dolphy heavily on both alto saxophone and bass clarinet, with Dolphy the featured soloist on their renditions of " [Naima](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naima "Naima")".[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-31) A 2001 [Pablo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pablo_Records "Pablo Records") box set, drawing on recordings of Coltrane's performances from his European tours of the early 1960s, features tunes absent from the 1961 Village Vanguard material, such as " [My Favorite Things](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My_Favorite_Things_(song) "My Favorite Things (song)")", which Dolphy performs on flute.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-32) #### Booker Little Trumpeter [Booker Little](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Booker_Little "Booker Little") and Dolphy had a short-lived musical partnership.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-33) Little's leader date for [Candid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candid_Records "Candid Records"), _[Out Front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_Front_(Booker_Little_album) "Out Front (Booker Little album)")_, featured Dolphy mainly on alto sax, though he played bass clarinet and flute on some ensemble passages. In addition, Dolphy's album _[Far Cry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Far_Cry_(album) "Far Cry (album)")_, recorded for [Prestige](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prestige_Records "Prestige Records"), features Little on five tunes (one of which, "Serene", was not included on the original LP release). Dolphy and Little also co-led a quintet at the Five Spot during 1961. The rhythm section consisted of [Richard Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Davis_(double_bassist) "Richard Davis (double bassist)"), [Mal Waldron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mal_Waldron "Mal Waldron") and [Ed Blackwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Blackwell "Ed Blackwell").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-baker-1) One night was documented and has been released as _[At the Five Spot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/At_the_Five_Spot "At the Five Spot")_ (plus a _Memorial Album_) as well as the compilation _[Here and There](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Here_and_There_(Eric_Dolphy_album) "Here and There (Eric Dolphy album)")_. In addition, both Dolphy and Little backed [Abbey Lincoln](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbey_Lincoln "Abbey Lincoln") on her album _[Straight Ahead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Straight_Ahead_(Abbey_Lincoln_album) "Straight Ahead (Abbey Lincoln album)")_ and played on [Max Roach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Roach "Max Roach")'s _[Percussion Bitter Sweet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percussion_Bitter_Sweet "Percussion Bitter Sweet")_. Little died at the age of 23 in October 1961. #### Others Dolphy also performed on key recordings by [George Russell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Russell_(composer) "George Russell (composer)") ( _[Ezz-thetics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ezz-thetics "Ezz-thetics")_), [Oliver Nelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Nelson "Oliver Nelson") ( _[Screamin' the Blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Screamin'_the_Blues "Screamin' the Blues")_, _[The Blues and the Abstract Truth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Blues_and_the_Abstract_Truth "The Blues and the Abstract Truth")_, and _[Straight Ahead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Straight_Ahead_(Oliver_Nelson_album) "Straight Ahead (Oliver Nelson album)")_), and [Ornette Coleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman "Ornette Coleman") ( _[Free Jazz: A Collective Improvisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Jazz:_A_Collective_Improvisation "Free Jazz: A Collective Improvisation")_ and the _Free Jazz_ outtake on _[Twins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twins_(Ornette_Coleman_album) "Twins (Ornette Coleman album)")_). He also worked and recorded with [Gunther Schuller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunther_Schuller "Gunther Schuller") ( _[Jazz Abstractions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_Abstractions "Jazz Abstractions")_), multi-instrumentalist [Ken McIntyre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Makanda_Ken_McIntyre "Makanda Ken McIntyre") ( _[Looking Ahead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Looking_Ahead_(Makanda_Ken_McIntyre_album) "Looking Ahead (Makanda Ken McIntyre album)")_), bassist [Ron Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ron_Carter "Ron Carter") ( _[Where?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Where%3F_(album) "Where? (album)")_), and pianist [Mal Waldron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mal_Waldron "Mal Waldron") ( _[The Quest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Quest_(Mal_Waldron_album) "The Quest (Mal Waldron album)")_). ### As a leader Dolphy's recording career as a leader began with [Prestige](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prestige_Records "Prestige Records"). His association with the label spanned 13 albums recorded from April 1960 to September 1961, though he was not the leader for all of the sessions. [Fantasy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fantasy_Records "Fantasy Records") released a 9-CD box set in 1995 containing all of Dolphy's recorded output for Prestige.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-34) Dolphy's first two albums as leader were _[Outward Bound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outward_Bound_(Eric_Dolphy_album) "Outward Bound (Eric Dolphy album)")_ and _[Out There](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_There_(Eric_Dolphy_album) "Out There (Eric Dolphy album)")_; both featured cover artwork by [Richard "Prophet" Jennings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Slater_Jennings "Richard Slater Jennings").[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-35)[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-baker-1) The first, sounding closer to hard bop than some later releases,[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-36)[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-37) was recorded at [Rudy Van Gelder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudy_Van_Gelder "Rudy Van Gelder")'s studio in New Jersey with trumpeter [Freddie Hubbard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freddie_Hubbard "Freddie Hubbard"), who shared rooms with Dolphy for a time when the two men first arrived in New York.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-38) The album features three Dolphy compositions: "G.W.", dedicated to [Gerald Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerald_Wilson "Gerald Wilson"), and the blues "Les" and "245". _Out There_ is closer to [third stream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_stream "Third stream") music,[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-39) which would also form part of Dolphy's work, and features [Ron Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ron_Carter "Ron Carter") on cello. [Charles Mingus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus "Charles Mingus")'s "Eclipse" from this album is one of the rare instances where Dolphy solos on [soprano clarinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soprano_clarinet "Soprano clarinet") (others being "Warm Canto" from [Mal Waldron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mal_Waldron "Mal Waldron")'s _[The Quest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Quest_(Mal_Waldron_album) "The Quest (Mal Waldron album)")_,[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-40) "Densities" from the compilation _[Vintage Dolphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vintage_Dolphy "Vintage Dolphy")_,[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-41) and "Song For The Ram's Horn" from an unreleased recording from a 1962 Town Hall concert). Dolphy occasionally recorded unaccompanied saxophone solos;[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-42) his only predecessors were the tenor players [Coleman Hawkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coleman_Hawkins "Coleman Hawkins") ("Picasso", 1948)[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-43) and [Sonny Rollins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonny_Rollins "Sonny Rollins") (for example, "Body and Soul", 1958),[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-44) making Dolphy the first to do so on alto. The album _Far Cry_ contains his performance of the [Gross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Gross_(musician) "Walter Gross (musician)")- [Lawrence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Lawrence_(songwriter) "Jack Lawrence (songwriter)") standard " [Tenderly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenderly "Tenderly")" on alto saxophone,[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-45) and, on his subsequent tour of Europe, [Billie Holiday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billie_Holiday "Billie Holiday")'s " [God Bless the Child](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/God_Bless_the_Child_(Billie_Holiday_song) "God Bless the Child (Billie Holiday song)")" was featured in his sets.[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-46) (The earliest known version was recorded at the Five Spot during his residency with [Booker Little](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Booker_Little "Booker Little").) He also recorded two takes of a short solo rendition of "Love Me" in 1963, released on _Conversations_ and _Muses_. [Twentieth-century classical music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twentieth_century_classical_music "Twentieth century classical music") was also part of Dolphy's musical career. He was very familiar with the music of composers such as [Anton Webern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anton_Webern "Anton Webern") and [Alban Berg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alban_Berg "Alban Berg"),[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-thomas_80-27) had a large record collection that included music by these composers, as well as by [Debussy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Debussy "Claude Debussy"), [Ravel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_Ravel "Maurice Ravel"), [Stravinsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Igor_Stravinsky "Igor Stravinsky"), and [Bartók](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%A9la_Bart%C3%B3k "Béla Bartók"),[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-47) and owned scores by composers such as [Milton Babbitt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milton_Babbitt "Milton Babbitt"), [Donald Erb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Erb "Donald Erb"), [Charles Ives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Ives "Charles Ives"), and [Olivier Messiaen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olivier_Messiaen "Olivier Messiaen").[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-48)[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-49)[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-50) He visited [Edgard Varèse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edgard_Var%C3%A8se "Edgard Varèse") at his home,[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-51) and performed the composer's _[Density 21.5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Density_21.5 "Density 21.5")_ for solo flute at the [Ojai Music Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ojai_Music_Festival "Ojai Music Festival") in 1962.[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-52) Dolphy also participated in [Gunther Schuller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunther_Schuller "Gunther Schuller")'s and [John Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Lewis_(pianist) "John Lewis (pianist)")'s [Third Stream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Stream "Third Stream") efforts of the 1960s, appearing on the album _[Jazz Abstractions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_Abstractions "Jazz Abstractions")_, and admired the Italian flute virtuoso [Severino Gazzelloni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Severino_Gazzelloni "Severino Gazzelloni"), after whom he named his composition _Gazzelloni_.[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-53) Around 1962–63, one of Dolphy's working bands included the pianist [Herbie Hancock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock "Herbie Hancock"), who can be heard on _[The Illinois Concert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Illinois_Concert "The Illinois Concert")_, _Gaslight 1962_, and the unissued Town Hall concert with poet [Ree Dragonette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ree_Dragonette "Ree Dragonette"). In July 1963, producer [Alan Douglas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Douglas_(record_producer) "Alan Douglas (record producer)") arranged recording sessions for which Dolphy's sidemen were emerging musicians of the day, and the results produced the albums _[Iron Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_Man_(Eric_Dolphy_album) "Iron Man (Eric Dolphy album)")_ and _[Conversations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conversations_(Eric_Dolphy_album) "Conversations (Eric Dolphy album)")_, as well as the _Muses_ album released in Japan in late 2013. These sessions marked the first time Dolphy played with [Bobby Hutcherson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Hutcherson "Bobby Hutcherson"), whom he knew from Los Angeles, and whose sister he dated at one point.[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-54) The sessions are perhaps best known for the three duets Dolphy performs with bassist [Richard Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Davis_(double_bassist) "Richard Davis (double bassist)") on "Alone Together", "Ode To Charlie Parker", and "Come Sunday"; the aforementioned release _Muses_ adds another take of "Alone Together" and an original composition for duet from which the album takes its name. In 1964, Dolphy signed with [Blue Note Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records "Blue Note Records") and recorded _[Out to Lunch!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_to_Lunch! "Out to Lunch!")_ with [Freddie Hubbard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freddie_Hubbard "Freddie Hubbard"), [Bobby Hutcherson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Hutcherson "Bobby Hutcherson"), [Richard Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Davis_(double_bassist) "Richard Davis (double bassist)") and [Tony Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Williams_(drummer) "Tony Williams (drummer)"). This album features Dolphy's fully developed avant-garde yet structured compositional style rooted in tradition. It is often considered his _magnum opus_.[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-Huey-55) ### European career After _[Out to Lunch!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_to_Lunch! "Out to Lunch!")_ and an appearance on pianist/composer [Andrew Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Hill_(jazz_musician) "Andrew Hill (jazz musician)")'s Blue Note album _[Point of Departure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_of_Departure_(Andrew_Hill_album) "Point of Departure (Andrew Hill album)")_, Dolphy left for Europe with Charles Mingus' sextet in early 1964. Before a concert in [Oslo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo "Oslo"), Norway, he informed Mingus that he planned to stay in Europe after their tour was finished, partly because he had become disillusioned with the United States' reception of musicians who were trying something new. Mingus then named the blues they had been performing "So Long Eric". Dolphy intended to settle in Europe with his fiancée Joyce Mordecai, who was working in the ballet scene in [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris "Paris"), France.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-Ratliff-12) After leaving Mingus, he performed and recorded a few sides with various European bands, and American musicians living in Paris, such as [Donald Byrd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Byrd "Donald Byrd") and [Nathan Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathan_Davis_(saxophonist) "Nathan Davis (saxophonist)"). _[Last Date](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Last_Date_(Eric_Dolphy_album) "Last Date (Eric Dolphy album)")_, originally a radio broadcast of a concert in [Hilversum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilversum "Hilversum") in the Netherlands, features [Misha Mengelberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Misha_Mengelberg "Misha Mengelberg") and [Han Bennink](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Han_Bennink "Han Bennink"), although it was not Dolphy's last public performance. Dolphy was also planning to join [Albert Ayler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler "Albert Ayler")'s group,[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-sparked-11) and, according to Jeanne Phillips, quoted in [A. B. Spellman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A._B._Spellman "A. B. Spellman")'s _Four Jazz Lives_, was preparing himself to play with [Cecil Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor "Cecil Taylor").[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-56) He also planned to form a band with [Woody Shaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woody_Shaw "Woody Shaw"), Richard Davis, and [Billy Higgins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Higgins "Billy Higgins"),[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-57) and was writing a [string quartet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/String_quartet "String quartet"), _Love Suite_.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-baker-1) ## Personal life and death Dolphy was engaged to marry Joyce Mordecai, a classically trained dancer who lived in Paris.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-Ratliff-12) He did not smoke[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-sparked-11) and did not use drugs or alcohol.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-sparked-11)[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-58) Before he left for Europe in 1964, Dolphy left papers and other effects with his friends [Hale Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hale_Smith "Hale Smith") and Juanita Smith. Eventually much of this material was passed on to the musician [James Newton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Newton_(flutist) "James Newton (flutist)").[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-Ratliff-12) It was announced in May 2014 that six boxes of music papers had been donated to the [Library of Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library_of_Congress "Library of Congress").[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-Ratliff-12)[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-59) On June 27, 1964, Dolphy traveled to [West Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Berlin "West Berlin") to play with a trio led by [Karl Berger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Berger "Karl Berger") at the opening of a jazz club called The Tangent.[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-bio85-60) He was apparently seriously ill when he arrived, and during the first concert was barely able to play. He was hospitalized that night, but his condition worsened.[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-61) On June 29, Dolphy died after falling into a [diabetic coma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diabetic_coma "Diabetic coma"). While certain details of his death are still disputed, it is largely accepted that he fell into a coma caused by undiagnosed diabetes. The liner notes to the _Complete Prestige Recordings_ box set say that Dolphy "collapsed in his hotel room in Berlin and when brought to the hospital he was diagnosed as being in a diabetic coma. After being administered a shot of [insulin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insulin "Insulin") he lapsed into [insulin shock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insulin_shock "Insulin shock") and died". A later documentary and liner notes dispute this, saying Dolphy collapsed on stage in Berlin and was brought to a hospital. Allegedly, the attending hospital physicians did not know Dolphy was a diabetic and assumed, based on a stereotype of jazz musicians, that he had overdosed on drugs.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-sparked-11) In this account, he was left in a hospital bed for the drugs to run their course.[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-62) [Ted Curson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Curson "Ted Curson") recalled the following: "That really broke me up. When Eric got sick on that date \[in Berlin\], and him being black and a jazz musician, they thought he was a [junkie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Addiction "Addiction"). Eric didn't use any drugs. He was a diabetic—all they had to do was take a blood test and they would have found that out. So he died for nothing. They gave him some detox stuff and he died, and nobody ever went into that club in Berlin again. That was the end of that club."[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-63) Shortly after Dolphy's death, Curson recorded and released _[Tears for Dolphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tears_for_Dolphy "Tears for Dolphy")_, featuring a title track that served as an elegy for his friend. Charles Mingus remarked of Dolphy shortly after his death that "Usually, when a man dies, you remember—or you say you remember—only the good things about him. With Eric, that's all you could remember. I don't remember any drags he did to anybody. The man was absolutely without a need to hurt."[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-limelight-22) Dolphy is buried in [Angelus-Rosedale Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angelus-Rosedale_Cemetery "Angelus-Rosedale Cemetery") in Los Angeles. His headstone bears the inscription: "He Lives In His Music."[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-64) ## Legacy John Coltrane acknowledged Dolphy's influence in a 1962 _[DownBeat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DownBeat "DownBeat")_ interview, stating: "After he sat in... We began to play some of the things we had only talked about before. Since he's been in the band, he's had a broadening effect on us. There are a lot of things we try now that we never tried before. This helped me... We're playing things that are freer than before."[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-65) Coltrane biographer [Eric Nisenson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Nisenson "Eric Nisenson") stated: "Dolphy's effect on Coltrane ran deep. Coltrane's solos became far more adventurous, using musical concepts that without the chemistry of Dolphy's advanced style he might have kept away from the ears of his public."[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-66) In his book _Free Jazz_, Ekkehard Jost provided specific examples of how Coltrane's playing began to change during the time he spent with Dolphy, noting that Coltrane started using wider melodic intervals like sixths and sevenths, and began focusing on integrating sound coloration and multiphonics into his solos.[\[67\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-67) Jost contrasted Coltrane's solo on "India", recorded in November 1961 while Dolphy was with the group, and released on _[Impressions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impressions_(John_Coltrane_album) "Impressions (John Coltrane album)")_, with his solo on " [My Favorite Things](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My_Favorite_Things_(song) "My Favorite Things (song)")", recorded roughly a year earlier, and released on the [Atlantic album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My_Favorite_Things_(John_Coltrane_album) "My Favorite Things (John Coltrane album)"),[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-68) and observed that on "My Favorite Things", Coltrane "accepted the mode as more or less binding, occasionally aiming away from it... at tones foreign to the scale,"[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-jost_29-69) whereas on "India", Coltrane, like Dolphy, played " _around_ the mode more than _in_ it."[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-jost_29-69) Dolphy's musical presence was also influential to many young jazz musicians who would later become prominent. Dolphy worked intermittently with [Ron Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ron_Carter "Ron Carter") and [Freddie Hubbard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freddie_Hubbard "Freddie Hubbard") throughout his career, and in later years he hired [Herbie Hancock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock "Herbie Hancock"), [Bobby Hutcherson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Hutcherson "Bobby Hutcherson") and [Woody Shaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woody_Shaw "Woody Shaw") to work in his live and studio bands. _[Out to Lunch!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_to_Lunch! "Out to Lunch!")_ featured yet another young performer, drummer [Tony Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Williams_(drummer) "Tony Williams (drummer)"), and Dolphy's participation on Hill's _[Point of Departure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_of_Departure_(Andrew_Hill_album) "Point of Departure (Andrew Hill album)")_ session brought him into contact with the tenor player [Joe Henderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Henderson "Joe Henderson"). There is a [celebration held at Le Moyne College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le_Moyne_College#Dolphy_Day "Le Moyne College") based on a Frank Zappa song, " [The Eric Dolphy Memorial Barbecue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weasels_Ripped_My_Flesh "Weasels Ripped My Flesh")," inspired by him. Carter, Hancock and Williams would go on to become one of the quintessential rhythm sections of the decade, both together on their own albums and as the backbone of [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis")'s [second great quintet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis_Quintet#Second_Great_Quintet "Miles Davis Quintet"). This aspect of the second great quintet is an ironic footnote for Davis, who was critical of Dolphy's music: in a 1964 _DownBeat_ "Blindfold Test", Miles quipped: "The next time I see \[Dolphy\] I'm going to step on his foot."[\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-70) However, Davis new quintet's rhythm section had all worked under Dolphy, thus creating a band whose brand of " [out](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outside_(jazz) "Outside (jazz)")" was strongly influenced by Dolphy. Dolphy's instrumental abilities and unique style of jazz influenced such musicians as [Anthony Braxton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Braxton "Anthony Braxton"),[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-71) members of the [Art Ensemble of Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Ensemble_of_Chicago "Art Ensemble of Chicago"),[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-72) [Oliver Lake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Lake "Oliver Lake"),[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-73) [Arthur Blythe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Blythe "Arthur Blythe"),[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-74) [Don Byron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Byron "Don Byron"),[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-75) and [Evan Parker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evan_Parker "Evan Parker").[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-76) ## Awards, honors, and tributes Dolphy was posthumously inducted into the _DownBeat_ magazine Hall of Fame in 1964.[\[77\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-77) [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane") paid tribute to Dolphy in an interview: "Whatever I'd say would be an understatement. I can only say my life was made much better by knowing him. He was one of the greatest people I've ever known, as a man, a friend, and a musician."[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-78) After Dolphy died, his mother gave Coltrane his flute and bass clarinet, and Coltrane, who traveled with Dolphy's photograph, hanging it on his hotel room walls,[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-Ratliff_2007_68-26) proceeded to play the instruments on several subsequent recordings.[\[79\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-79) [Frank Zappa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa "Frank Zappa") acknowledged Dolphy as a musical influence in the liner notes to the 1966 album _[Freak Out!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freak_Out! - [experimental rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Experimental_rock "Experimental rock") | | Cultural origins | Late 1960s, [Canterbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury "Canterbury"), England | | Other topics | | - [Rock in Opposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_in_Opposition "Rock in Opposition") | The **Canterbury scene** (or **Canterbury sound**) is a musical scene that originated in the city of [Canterbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury "Canterbury"), [Kent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent "Kent"), England during the late 1960s and early 1970s.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury_scene#cite_note-All-1) Associated with [progressive rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock "Progressive rock"),[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury_scene#cite_note-O'Dair2015-2) the term describes a loosely defined, [improvisational](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Improvisation "Improvisation") style that blended elements of [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz"), [rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music"), and [psychedelia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychedelic_music "Psychedelic music").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury_scene#cite_note-All-1) The Canterbury scene was born from the ashes of [The Wilde Flowers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wilde_Flowers "The Wilde Flowers"), a psych-pop outfit active in the mid to late 60s. After the band broke up in 1969, its members soon went on to play together in numerous bands (e.g. [Soft Machine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine "Soft Machine"), [Caravan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caravan_(band) "Caravan (band)"), [Gong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gong_(band) "Gong (band)"), [Hatfield and the North](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hatfield_and_the_North "Hatfield and the North"), [Egg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egg_(band) "Egg (band)"), and [National Health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Health "National Health")), with ever-changing and overlapping personnel, creating some similarities in their musical output [\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury_scene#cite_note-ProgArchives-3). Many prominent British [avant-garde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde_jazz "Avant-garde jazz") or [fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") musicians began their career in Canterbury bands, including [Hugh Hopper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugh_Hopper "Hugh Hopper"), [Steve Hillage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Hillage "Steve Hillage"), [Dave Stewart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Stewart_(musician,_born_1950) "Dave Stewart (musician, born 1950)"), [Robert Wyatt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Wyatt "Robert Wyatt"), [Kevin Ayers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Ayers "Kevin Ayers"), [Richard Sinclair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Sinclair "Richard Sinclair"), [Tony Coe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Coe "Tony Coe"), [Daevid Allen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daevid_Allen "Daevid Allen"), and [Mike Ratledge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Ratledge "Mike Ratledge").[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury_scene#cite_note-AM-CS-4) ## Definition and history The Canterbury scene is largely defined by a set of musicians and bands with intertwined members. These are not tied by very strong musical similarities, but a certain whimsicality, touches of [psychedelia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychedelia "Psychedelia"), rather abstruse lyrics, and a use of [improvisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Improvisation "Improvisation") derived from [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") are common elements in their work.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury_scene#cite_note-AM-CS-4) "The real essence of 'Canterbury Sound' is the tension between complicated harmonies, extended improvisations, and the sincere desire to write catchy pop songs." "In the very best Canterbury music...the musically silly and the musically serious are juxtaposed in an amusing and endearing way."[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury_scene#cite_note-5) There is variation within the scene, for example from pop/rock like early [Soft Machine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine "Soft Machine") and much [Caravan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caravan_(band) "Caravan (band)") to avant-garde composed pieces as with early [National Health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Health "National Health") to improvised jazz as with later Soft Machine or [In Cahoots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_Cahoots "In Cahoots"). [Didier Malherbe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Didier_Malherbe "Didier Malherbe") (of [Gong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gong_(band) "Gong (band)")) has defined the scene as having "certain chord changes, in particular the use of minor second chords, certain harmonic combinations, and a great clarity in the aesthetics, and a way of improvising that is very different from what is done in jazz."[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury_scene#cite_note-whatis-6) There is debate about the existence and definition of the scene. [Dave Stewart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Stewart_(musician,_born_1950) "Dave Stewart (musician, born 1950)") has complained at the nomenclature as he and many other musicians identified with the Canterbury scene never had anything to do with Canterbury, the place. The former Soft Machine bassist [Hugh Hopper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugh_Hopper "Hugh Hopper"), who lived in [Whitstable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitstable "Whitstable"), near Canterbury, said: "I think it's a rather artificial label, a journalistic thing... I don't mind it, but people like [Robert \[Wyatt\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Wyatt "Robert Wyatt"), he in fact hates that idea, because he was born somewhere else and just happened to go to school here. In the time when [the Wilde Flowers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wilde_Flowers "The Wilde Flowers") started we hardly ever worked in Canterbury. It wasn't until Robert and [Daevid \[Allen\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daevid_Allen "Daevid Allen") went to London to start Soft Machine that anything happened at all. They weren't really a Canterbury band \[...\] if it helps people understand or listen to more music then it is fine."[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury_scene#cite_note-whatis-6) In the 21st century, the Canterbury group [Syd Arthur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syd_Arthur "Syd Arthur") have been seen as latter-day practitioners.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury_scene#cite_note-7) ## Others Poet, painter, and singer [Lady June](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lady_June "Lady June") was regarded an "honorary member" of the Canterbury scene for having performed and recorded with some of the members, and being a "landlady" to many in her flat in [Maida Vale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maida_Vale "Maida Vale"), London.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury_scene#cite_note-8)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury_scene#cite_note-9) ## References 1. Unsourced material may be challenged and removed.
_Find sources:_ ["Spontaneous composition"](https://www.google.com/search?as_eq=wikipedia&q=%22Spontaneous+composition%22)– [news](https://www.google.com/search?tbm=nws&q=%22Spontaneous+composition%22+-wikipedia&tbs=ar:1) **·** [newspapers](https://www.google.com/search?&q=%22Spontaneous+composition%22&tbs=bkt:s&tbm=bks) **·** [books](https://www.google.com/search?tbs=bks:1&q=%22Spontaneous+composition%22+-wikipedia) **·** [scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=%22Spontaneous+composition%22) **·** [JSTOR](https://www.jstor.org/action/doBasicSearch?Query=%22Spontaneous+composition%22&acc=on&wc=on)_(June 2009)__([Learn how and when to remove this message](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Maintenance_template_removal "Help:Maintenance template removal"))_ | **Spontaneous composition** is [music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music "Music") performed, occurring, or resulting from a sudden natural impulse, tendency, or inclination; without effort or premeditation; natural and unconstrained; unplanned.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spontaneous_composition#cite_note-1) Spontaneity in music is mostly associated with [improvised music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_improvisation "Musical improvisation") and jazz, but through the course of the last century it became practiced in other genres as well. [Improvisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_improvisation "Musical improvisation") is one possible [compositional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_composition "Musical composition") tool used in creating a **spontaneous composition**.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spontaneous_composition#cite_note-2) Keith Jarrett, an American pianist, is known for his work, which is almost exclusively based on improvisation. Keith Jarrett considers spontaneity to be an essential element of his music. He never writes musical notations for his works and makes no plans before a performance. Jarrett describes his compositional process as “being three people at once while improvising: the Improviser, the Spontaneous Composer, and the Keyboardist (the man at the keyboard). Jarrett himself is performing all of the tasks he describes simultaneously, but in an attempt to explain improvisation as an activity, he breaks down the task of performing into separate but interdependent “jobs” completed by his personae. (…) Jarrett describes the perfect work of his personae as the height of improvisational experience; when each of his personae are able to work freely and in harmony with the others (…).”[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spontaneous_composition#cite_note-3) Jarrett further explains: "If I remain the listener and not think I'm the player, if I remain the listener and not control the thing, something happens."[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spontaneous_composition#cite_note-4) The term "spontaneous composition" is closely associated with the music of Art Ensemble of Chicago. The band is best known for their innovative combining of absolute free playing with composed parts, building their compositions on improvisation, augmented communication between the players and prearranged sequences. Their music is often associated with avant-garde jazz, but they played freely through various musical zones, from the most reverent, like traditional, gospel, or so-called “Great Black Music”, to the most radical, like free-jazz or experimental. However, they never confined themselves to a single musical style or strict rules. They simply called it “creative music”.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spontaneous_composition#cite_note-5) Unlike Keith Jarrett's compositions, which were created entirely spontaneously, the music of Art Ensemble of Chicago was built through various combinations in the range between free and prearranged music. Its member, Roscoe Mitchell, multi-instrumentalist and inventor of new percussions, describes their way of composing as follows: ”I’m interested in all aspects of creativity. And one goal has always been to be a really good improviser who really does create spontaneous composition. So I study all the time, trying to develop ways to improve communication amongst the players and to shape and control the improvisations. There are so many paths to investigate, and not just contemporary paths.”[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spontaneous_composition#cite_note-6) [Scott Barry Kaufman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_Barry_Kaufman "Scott Barry Kaufman"), a psychologist known for his work on creativity, human potential and intelligence, explores concepts related to spontaneity in creative processes. He postulates that spontaneity is essential for creative process and he analyzed it by exploring processes like improvisation, brainstorming, openness, or playfulness.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spontaneous_composition#cite_note-7) ## References 1. From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

(Redirected from [Backbeat](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Backbeat&redirect=no "Backbeat"))

Basic unit of time in music and music theory

For other uses, see [beat music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_music "Beat music"), [beat (acoustics)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(acoustics) "Beat (acoustics)"), [drum beat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drum_beat "Drum beat"), and [beat (disambiguation)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(disambiguation) "Beat (disambiguation)").

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/82/Metric_levels.svg/500px-Metric_levels.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Metric_levels.svg) Metric levels: beat level shown in middle with division levels above and multiple levels below.

In [music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music "Music") and [music theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_theory "Music theory"), the **beat** is the basic unit of time, the [pulse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulse_(music) "Pulse (music)") (regularly repeating event), of the _mensural level_[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#cite_note-1) (or _beat level_).[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#cite_note-2) The beat is often defined as the rhythm listeners would tap their toes to when listening to a piece of music, or the numbers a musician [counts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counting_(music) "Counting (music)") while performing, though in practice this may be technically incorrect (often the first multiple level).\[ _[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_\] In popular use, _beat_ can refer to a variety of related concepts, including [pulse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulse_(music) "Pulse (music)"), [tempo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tempo "Tempo"), [meter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meter_(music) "Meter (music)"), specific [rhythms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm "Rhythm"), and [groove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groove_(popular_music) "Groove (popular music)").

Rhythm in music is characterized by a repeating sequence of [stressed and unstressed beats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#On-beat_and_off-beat) (often called "strong" and "weak") and divided into [bars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bar_(music) "Bar (music)") organized by [time signature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_signature "Time signature") and [tempo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tempo "Tempo") indications.

Beats are related to and distinguished from pulse, rhythm (grouping), and meter:

> Meter is the measurement of the number of pulses between more or less regularly recurring accents. Therefore, in order for meter to exist, some of the pulses in a series must be accented—marked for consciousness—relative to others. When pulses are thus counted within a metric context, they are referred to as _beats_.

— [Leonard B. Meyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_B._Meyer "Leonard B. Meyer") and [Cooper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grosvenor_Cooper?action=edit&redlink=1 "Grosvenor Cooper (page does not exist)") (1960)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#cite_note-3)

[Metric levels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meter_(music)#Metric_structure "Meter (music)") faster than the beat level are division levels, and slower levels are multiple levels. Beat has always been an important part of music. Some [music genres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_genre "Music genre") such as [funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funk "Funk") will in general de-emphasize the beat, while others such as [disco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disco "Disco") emphasize the beat to accompany dance.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#cite_note-hhd-4)

## Division

\[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beat_(music)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Division")\]

Main article: [Metre (music) §Metric structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metre_(music)#Metric_structure "Metre (music)")

As beats are combined to form measures, each beat is divided into parts. The nature of this combination and division is what determines meter. Music where two beats are combined is in [duple meter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duple_meter "Duple meter"), music where three beats are combined is in [triple meter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triple_meter "Triple meter"). Music where the beat is split in two are in simple meter, music where the beat is split in three are called compound meter. Thus, simple duple (**2**

**4**, **4**

**4**, etc.), simple triple (**3**

**4**), compound duple (**6**

**8**), and compound triple (**9**

**8**). Divisions which require numbers, [tuplets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuplet "Tuplet") (for example, dividing a [quarter note](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quarter_note "Quarter note") into five equal parts), are irregular divisions and subdivisions. Subdivision begins two levels below the beat level: starting with a quarter note or a dotted quarter note, subdivision begins when the note is divided into sixteenth notes.

## Downbeat and upbeat

\[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beat_(music)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Downbeat and upbeat")\]

[![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/65/Anacrusis-bwv736.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Anacrusis-bwv736.png) Beginning of [Bach's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_Sebastian_Bach "Johann Sebastian Bach") [BWV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BWV "BWV") 736, with upbeat (anacrusis) in red. [Play](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/4/41/Anacrusis-bwv736.mid/Anacrusis-bwv736.mid.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Anacrusis-bwv736.mid "File:Anacrusis-bwv736.mid")

The _downbeat_ is the first beat of the [bar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bar_(music) "Bar (music)"), i.e. number 1. The _upbeat_ is the last beat in the previous bar which immediately precedes, and hence anticipates, the downbeat.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#cite_note-Groveupbeat-5) Both terms correspond to the direction taken by the hand of a [conductor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conductor_(music) "Conductor (music)").

> This idea of directionality of beats is significant when you translate its effect on music. The crusis of a measure or a phrase is a beginning; it propels sound and energy forward, so the sound needs to lift and have forward motion to create a sense of direction. The anacrusis leads to the crusis, but doesn't have the same 'explosion' of sound; it serves as a preparation for the crusis.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#cite_note-6)

An anticipatory note or succession of notes occurring before the first barline of a piece is sometimes referred to as an upbeat figure, section or phrase. Alternative expressions include "pickup" and " [anacrusis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anacrusis "Anacrusis")" (the latter ultimately from Greek _ana_ \["up towards"\] and _krousis_ \["strike"/"impact"\] through French _anacrouse_). In English, _anákrousis_ translates literally as "pushing up". The term anacrusis was borrowed from the field of [poetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poetry "Poetry"), in which it refers to one or more unstressed extrametrical [syllables](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syllable "Syllable") at the beginning of a line.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#cite_note-Groveupbeat-5)

## On-beat and off-beat

\[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beat_(music)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: On-beat and off-beat")\]
