Off-beat or backbeat pattern, popular on snare drum[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#cite_note-Schroedl-7)

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d8/Backbeat_chop.png/330px-Backbeat_chop.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Backbeat_chop.png)" [Skank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skank_(guitar) "Skank (guitar)")" guitar rhythm[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#cite_note-8)[Play](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/9/98/Skank_on_Em64.mid/Skank_on_Em64.mid.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Skank_on_Em64.mid "File:Skank on Em64.mid"). Often referred to as "upbeats", in parallel with [upstrokes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upstroke "Upstroke").

In typical Western music [**4**\\
\\
**4** time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadruple_time "Quadruple time"), [counted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counting_(music) "Counting (music)") as "1234, 1234...", the first beat of the bar (downbeat) is usually the strongest [accent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accent_(music) "Accent (music)") in the melody and the likeliest place for a chord change, the third is the next strongest: these are "on" beats. The second and fourth are weaker—the "off-beats". Subdivisions (like eighth notes) that fall between the pulse beats are even weaker and these, if used frequently in a rhythm, can also make it "off-beat".[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#cite_note-beat-9)

The effect can be easily simulated by evenly and repeatedly counting to four. As a background against which to compare these various rhythms a bass drum strike on the downbeat and a constant eighth note subdivision on ride cymbal have been added, which would be counted as follows ( **bold** denotes a stressed beat):

- **1** 2 3 4 **1** 2 3 4 — [play eighth notes and bass drum alone](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/1/16/Backbeat_example_eighth_notes.mid/Backbeat_example_eighth_notes.mid.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Backbeat_example_eighth_notes.mid "File:Backbeat example eighth notes.mid")
- **1** 2 **3** 4 **1** 2 **3** 4 — the stress here on the "on" beat [play](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/4/4c/Backbeat_example_unsyncopated.mid/Backbeat_example_unsyncopated.mid.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Backbeat_example_unsyncopated.mid "File:Backbeat example unsyncopated.mid")

But one may syncopate that pattern and alternately stress the odd and even beats, respectively:

- 1 **2** 3 **4** 1 **2** 3 **4** — the stress on the "unexpected", or syncopated, beat [play](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/0/00/Backbeat_example.mid/Backbeat_example.mid.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Backbeat_example.mid "File:Backbeat example.mid")

So "off-beat" is a musical term, commonly applied to [syncopation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syncopation "Syncopation"), that emphasizes the weak even beats of a bar, as opposed to the usual on-beat. This is a fundamental technique of [African polyrhythm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_polyrhythm "African polyrhythm") that transferred to popular western music. According to Grove Music, the "Offbeat is \[often\] where the downbeat is replaced by a rest or is tied over from the preceding bar".[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#cite_note-beat-9) The downbeat can never be the off-beat because it is the strongest beat in **4**

**4** time.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#cite_note-10) Certain genres tend to emphasize the off-beat, where this is a defining characteristic of rock'n'roll and [ska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ska "Ska") music.

A **back beat**, or **backbeat**, is a [syncopated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syncopation "Syncopation") accentuation on the "off" beat. In a simple **4**

**4** rhythm these are beats 2 and 4.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#cite_note-Grove-13)

"A big part of R&B's attraction had to do with the stompin' backbeats that make it so eminently danceable," according to the _Encyclopedia of Percussion_.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#cite_note-14) An early record with an emphasised back beat throughout was " [Good Rockin' Tonight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Good_Rockin'_Tonight "Good Rockin' Tonight")" by [Wynonie Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wynonie_Harris "Wynonie Harris") in 1948.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#cite_note-15) Although drummer [Earl Palmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_Palmer "Earl Palmer") claimed the honor for " [The Fat Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fat_Man_(song) "The Fat Man (song)")" by [Fats Domino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fats_Domino "Fats Domino") in 1949, which he played on, saying he adopted it from the final "shout" or "out" chorus common in [Dixieland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dixieland "Dixieland") jazz. There is a hand-clapping back beat on " [Roll 'Em Pete](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roll_'Em_Pete "Roll 'Em Pete")" by [Pete Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Johnson_(musician) "Pete Johnson (musician)") and [Big Joe Turner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Joe_Turner "Big Joe Turner"), recorded in 1938. A distinctive back beat can be heard on "Back Beat Boogie" by [Harry James](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_James "Harry James") And His Orchestra, recorded in late 1939.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#cite_note-16) Other early recorded examples include the final verse of "Grand Slam" by [Benny Goodman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benny_Goodman "Benny Goodman") in 1942 and some sections of The [Glenn Miller Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenn_Miller_Orchestra "Glenn Miller Orchestra")'s "(I've Got A Gal In) Kalamazoo", while [amateur direct-to-disc recordings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Christian#Bebop_and_Minton.27s_Playhouse "Charlie Christian") of [Charlie Christian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Christian "Charlie Christian") jamming at [Minton's Playhouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minton's_Playhouse "Minton's Playhouse") around the same time have a sustained snare-drum backbeat on the hottest choruses.

Outside [U.S.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") popular music, there are early recordings of music with a distinctive backbeat, such as the 1949 recording of Mangaratiba by [Luiz Gonzaga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luiz_Gonzaga "Luiz Gonzaga") in Brazil.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#cite_note-17)

Delayed backbeat (last eighth note in each measure) as in funk music[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#cite_note-Mattingly-18)

Slap bass executions on the backbeat are found in styles of country western music of the 1930s, and the late 1940s early 1950s music of Hank Williams reflected a return to strong backbeat accentuation as part of the honky tonk style of country.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#cite_note-19)
In the mid-1940s " [hillbilly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_music "Country music")" musicians the [Delmore Brothers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delmore_Brothers "Delmore Brothers") were turning out [boogie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boogie "Boogie") tunes with a hard driving back beat, such as the No. 2 hit "Freight Train Boogie" in 1946, as well as in other boogie songs they recorded.\[ _[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] Similarly [Fred Maddox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_Maddox "Fred Maddox")'s characteristic backbeat, a [slapping bass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slapping_bass "Slapping bass") style, helped drive a rhythm that came to be known as [rockabilly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rockabilly "Rockabilly"), one of the early forms of [rock and roll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_and_roll "Rock and roll").[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#cite_note-20) Maddox had used this style as early as 1937.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#cite_note-21)

In today's popular music the [snare drum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snare_drum "Snare drum") is typically used to play the backbeat pattern.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#cite_note-Schroedl-7) Additionally, [hand claps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clapping "Clapping") and [stacked cymbals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cymbal "Cymbal") can fulfil this purpose. A [hi-hat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hi-hat "Hi-hat") is often used as a softer alternative in jazz. Early [funk music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funk_music "Funk music") often delayed one of the backbeats by an eighth note so as "to give a 'kick' to the \[overall\] beat".[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#cite_note-Mattingly-18)

Some songs, such as [The Beatles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Beatles "The Beatles")' " [Please Please Me](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Please_Please_Me_(song) "Please Please Me (song)")" and " [I Want to Hold Your Hand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Want_to_Hold_Your_Hand "I Want to Hold Your Hand")", [The Knack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Knack "The Knack")'s " [Good Girls Don't](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Good_Girls_Don't "Good Girls Don't")" and [Blondie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blondie_(band) "Blondie (band)")'s cover of [The Nerves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nerves "The Nerves")' " [Hanging on the Telephone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanging_on_the_Telephone "Hanging on the Telephone")", employ a double backbeat pattern.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#cite_note-wave-22) In a double backbeat, one of the off beats is played as two eighth notes rather than one quarter note.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#cite_note-wave-22)

Some drummers slightly delay the backbeat on the snare drum to create a more relaxed feel, a technique known as the "delayed" or "late backbeat." In such cases, the intervals between beats 2 and 3, and between beats 4 and 1, are slightly shortened to prevent the tempo from slowing down. This playing style is particularly common in rock and soul music from the late 1960s to the mid-1970s.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#cite_note-23) Notable examples can be heard in recordings such as " [Green Onions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Onions "Green Onions")" by [Booker T. & the M.G.'s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Booker_T._&_the_M.G.'s "Booker T. & the M.G.'s"), " [And Your Bird Can Sing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/And_Your_Bird_Can_Sing "And Your Bird Can Sing")" by [The Beatles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Beatles "The Beatles"), " [Hey Joe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hey_Joe "Hey Joe")" by [The Jimi Hendrix Experience](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Jimi_Hendrix_Experience "The Jimi Hendrix Experience"), and " [Easy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Easy_(Commodores_song) "Easy (Commodores song)")" by [The Commodores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commodores "Commodores"). Drummer [Charlie Watts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Watts "Charlie Watts") of [The Rolling Stones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rolling_Stones "The Rolling Stones") frequently employed this technique during this period, as heard in tracks like " [Monkey Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monkey_Man_(Rolling_Stones_song) "Monkey Man (Rolling Stones song)")," " [Wild Horses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_Horses_(Rolling_Stones_song) "Wild Horses (Rolling Stones song)")," " [Sister Morphine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sister_Morphine "Sister Morphine")," and " [Let It Bleed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Let_It_Bleed_(song) "Let It Bleed (song)")."[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#cite_note-24) A delayed backbeat can also be heard in the famous eight-bar " [Funky Drummer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funky_Drummer "Funky Drummer")" break, played by [Clyde Stubblefield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clyde_Stubblefield "Clyde Stubblefield").[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#cite_note-25) _Early_ backbeats can be heard in [Bruce Springsteen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruce_Springsteen "Bruce Springsteen")'s "The River," [The Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Police "The Police")'s " [Every Breath You Take](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Every_Breath_You_Take "Every Breath You Take")," and [D'Angelo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D'Angelo "D'Angelo")'s "The Line."[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#cite_note-26)

## Cross-beat

\[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beat_(music)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Cross-beat")\]

Main article: [Cross-beat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross-beat "Cross-beat")

> Cross-rhythm. A rhythm in which the regular pattern of accents of the prevailing meter is contradicted by a conflicting pattern and not merely a momentary displacement that leaves the prevailing meter fundamentally unchallenged
>
> — _New Harvard Dictionary of Music_ (1986: 216).[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#cite_note-27)[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#cite_note-Neal_2000_https://archive.org/details/countrymusicannu00char/page/115_115-28)

## Hyperbeat

\[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beat_(music)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Hyperbeat")\]

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3b/Hypermeter.png/330px-Hypermeter.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hypermeter.png) Hypermeter: 4 beat measure, 4 measure hypermeasure, and 4 hypermeasure verses. Hyperbeats in red.

A **hyperbeat** is one unit of [hypermeter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypermeter "Hypermeter"), generally a measure. "Hypermeter is meter, with all its inherent characteristics, at the level where measures act as beats."[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#cite_note-Neal_2000_https://archive.org/details/countrymusicannu00char/page/115_115-28)[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#cite_note-29)

## Beat perception

\[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beat_(music)&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Beat perception")\]

Beat perception refers to the human ability to extract a periodic time structure from a piece of music.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#cite_note-30)[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#cite_note-31)
This ability is evident in the way people instinctively move their body in time to a musical beat, made possible by a form of [sensorimotor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sensorimotor_network "Sensorimotor network") [synchronization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synchronization "Synchronization") called 'beat-based timing'. This involves identifying the beat of a piece of music and timing the frequency of movements to match it.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#cite_note-32)[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#cite_note-33)[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#cite_note-34)
Infants across cultures display a rhythmic [motor response](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sensorimotor_network "Sensorimotor network") but it is not until between the ages of 2 years 6 months and 4 years 6 months that they are able to match their movements to the beat of an auditory stimulus.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#cite_note-35)[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#cite_note-36)

## Related concepts

\[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beat_(music)&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Related concepts")\]

- _[Tatum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tatum_(music) "Tatum (music)")_ refers to a subdivision of a beat which represents the "time division that most highly coincides with note onsets".[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#cite_note-37)
- _Afterbeat_ refers to a [percussion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percussion_instrument "Percussion instrument") style where a strong accent is sounded on the second, third and fourth beats of the bar, following the downbeat.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#cite_note-Grove-13)
- In [reggae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reggae "Reggae") music, the term _[one drop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_drop_rhythm "One drop rhythm")_ refers to the complete de-emphasis (to the point of silence) of the first beat in the cycle.
- [James Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Brown "James Brown")'s signature [funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funk "Funk") groove emphasized the downbeat–that is, with heavy emphasis "on the one" (the first beat of every measure)–to etch his distinctive sound, rather than the back beat (familiar to many R&B musicians) which places the emphasis on the second beat.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#cite_note-nytimes.com-38)[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#cite_note-fa_maceo-39)[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#cite_note-40)

**ECM** (Edition of Contemporary Music) is an independent [record label](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Record_label "Record label") founded by Karl Egger, [Manfred Eicher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manfred_Eicher "Manfred Eicher") and Manfred Scheffner in [Munich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich "Munich") in 1969. While ECM is best known for [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") music, the label has released a variety of recordings, and ECM's artists often refuse to acknowledge boundaries between genres. ECM's motto is "the most beautiful sound next to silence", taken from a 1971 review of ECM releases in _[Coda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coda_(magazine) "Coda (magazine)")_, a Canadian jazz magazine.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records#cite_note-1)

ECM has been distributed in the U.S. by [Warner Bros. Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Bros._Records "Warner Bros. Records"), [PolyGram Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PolyGram_Records "PolyGram Records"), [BMG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bertelsmann_Music_Group "Bertelsmann Music Group"), and, since 1999, [Universal Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Music "Universal Music"), the successor of PolyGram, worldwide. Its album covers were profiled in two books: _Sleeves of Desire_ and _Windfall Light_, both published by Lars Müller.

## History

\[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=ECM_Records&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")\]

The first ECM release produced by Manfred Scheffner was pianist [Mal Waldron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mal_Waldron "Mal Waldron")'s 1969 recording _[Free at Last](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_at_Last_(Mal_Waldron_album) "Free at Last (Mal Waldron album)")_. The label went on to release recordings by many prominent jazz musicians, including [Paul Bley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Bley "Paul Bley"), [Jack DeJohnette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_DeJohnette "Jack DeJohnette"), [Keith Jarrett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett "Keith Jarrett"), [Jan Garbarek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Garbarek "Jan Garbarek"), [Pat Metheny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pat_Metheny "Pat Metheny"), [Gary Burton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Burton "Gary Burton"), [Chick Corea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chick_Corea "Chick Corea"), [Charlie Haden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Haden "Charlie Haden"), [John Abercrombie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Abercrombie_(guitarist) "John Abercrombie (guitarist)"), [Dave Liebman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Liebman "Dave Liebman"), [Eberhard Weber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eberhard_Weber "Eberhard Weber"), [Egberto Gismonti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egberto_Gismonti "Egberto Gismonti"), [Dave Holland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Holland_(bassist) "Dave Holland (bassist)"), [Terje Rypdal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terje_Rypdal "Terje Rypdal"), [Stefano Bollani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stefano_Bollani "Stefano Bollani") and [Ralph Towner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_Towner "Ralph Towner"). The label has also released recordings in the [world music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_music "World music") genre by artists including [Steve Tibbetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Tibbetts "Steve Tibbetts"), [Stephan Micus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephan_Micus "Stephan Micus"), [Codona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona "Codona"), [Anouar Brahem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anouar_Brahem "Anouar Brahem"), [L. Shankar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L._Shankar "L. Shankar"), [Jon Hassell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jon_Hassell "Jon Hassell"), and [Naná Vasconcelos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nan%C3%A1_Vasconcelos "Naná Vasconcelos").

Manfred Eicher continues to take an active interest in the music released by ECM, acting as [producer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Record_producer "Record producer") of the vast majority of its recordings, although Steve Lake, Thomas Stoewsand, Robert Hurwitz, Lee Townsend, Hans Wendl and Sun Chung have also produced discs for the label. The typical ECM session is just three days: two days to record, one day to [mix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audio_mixing_(recorded_music) "Audio mixing (recorded music)"). Many of the albums have been recorded with [Jan Erik Kongshaug](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Erik_Kongshaug "Jan Erik Kongshaug") (of Talent Studios and later Rainbow Studios) in Oslo, Norway, as sound engineer; other engineers have included Martin Wieland (who recorded Jarrett's "The Köln Concert"), James Farber, Stefano Amerio and, on classical recordings, Peter Laenger.

### New Series and commemorative editions

\[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=ECM_Records&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: New Series and commemorative editions")\]

The _ECM New Series_ was created in 1984 to document Western classical works. It has released works by composers from the early ( [Thomas Tallis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Tallis "Thomas Tallis"), [Carlo Gesualdo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlo_Gesualdo "Carlo Gesualdo"), [Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giovanni_Pierluigi_da_Palestrina "Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina")) to the contemporary ( [John Cage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Cage "John Cage"), [Elliott Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elliott_Carter "Elliott Carter"), [Steve Reich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Reich "Steve Reich") and [John Adams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Adams_(composer) "John Adams (composer)")). The series was initiated for [Arvo Pärt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arvo_P%C3%A4rt "Arvo Pärt")'s record debut _Tabula Rasa_, which Eicher recorded and produced in 1977, 1983, and 1984. Since then Pärt and Eicher have built a strong relationship: all works premiere on recordings for the label and all are done in presence of the composer. Keith Jarrett, better known as a jazz musician, contributed together with [Gidon Kremer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gidon_Kremer "Gidon Kremer") amongst others to _Tabula Rasa_. He later recorded several classical works by [Bach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_Sebastian_Bach "Johann Sebastian Bach"), [Mozart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolfgang_Amadeus_Mozart "Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart"), [Shostakovich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dmitri_Shostakovich "Dmitri Shostakovich"), and others for the series.

The three albums _[Music for 18 Musicians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_for_18_Musicians "Music for 18 Musicians")_, _[Octet/Music for a Large Ensemble/Violin Phase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Octet/Music_for_a_Large_Ensemble/Violin_Phase "Octet/Music for a Large Ensemble/Violin Phase")_, and _[Tehillim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tehillim_(Reich) "Tehillim (Reich)")_ by Reich were recorded before 1984 (all with the composer performing) and were later moved to the classical department together with some by [Meredith Monk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meredith_Monk "Meredith Monk"), [Thomas Demenga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Demenga "Thomas Demenga") and [Harald Weiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harald_Weiss "Harald Weiss").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records#cite_note-2) Several of John Adams' works from his minimalist period have been released through the label as well, including _[Harmonium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmonium_(Adams) "Harmonium (Adams)")_ and _[Harmonielehre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmonielehre "Harmonielehre")_.

Over the years, many other works by contemporary composers such as [Valentyn Sylvestrov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valentyn_Sylvestrov "Valentyn Sylvestrov"), [Tigran Mansurian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tigran_Mansurian "Tigran Mansurian"), [Erkki-Sven Tüür](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erkki-Sven_T%C3%BC%C3%BCr "Erkki-Sven Tüür"), [Heinz Holliger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heinz_Holliger "Heinz Holliger"), [Giya Kancheli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giya_Kancheli "Giya Kancheli"), [György Kurtág](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gy%C3%B6rgy_Kurt%C3%A1g "György Kurtág"), or [Heiner Goebbels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heiner_Goebbels "Heiner Goebbels") as well as the soundtracks of several works by the filmmaker [Jean-Luc Godard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Luc_Godard "Jean-Luc Godard") have been issued on the _ECM New Series_ label. Interpreters who released records in classical genres include [Kim Kashkashian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Kashkashian "Kim Kashkashian"), [András Schiff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andr%C3%A1s_Schiff "András Schiff"), [Gidon Kremer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gidon_Kremer "Gidon Kremer"), the [Hilliard Ensemble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilliard_Ensemble "Hilliard Ensemble"), [Thomas Zehetmair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Zehetmair "Thomas Zehetmair"), [Carolin Widmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carolin_Widmann "Carolin Widmann"), [Till Fellner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Till_Fellner "Till Fellner"), Herbert Henck, [Alexei Lubimov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexei_Lubimov "Alexei Lubimov"), [András Keller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andr%C3%A1s_Keller "András Keller"), [Miklós Perényi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mikl%C3%B3s_Per%C3%A9nyi "Miklós Perényi"), [John Holloway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Holloway_(musician) "John Holloway (musician)"), [John Potter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Potter_(musician) "John Potter (musician)") or most recently [Patricia Kopatchinskaja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patricia_Kopatchinskaja "Patricia Kopatchinskaja").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records#cite_note-3)[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records#cite_note-4)[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records#cite_note-5)[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records#cite_note-6)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records#cite_note-7)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records#cite_note-8)

On many releases, the orientations towards jazz and classical music of ECM are combined: For example, Garbarek's _[Officium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Officium_(album) "Officium (album)")_ (1994) features him playing saxophone solos over the [Hilliard Ensemble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilliard_Ensemble "Hilliard Ensemble") singing [Gregorian chant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gregorian_chant "Gregorian chant"), early [polyphony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polyphony "Polyphony") and [Renaissance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renaissance_music "Renaissance music") works. Garbarek's work with guitarist Ralph Towner continued, and has been influenced by 20th century chamber music as much as by jazz-oriented material. [John Potter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Potter_(musician) "John Potter (musician)"), formerly of the Hilliard Ensemble, recorded works by [John Dowland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dowland "John Dowland") with jazz saxophonist [John Surman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Surman "John Surman") and others, and Surman's _Proverbs and Songs_ is a suite of choral settings of [Old Testament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Testament "Old Testament") texts, recorded in [Salisbury Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salisbury_Cathedral "Salisbury Cathedral"). The label has also released unique works that fit into no obvious genre at all (like the records of composer Meredith Monk).

In 2002 and 2004, ECM released a series of compilation CDs titled _:rarum_. Twenty of the label's artists were asked to compile a single CD of their work. (Garbarek's and Jarrett's compilations are double CDs.) Artists who contributed to this series are Keith Jarrett, Jan Garbarek, Chick Corea, Gary Burton, Bill Frisell, Art Ensemble of Chicago, Terje Rypdal, Bobo Stenson, Pat Metheny, Dave Holland, Egberto Gismonti, Jack DeJohnette, John Surman, John Abercrombie, Carla Bley, Paul Motian, Tomasz Stańko, Eberhard Weber, Arild Andersen, Jon Christensen.

After working as a writer for _Melody Maker_ magazine, Steve Lake first joined the ECM-staff in 1978.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records#cite_note-9) While working predominantly for the writing department he now has also produced more than 40 records which are more in the experimental areas of jazz like ones of [Evan Parker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evan_Parker "Evan Parker"), [Roscoe Mitchell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roscoe_Mitchell "Roscoe Mitchell"), [Hal Russell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hal_Russell "Hal Russell"), [Robin Williamson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Williamson "Robin Williamson"), [Joe Maneri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Maneri "Joe Maneri") or [Mat Maneri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mat_Maneri "Mat Maneri").[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records#cite_note-10) Furthermore, he published the book _Horizons Touched: The Music of ECM_ (2007) with music critic/novelist [Paul Griffiths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Griffiths_(writer) "Paul Griffiths (writer)") and made contributions to the books _Sleeves of Desire: a Cover Story_ (1996), _Windfall Light: The Visual Language of ECM_ (2010) and _ECM - A Cultural Archaeology_ (2012).[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records#cite_note-11)

### Recent developments in online distribution

\[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=ECM_Records&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Recent developments in online distribution")\]

On November 14, 2017, ECM announced in a press release that its entire catalog would be made available for [streaming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Streaming_media "Streaming media") on all major music streaming platforms (Apple Music, Amazon, Spotify, Deezer, Tidal and Qobuz). Previously, ECM recordings had never been available for streaming, save for a few select compilations of major performers. In a press release on its website, ECM explained its decision:

> In recent years, ECM and the musicians have had to face unauthorized streaming of recordings via video sharing websites, plus piracy, bootlegs, and a proliferation of illegal download sites. It was important to make the catalogue accessible within a framework, where copyrights are respected.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records#cite_note-ecmrecords2-12)

ECM further added that the physical recordings (CD & vinyl records) still constitute the "preferred mediums".[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records#cite_note-ecmrecords2-12)

## Exhibitions about ECM

\[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=ECM_Records&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Exhibitions about ECM")\]

In fall 2012, the Munich museum [Haus der Kunst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haus_der_Kunst "Haus der Kunst") opened an exhibition about the work of the label called _ECM – A Cultural Archaeology_. It pointed out the early jazz-focused years until the mid-1980s, before the _New Series_ was initiated. In close relation with Eicher and ECM, the exhibition was created by art curator [Okwui Enwezor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Okwui_Enwezor "Okwui Enwezor") and Markus Müller. To complement the historically oriented content of the exhibition, it was accompanied with a concert series of current artists of the label, which included [François Couturier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Couturier "François Couturier"), [Enrico Rava](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enrico_Rava "Enrico Rava"), [Meredith Monk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meredith_Monk "Meredith Monk"), [András Schiff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andr%C3%A1s_Schiff "András Schiff"), [Evan Parker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evan_Parker "Evan Parker"), [Gidon Kremer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gidon_Kremer "Gidon Kremer") or [Tomasz Stańko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomasz_Sta%C5%84ko "Tomasz Stańko").[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records#cite_note-13) Some of these artists have a long relationship with the label—even if their 'home' is _ECM_ or _New Series_.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records#cite_note-14)[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records#cite_note-15)

Additionally, Eicher curated a film series of eleven selected movies, which relate to the label. While some of its filmmakers have been related to ECM, like [Theo Angelopoulos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theo_Angelopoulos "Theo Angelopoulos") or [Jean-Luc Godard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Luc_Godard "Jean-Luc Godard"), others gave inspiration to the label, like [Ingmar Bergman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ingmar_Bergman "Ingmar Bergman") or [Andrei Tarkovsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrei_Tarkovsky "Andrei Tarkovsky"), and others used music by ECM.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records#cite_note-16) The physical catalogue of the exhibition was published by [Prestel Verlag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prestel_Verlag "Prestel Verlag") in German and English.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records#cite_note-17) Another extended exhibition was displayed in Seoul, Korea, from September until November 2013. Under the [Gertrude Stein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gertrude_Stein "Gertrude Stein") quote _Think of your Ears as Eyes_, the exhibition took a wider view on the label's history than the one in Munich. Again, it was accompanied by a concert series, including [Kim Kashkashian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Kashkashian "Kim Kashkashian"), András Schiff, [Myung-whun Chung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myung-whun_Chung "Myung-whun Chung"), [Heinz Holliger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heinz_Holliger "Heinz Holliger"), [Norma Winstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norma_Winstone "Norma Winstone"), [Ralph Towner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_Towner "Ralph Towner") and [Yeahwon Shin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yeahwon_Shin "Yeahwon Shin").[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records#cite_note-18)

## ECM and film

\[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=ECM_Records&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: ECM and film")\]

The label has a special relation towards film and directors.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records#cite_note-19) Founder [Manfred Eicher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manfred_Eicher "Manfred Eicher") himself is a very passionate movie viewer and directed in 1990 an adaption of [Max Frisch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Frisch "Max Frisch")'s _[Holozän](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_the_Holocene "Man in the Holocene")_ together with [Heinz Bütler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heinz_B%C3%BCtler?action=edit&redlink=1 "Heinz Bütler (page does not exist)").[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records#cite_note-20)[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records#cite_note-ecmrecords1-21) The label has also released some soundtracks e.g. for [_The Return_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Return_(2003_film) "The Return (2003 film)") (2003) by [Andrey Zvyagintsev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrey_Zvyagintsev "Andrey Zvyagintsev") or _[Nouvelle Vague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nouvelle_Vague_(1990_film) "Nouvelle Vague (1990 film)")_ (ECM NewSeries 1600-01) and _[Histoire(s) du cinéma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Histoire(s)_du_cin%C3%A9ma "Histoire(s) du cinéma")_ (ECM NewSeries 1706) by French-Swiss director [Jean-Luc Godard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Luc_Godard "Jean-Luc Godard"). This collaboration expanded over the years and led on the one hand into the contribution of several stills from Godard's movies for covers like _Morimur_ (ECM NewSeries 1765) by [Christoph Poppen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christoph_Poppen "Christoph Poppen"), _Asturiana - Songs from Spain and Argentinia_ (ECM NewSeries 1975) by [Kim Kashkashian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Kashkashian "Kim Kashkashian") or the 2011 _Live at Birdland_ (ECM 2162) by [Lee Konitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Konitz "Lee Konitz")/ [Brad Mehldau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brad_Mehldau "Brad Mehldau")/ [Charlie Haden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Haden "Charlie Haden")/ [Paul Motian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Motian "Paul Motian").[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records#cite_note-22) On the other hand, Eicher took over the musical direction of many of Godard's films like _[Germany Year 90 Nine Zero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany_Year_90_Nine_Zero "Germany Year 90 Nine Zero")_, _[Hélas pour moi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9las_pour_moi "Hélas pour moi")_, _[JLG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JLG/JLG_%E2%80%93_Self-Portrait_in_December "JLG/JLG – Self-Portrait in December")_ or _[For Ever Mozart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/For_Ever_Mozart "For Ever Mozart")_. Besides these Eicher was also the head behind the music of [Xavier Koller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Koller "Xavier Koller")'s _[Reise der Hoffnung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journey_of_Hope_(film) "Journey of Hope (film)")_, [Sandra Nettelbeck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandra_Nettelbeck "Sandra Nettelbeck")'s _[Mostly Martha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mostly_Martha_(film) "Mostly Martha (film)")_ and the Oscar-nominated documentary _[War Photographer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_Photographer "War Photographer")_ by [Christian Frei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_Frei "Christian Frei").[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records#cite_note-ecmrecords1-21) Additionally Godard has released a collection of short films on the label with [Anne-Marie Miéville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anne-Marie_Mi%C3%A9ville "Anne-Marie Miéville") called _Four Short Films_ (ECM 5001).[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records#cite_note-23)

Apart from her own work Greek composer [Eleni Karaindrou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eleni_Karaindrou "Eleni Karaindrou") wrote scores for stage and for movies, which include _[Ulysses' Gaze](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses'_Gaze "Ulysses' Gaze")_ (1995), _[Eternity and a Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eternity_and_a_Day "Eternity and a Day")_ (1998) and _[The Dust of Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Dust_of_Time "The Dust of Time")_ (1999), among others by filmmaker [Theo Angelopoulos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theo_Angelopoulos "Theo Angelopoulos") released on ECM.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records#cite_note-24) The Swiss actor [Bruno Ganz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruno_Ganz "Bruno Ganz"), who has also worked with Angelopoulos, has recorded two spoken word-albums for the label: one in 1984 with poems by [Friedrich Hölderlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedrich_H%C3%B6lderlin "Friedrich Hölderlin") (ECM New Series 1285) and one in 1999 called _Wenn Wasser Wäre_ (ECM New Series 1723) with works of [T. S. Eliot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T._S._Eliot "T. S. Eliot") and [Giorgos Seferis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giorgos_Seferis "Giorgos Seferis"). Another nameable release is the record _[Scardanelli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scardanelli_(album) "Scardanelli (album)")_ (ECM 1761) with texts and music from [Harald Bergmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harald_Bergmann "Harald Bergmann")'s film of the same name from 2000, which reflects the work of Hölderlin in his last years. In the title role, it features Austrian actor [Walter Schmidinger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Schmidinger "Walter Schmidinger") who's reading the poems and texts on this record taken from the movie.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records#cite_note-25) In fall 2012, ECM released a record called _Turmgedichte_ (ECM New Series 2285) by actor/voice actor/vocalist [Christian Reiner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_Reiner?action=edit&redlink=1 "Christian Reiner (page does not exist)") also with poems by Hölderlin.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records#cite_note-26)

Furthermore, ECM has many projects and albums dedicated to people involved with motion pictures. For example, Italian piano player [Stefano Battaglia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stefano_Battaglia "Stefano Battaglia") pays tribute to the work of director [Pier Paolo Pasolini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pier_Paolo_Pasolini "Pier Paolo Pasolini") on his 2007 _[Re: Pasolini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Re:_Pasolini "Re: Pasolini")_ (ECM 1998-99). Its cover pictures a still from Pasolini's 1964 _[The Gospel According to St. Matthew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Gospel_According_to_St._Matthew_(film) "The Gospel According to St. Matthew (film)")_.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records#cite_note-Kern_2010_p._83-89-27) In 2022 a recording of texts by the Italian film maker called _Pier Paolo Pasolini: Land der Arbeit_ (ECM 2768) spoken in German by Reiner was released.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records#cite_note-28) Polish jazz trumpeter [Tomasz Stańko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomasz_Sta%C5%84ko "Tomasz Stańko") recorded in 1994 _[Matka Joanna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matka_Joanna "Matka Joanna")_ (ECM 1544) as an homage to Polish film director [Jerzy Kawalerowicz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerzy_Kawalerowicz "Jerzy Kawalerowicz")'s movie _[Matka Joanna od Aniołów](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mother_Joan_of_the_Angels "Mother Joan of the Angels")_ (1961). Three years later on his 1997 _[Litania: Music of Krzysztof Komeda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Litania:_Music_of_Krzysztof_Komeda "Litania: Music of Krzysztof Komeda")_ (ECM 1636) Stańko honors the work of another countryman and film composer [Krzysztof Komeda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krzysztof_Komeda "Krzysztof Komeda") who is widely known for the scores of several films by [Roman Polanski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Polanski "Roman Polanski") but was also a jazz pianist. Polanski also contributed a preface for the booklet of _Litania_. The album _[Dans la Nuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dans_la_Nuit_(Louis_Sclavis_album) "Dans la Nuit (Louis Sclavis album)")_ (ECM 1805) by French woodwind player [Louis Sclavis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Sclavis "Louis Sclavis"), who also was active as a film composer, is a new score for [Charles Vanel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Vanel "Charles Vanel")'s 1930 silent movie _[Dans la nuit (film)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dans_la_nuit_(film) "Dans la nuit (film)")_.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records#cite_note-29)

The French pianist [François Couturier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Couturier "François Couturier") dedicated a couple of his works to the Soviet/Russian director [Andrei Tarkovsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrei_Tarkovsky "Andrei Tarkovsky").[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records#cite_note-Kern_2010_p._83-89-27) This includes pieces on his 2010 solo record _Un jour si blanc_ (ECM 2103) and the albums _Nostalghia - Song for Tarkovsky_ (ECM 1979) from 2006 as well as the _Tarkovsky Quartet_ (ECM 2159) from 2011 - both with photographs and movie stills of Tarkovsky in the booklet.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records#cite_note-30) Other examples of works dedicated to the director are _Arbos_ (ECM NewSeries 1325) by Estonian composer [Arvo Pärt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arvo_P%C3%A4rt "Arvo Pärt"), the piece _Eight Hymns in memoriam Andrei Tarkovsky_ by composer [Stevan Kovacs Tickmayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stevan_Kovacs_Tickmayer?action=edit&redlink=1 "Stevan Kovacs Tickmayer (page does not exist)") which can be found on [Gidon Kremer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gidon_Kremer "Gidon Kremer")'s 2010 _[Hymns and Prayers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hymns_and_Prayers?action=edit&redlink=1 "Hymns and Prayers (page does not exist)")_ (ECM NewSeries 2161) or _3rd Piece_ by Jan Garbarek on his solo record _[All Those Born with Wings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_Those_Born_with_Wings "All Those Born with Wings")_ (ECM 1324).[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records#cite_note-31) In Spring 2013 ECM released the record _[La notte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Notte_(album) "La Notte (album)")_ by [Ketil Bjørnstad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ketil_Bj%C3%B8rnstad "Ketil Bjørnstad") which took its inspiration from Italian filmmaker [Michelangelo Antonioni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelangelo_Antonioni "Michelangelo Antonioni"); its title and cover were taken from the 1961 [movie of the same name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Notte "La Notte").[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records#cite_note-32) Later that year an [album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/39_Steps_(album) "39 Steps (album)") by [John Abercrombie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Abercrombie_(guitarist) "John Abercrombie (guitarist)") was released with four allusions towards [Hitchcock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Hitchcock "Alfred Hitchcock") movies including the name of the title track taken from _[39 Steps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_39_Steps_(1935_film) "The 39 Steps (1935 film)")_.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records#cite_note-33) On her 2018 album _Descansado: Songs for Films_ (ECM 2567) English singer [Norma Winstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norma_Winstone "Norma Winstone") pays tribute to composers like [Nino Rota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nino_Rota "Nino Rota"), [Michel Legrand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michel_Legrand "Michel Legrand"), [William Walton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Walton "William Walton"), [Bernard Herrmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_Herrmann "Bernard Herrmann"), and [Ennio Morricone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ennio_Morricone "Ennio Morricone") \- all strongly connected to movies - by rearranging their pieces.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records#cite_note-34)

The connection with motion pictures spans further and is reflected in the design of the booklet of _[Mnemosyne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mnemosyne_(album) "Mnemosyne (album)")_ (ECM NewSeries 1700) by [Jan Garbarek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Garbarek "Jan Garbarek") and the [Hilliard Ensemble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilliard_Ensemble "Hilliard Ensemble")—the successor of its highly successful album _[Officium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Officium_(album) "Officium (album)")_ (ECM 1525). It includes stills from _[The Seventh Seal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Seventh_Seal "The Seventh Seal")_ (1957) by Swedish director [Ingmar Bergman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ingmar_Bergman "Ingmar Bergman").[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records#cite_note-35)

In 1986, director Jan Horne shot the 60-minute documentary _Bare Stillheten_ about Eicher and the label in Munich, Oslo, and Tokyo for television with Garbarek, [Terje Rypdal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terje_Rypdal "Terje Rypdal"), [Jon Christensen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jon_Christensen_(musician) "Jon Christensen (musician)"), [Arild Andersen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arild_Andersen "Arild Andersen"), [John Surman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Surman "John Surman"), [Eberhard Weber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eberhard_Weber "Eberhard Weber"), and others participating.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records#cite_note-36) There is also a documentary by Peter Guyer and Norbert Wiedmer called _[Sounds and Silence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sounds_and_Silence?action=edit&redlink=1 "Sounds and Silence (page does not exist)")_ (2010) which portraits exemplary the daily work of [Manfred Eicher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manfred_Eicher "Manfred Eicher") with various musicians including Arvo Pärt, [Nik Bärtsch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nik_B%C3%A4rtsch "Nik Bärtsch"), [Anouar Brahem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anouar_Brahem "Anouar Brahem"), [Dino Saluzzi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dino_Saluzzi "Dino Saluzzi") and [Anja Lechner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anja_Lechner?action=edit&redlink=1 "Anja Lechner (page does not exist)"), Jan Garbarek and [Kim Kashkashian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Kashkashian "Kim Kashkashian") or [Gianluigi Trovesi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gianluigi_Trovesi "Gianluigi Trovesi") and [Gianni Coscia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gianni_Coscia "Gianni Coscia"). The soundtrack with tracks from the recording sessions seen in the movie was as well as the documentary also released on ECM called _Music for the Film - Sounds and Silence_ (ECM 2250).[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records#cite_note-37) A documentary about reed player [Charles Lloyd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Lloyd_(jazz_musician) "Charles Lloyd (jazz musician)") called _Arrows Into Infinity_ (ECM 5052), directed by his wife Dorothy Darr together with Jeffery Morse, was released in July 2014.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records#cite_note-38) Another project from 2014 shows moving images by [Prashant Bhargava](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prashant_Bhargava "Prashant Bhargava") with music by [Vijay Iyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vijay_Iyer "Vijay Iyer") called _[Radhe Radhe: Rites of Holi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radhe_Radhe:_Rites_of_Holi "Radhe Radhe: Rites of Holi")_ (ECM 5507).[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records#cite_note-39) In 2018 followed a portrait about Abercrombie called _Open Land: Meeting John Abercrombie_ (ECM 5053), filmed by [Arno Oehri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arno_Oehri?action=edit&redlink=1 "Arno Oehri (page does not exist)") and [Oliver Primus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Primus "Oliver Primus").[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records#cite_note-40)
Besides these movies, ECM has also released concert videos of Karaindrou, Marc Sinan, [Keith Jarrett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett "Keith Jarrett") solo and with his _Standards_ trio.[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records#cite_note-41)

[Jump to content](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESP-Disk%27#bodyContent) From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia (Redirected from [ESP-Disk](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=ESP-Disk&redirect=no "ESP-Disk")) American record company and label Record label | ESP-Disk' | | --- | | [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/3/38/Esp-disk-logo.jpg/120px-Esp-disk-logo.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Esp-disk-logo.jpg) | | Founded | 1963(1963) | | Founder | [Bernard Stollman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_Stollman "Bernard Stollman") | | Genre | [Free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz"), [free improvisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_improvisation "Free improvisation"), [folk rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk_rock "Folk rock"), [underground rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underground_rock "Underground rock") | | Country of origin | U.S. | | Location | [Brooklyn, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn,_New_York "Brooklyn, New York") | | Official website | [www.espdisk.com](http://www.espdisk.com/) | **ESP-Disk'** is a New York–based record company and [label](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Record_label "Record label") founded in 1963[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESP-Disk%27#cite_note-1) by lawyer [Bernard Stollman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_Stollman "Bernard Stollman"). ## History \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=ESP-Disk%27&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: History")\] [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/85/Helix%2C_v.4%2C_no.6%2C_Aug._29%2C_1968_-_DPLA_-_73a8fb15a58855b090d500dba021b984_%28page_21%29.jpg/250px-Helix%2C_v.4%2C_no.6%2C_Aug._29%2C_1968_-_DPLA_-_73a8fb15a58855b090d500dba021b984_%28page_21%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Helix,_v.4,_no.6,_Aug._29,_1968_-_DPLA_-_73a8fb15a58855b090d500dba021b984_(page_21).jpg) A 1968 ad in Seattle underground paper _[Helix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helix_(newspaper) "Helix (newspaper)")_ offers a free ESP-Disk' with a year's subscription. Though it originally existed to release [Esperanto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esperanto "Esperanto")-based [music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esperanto_music "Esperanto music"), beginning with its second release (Albert Ayler's _[Spiritual Unity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity "Spiritual Unity")_), ESP became the most important exponent of what is commonly referred to as [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESP-Disk%27#cite_note-2) Early releases included albums by [Paul Bley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Bley "Paul Bley"), [Pharoah Sanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pharoah_Sanders "Pharoah Sanders") and [Sun Ra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_Ra "Sun Ra").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESP-Disk%27#cite_note-3) ESP also released recordings by uncommercial [underground rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underground_rock "Underground rock") acts including [the Fugs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fugs "The Fugs"), [The Godz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Godz_(New_York_band) "The Godz (New York band)") and [Pearls Before Swine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearls_Before_Swine_(band) "Pearls Before Swine (band)"). The label's motto is "The artists alone decide what you will hear."[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESP-Disk%27#cite_note-4) [Bernard Stollman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_Stollman "Bernard Stollman") faced allegations of not paying [royalties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royalties "Royalties") to the artists that were signed to ESP-Disk'.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESP-Disk%27#cite_note-5) [Tom Rapp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Rapp "Tom Rapp") of the band [Pearls Before Swine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearls_Before_Swine_(band) "Pearls Before Swine (band)") claimed that: "We never got any money from ESP. Never, not even like a hundred dollars or something. My real sense is that he \[Stollman\] was abducted by aliens, and when he was probed it erased his memory of where all the money was".[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESP-Disk%27#cite_note-6) [Peter Stampfel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Stampfel "Peter Stampfel") of the band [Holy Modal Rounders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Modal_Rounders "Holy Modal Rounders") and [The Fugs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fugs "The Fugs") claimed that Stollman told him that "the contract says that all rights belong to me. You have no royalties ever, ever, ever. The publishing is mine. You don't own the songs anymore. We don't owe you anything".[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESP-Disk%27#cite_note-7) Members of The Fugs have also stated claims that they received an unfavourable record contract. [Ed Sanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Sanders "Ed Sanders") said that "our royalty rate was less than 3%, one of the lower percentages in the history of western civilization".[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESP-Disk%27#cite_note-8) _801 Magazine_, which featured an interview with Stollman in 2008, said that Stollman claimed that "he paid all the recording costs and gave the musicians small advances", and that "he never made any money from the music".[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESP-Disk%27#cite_note-9) ## Discography \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=ESP-Disk%27&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Discography")\] Main article: [ESP-Disk' discography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESP-Disk'_discography "ESP-Disk' discography") ## See also \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=ESP-Disk%27&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: See also")\] - [BYG Actuel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BYG_Actuel "BYG Actuel") - [AACM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Creative_Musicians "Association for the Advancement of Creative Musicians") - [List of record labels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_record_labels "List of record labels") ## References \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=ESP-Disk%27&action=edit§ion=4 "Edit section: References")\] 1. Jean-Luc Young
Fernand Boruso | | Defunct | 1973(1973) | | Genre | [Free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz"), [Avant-garde jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde_jazz "Avant-garde jazz") | | Country of origin | [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France") | | Location | [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris "Paris") | **BYG Records** was a French [record label](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Record_label "Record label") known for the **Actuel** series specializing in [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz"). However, the label released a handful of non-jazz recordings by artists such as [Musica Elettronica Viva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musica_Elettronica_Viva "Musica Elettronica Viva"), [Terry Riley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terry_Riley "Terry Riley"), [Freedom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_(band) "Freedom (band)") and [Gong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gong_(band) "Gong (band)"). ## History \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=BYG_Records&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: History")\] BYG Records was founded in March 1967 by [Jean Georgakarakos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Georgakarakos "Jean Georgakarakos"), Jean-Luc Young, and Fernand Boruso. The name of the label was formed from the initial letters of the founders' surnames. Georgakarakos had previously established himself as a record distributor and importer, while Young worked for [Barclay Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barclay_Records "Barclay Records") and Boruso for [Saravah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saravah "Saravah"), the record label formed by Pierre Barouh. The label invited American free jazz musicians to [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris "Paris") to record in the summer of 1969, a time when they were receiving little support or attention in the United States. Many of these musicians were already overseas at the time, having appeared at the Pan-African Music Festival in [Algiers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algiers "Algiers") in July 1969.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BYG_Actuel#cite_note-1) (Jazz photographer Jacques Bisceglia was largely responsible for connecting the label and musicians, and the "B" in BYG is often wrongly held to refer to Bisceglia.) The resulting albums are an important repository of free jazz recordings from the period. BYG Actuel was also responsible for organising the Actuel festival, which took place in late October 1969 in the small Belgian town of Amougies. The festival was initially intended to take place in or near Paris, but was banned by the French authorities. It featured many leading exponents of progressive rock, such as [Frank Zappa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa "Frank Zappa"), [Pink Floyd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pink_Floyd "Pink Floyd"), [Captain Beefheart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain_Beefheart "Captain Beefheart"), [Soft Machine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine "Soft Machine"), [Ten Years After](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ten_Years_After "Ten Years After"), [Yes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band) "Yes (band)") and [The Nice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nice "The Nice"). The festival was a popular success, with around 20,000 visitors over five nights, but it was a financial failure. In July 1970, Georgakarakos organised the Popanalia festival at Biot on the [French Riviera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Riviera "French Riviera"), but this was also financially unsuccessful. By 1972, financial problems had plagued BYG to the point where it virtually went underground. Georgakarakos and Young later formed their own record labels, [Celluloid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celluloid_Records "Celluloid Records") (Georgakarakos) and [Charly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charly_Records "Charly Records") (Young). In 2002 a compilation album featuring the best of the label, _JazzActuel: a collection of avant garde/free jazz/psychedelia from the BYG/Actuel catalogue of 1969–1971_, was released by Charly (as a 3-CD set) and Get Back Records of Italy (as a 6-LP set). The collection was curated by [Thurston Moore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thurston_Moore "Thurston Moore") of [Sonic Youth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonic_Youth "Sonic Youth") and journalist [Byron Coley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byron_Coley "Byron Coley").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BYG_Actuel#cite_note-2) ## Discography \[ # Prestige Records Prestige Records American jazz record label Not to be confused with the namesake Prestige Records, a British label that releases the work of [Imran Khan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imran_Khan_(singer) "Imran Khan (singer)"). Record label | Prestige Records | | --- | | [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/28/Prestige_Records_logo.svg/500px-Prestige_Records_logo.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Prestige_Records_logo.svg) | | Parent company | [Concord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concord_(entertainment_company) "Concord (entertainment company)") | | Founded | 1949;76years ago(1949)[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prestige_Records#cite_note-1) | | Founder | [Bob Weinstock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Weinstock "Bob Weinstock") | | Genre | [Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") | | Country of origin | United States | | Location | [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") | | Official website | [concordmusicgroup.com/labels/Prestige](http://concordmusicgroup.com/labels/Prestige) | **Prestige Records** is a [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") record company and label founded in 1949 by [Bob Weinstock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Weinstock "Bob Weinstock") in New York City which issued recordings in the mainstream, bop, and cool jazz idioms.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prestige_Records#cite_note-New_Grove-2) The company recorded hundreds of albums by many of the leading jazz musicians of the day, sometimes issuing them on subsidiary labels. The company's began releasing jazz records in 78 and 45 RPM formats in 1950. The Prestige label includes the 13000 and 25000 cat# series. Prestige International was a sub-label of Prestige, active from 1960 to 1969, that mostly released folk music. In 1971, the company was sold to [Fantasy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fantasy_Records "Fantasy Records"), which was later absorbed by [Concord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concord_Records "Concord Records"). ## History The Prestige office was located at 446 West 50th Street, [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prestige_Records#cite_note-3) Its catalogue included [Gene Ammons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gene_Ammons "Gene Ammons"), [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane"), [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis"), [Stan Getz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Getz "Stan Getz"), [Wardell Gray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wardell_Gray "Wardell Gray"), [Thelonious Monk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thelonious_Monk "Thelonious Monk"), and [Sonny Rollins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonny_Rollins "Sonny Rollins").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prestige_Records#cite_note-New_Grove-2) Audio engineer [Rudy Van Gelder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudy_Van_Gelder "Rudy Van Gelder") was the recording engineer of many Prestige albums in the 1950s and early-to-mid-1960s. Prestige created new labels in 1960: Swingville, Moodsville, covering jazz, [Bluesville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bluesville_Records "Bluesville Records") featuring blues revival artists, Lively Arts featuring spoken word recordings and Prestige International, Prestige Folklore, Irish and Near East with folk and world music.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prestige_Records#cite_note-New_Grove-2) By the later 1950s, Weinstock ceased supervising recording sessions directly, employing [Chris Albertson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Albertson "Chris Albertson"), [Ozzie Cadena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzie_Cadena "Ozzie Cadena"), [Esmond Edwards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esmond_Edwards "Esmond Edwards"), [Don Schlitten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Schlitten "Don Schlitten"), and producer/music supervisor [Bob Porter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Porter_(record_producer) "Bob Porter (record producer)"), among others, to fulfill this function.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prestige_Records#cite_note-New_Grove-2) Musicians recording for the label in the 1960s included [Jaki Byard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaki_Byard "Jaki Byard") and [Booker Ervin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Booker_Ervin "Booker Ervin"), while Prestige remained commercially viable by recording a number of [soul jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_jazz "Soul jazz") artists like [Charles Earland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Earland "Charles Earland"). In 1966 the company's headquarters were located at 203 South Washington Avenue in [Bergenfield, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bergenfield,_New_Jersey "Bergenfield, New Jersey").[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prestige_Records#cite_note-4) The company was sold[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prestige_Records#cite_note-label-5) to [Fantasy Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fantasy_Records "Fantasy Records") in 1971, and original releases on the label formed a significant proportion of its [Original Jazz Classics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Original_Jazz_Classics "Original Jazz Classics") line. Fantasy was purchased by [Concord Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concord_Records "Concord Records") in 2005.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prestige_Records#cite_note-label-5) In 2017, Concord Music Group revived the Prestige label. The first album released under the label's reactivation was _A Social Call_ from Texas native [Jazzmeia Horn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazzmeia_Horn "Jazzmeia Horn").[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prestige_Records#cite_note-6)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prestige_Records#cite_note-7) ## Discography Main article: [Prestige Records discography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prestige_Records_discography "Prestige Records discography") ## References 1. Savoy disc from the 1940s | | Parent company | [Concord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concord_(entertainment_company) "Concord (entertainment company)") | | Founded | 1942;84years ago(1942) | | Founder | [Herman Lubinsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herman_Lubinsky "Herman Lubinsky") | | Distributor | [Universal Music Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Music_Group "Universal Music Group") | | Genre | [Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz"), [R&B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_and_blues "Rhythm and blues"), [gospel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gospel_music "Gospel music") | | Country of origin | U.S. | | Location | [Newark, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newark,_New_Jersey "Newark, New Jersey") | **Savoy Records** is an American record company and label established by [Herman Lubinsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herman_Lubinsky "Herman Lubinsky") in 1942 in Newark, New Jersey.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savoy_Records#cite_note-New_Grove-1) Savoy specialized in [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz"), [rhythm and blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_and_blues "Rhythm and blues"), and [gospel music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gospel_music "Gospel music"). In September 2017, Savoy was acquired by [Concord Bicycle Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concord_Bicycle_Music "Concord Bicycle Music").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savoy_Records#cite_note-2) ## History In the 1940s, Savoy recorded some of the biggest names in jazz, including [Charlie Parker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Parker "Charlie Parker"), [Erroll Garner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erroll_Garner "Erroll Garner"), [Dexter Gordon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dexter_Gordon "Dexter Gordon"), [J. J. Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._J._Johnson "J. J. Johnson"), [Fats Navarro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fats_Navarro "Fats Navarro"), and [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis"). In 1948, it began buying other labels: Bop, [Discovery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_Records "Discovery Records"), [National](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Records "National Records"), and [Regent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regent_Records_(US) "Regent Records (US)"). It also reissued music from Jewel Records.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savoy_Records#cite_note-New_Grove-1) In the early 1960s, Savoy briefly recorded several [avant-garde jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde_jazz "Avant-garde jazz") artists. These included [Paul Bley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Bley "Paul Bley"), [Bill Dixon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Dixon "Bill Dixon"), [Charles Moffett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Moffett "Charles Moffett"), [Perry Robinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perry_Robinson "Perry Robinson"), [Archie Shepp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Shepp "Archie Shepp"), [Sun Ra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_Ra "Sun Ra"), [Marzette Watts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marzette_Watts "Marzette Watts"), and [Valdo Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valdo_Williams "Valdo Williams"). After Lubinsky's death in 1974, [Clive Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clive_Davis "Clive Davis"), then manager of [Arista Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arista_Records "Arista Records"), acquired Savoy's catalogue. After that, [Joe Fields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Fields_(producer) "Joe Fields (producer)") of [Muse Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muse_Records "Muse Records") purchased the catalogue from Arista. In 1986, [Malaco Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaco_Records "Malaco Records") acquired Savoy's black gospel titles and contracts.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savoy_Records#cite_note-3) In 1991, [Nippon Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nippon_Columbia "Nippon Columbia") acquired Savoy and its library, and distributed Savoy releases through its wholly owned subsidiary, Savoy Jazz. In 2003, Savoy Jazz acquired the rights to the [Muse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muse_Records "Muse Records") and [Landmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landmark_Records "Landmark Records") catalogues from [32 Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/32_Jazz "32 Jazz").[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savoy_Records#cite_note-porter-4) In 2009, the label entered a distribution arrangement with [Warner Music Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Music_Group "Warner Music Group").[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savoy_Records#cite_note-wmg-5) Savoy included the rock imprint [429 Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/429_Records "429 Records"). Many of the label's African American artists begrudged the label's founder, Herman Lubinsky, feeling underpaid for their work. Tiny Price, a journalist for the African American newspaper _The Newark Herald News_, said of Savoy and Lubinsky: > There's no doubt everybody hated Herman Lubinsky. If he messed with you, you were messed. At the same time, some of those people, many of them Newark's top singers and musicians, would never have been exposed on records if he didn't do what he did. Except for Lubinsky, all the hot little numbers, like Buddy Johnson's "Cherry", would have been lost. The man may have been hated, but he saved a lot of our history for us and for future generations.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savoy_Records#cite_note-6) Savoy's artistic directors included [Buck Ram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buck_Ram "Buck Ram"), [Teddy Reig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teddy_Reig "Teddy Reig"), [Ralph Bass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_Bass "Ralph Bass") (1948–1952), [Fred Mendelsohn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_Mendelsohn "Fred Mendelsohn") (1953), and [Ozzie Cadena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzie_Cadena "Ozzie Cadena") (1954–1962). ## Discography _The following are 12" LPs and have the prefix MG._ | Cat | Artist | Album | | --- | --- | --- | | 12000 | [Charlie Parker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Parker "Charlie Parker") | _Memorial 1_ | | 12001 | Charlie Parker | _Immortal Charlie Parker, The_ | | 12002 | [Erroll Garner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erroll_Garner "Erroll Garner") | _Penthouse Serenade_ | | 12003 | Erroll Garner | _Serenade to Laura_ | | 12004 | [Marian McPartland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marian_McPartland "Marian McPartland") | _At Storyville/At the Hickory House_ | | 12005 | Marian McPartland | _Lullaby of Birdland_ | | 12006 | [Kenny Clarke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenny_Clarke "Kenny Clarke") | _[Telefunken Blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telefunken_Blues "Telefunken Blues")_ | | 12007 | Kenny Clarke and [Ernie Wilkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernie_Wilkins "Ernie Wilkins") | _[Kenny Clarke & Ernie Wilkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenny_Clarke_&_Ernie_Wilkins "Kenny Clarke & Ernie Wilkins")_ | | 12008 | Erroll Garner/ [Billy Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Taylor "Billy Taylor") | _Back to Back_ | | 12009 | Charlie Parker | _Memorial 1_ | | 12010 | [J.
