[Andrew White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_White_(saxophonist) "Andrew White (saxophonist)") | **Weather Report** was an American [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") band active from 1970 to 1986. The band was founded in 1970 by Austrian keyboardist [Joe Zawinul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Zawinul "Joe Zawinul"), American saxophonist [Wayne Shorter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter "Wayne Shorter"), Czech bassist [Miroslav Vitouš](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miroslav_Vitou%C5%A1 "Miroslav Vitouš"), American drummer [Alphonse Mouzon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alphonse_Mouzon "Alphonse Mouzon") and American percussionists [Don Alias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Alias "Don Alias") and Barbara Burton. The band was initially co-led by Zawinul and Shorter but as the 1970s progressed, Zawinul became the primary composer and creative director of the group. Other prominent members throughout the band's history included bassists [Jaco Pastorius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaco_Pastorius "Jaco Pastorius"), [Alphonso Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alphonso_Johnson "Alphonso Johnson") and [Victor Bailey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Bailey_(musician) "Victor Bailey (musician)"), drummers [Chester Thompson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chester_Thompson "Chester Thompson"), [Peter Erskine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Erskine "Peter Erskine") and [Omar Hakim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omar_Hakim "Omar Hakim"), and percussionists [Airto Moreira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airto_Moreira "Airto Moreira") and [Alex Acuña](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Acu%C3%B1a "Alex Acuña"). A quintet of Zawinul and Shorter plus a bassist, a drummer, and a percussionist was the standard formation for Weather Report. The band started as a free improvising group with avant-garde and experimental electronic leanings (pioneered by Zawinul); when Vitouš left Weather Report (due mostly to creative disagreements), Zawinul increasingly steered the band towards a funky, edgy sound incorporating elements of [R&B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_and_blues "Rhythm and blues") and native musics from around the world. Zawinul used the latest developments in synthesizer technology, and he took advantage of a large variety of sounds and tone colors to make the band stand out. During the first half of their career, Weather Report were seen as one of the defining acts in modern jazz, winning the [DownBeat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DownBeat "DownBeat") "best album award" five times in a row. Alongside bands such as [Mahavishnu Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahavishnu_Orchestra "Mahavishnu Orchestra"), [Return to Forever](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Return_to_Forever "Return to Forever"), and [Herbie Hancock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock "Herbie Hancock")'s [Headhunters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Headhunters "The Headhunters") (all with members inspired by and partially responsible for the fusion-era work of [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis")), Weather Report is widely considered one of the defining bands of the [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") genre. ## Musical style Over their 16-year career, Weather Report explored various types of music, predominantly centered on jazz (initially the " [free](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz")" variety), but also incorporating elements of [art music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_music "Art music"), [ethnic music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk_music "Folk music"), [R&B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_and_blues "Rhythm and blues"), [funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funk "Funk"), and [rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music"). While their work was categorized as "jazz fusion", the band members generally distanced themselves from that term. From the start, Weather Report took the unusual approach of abandoning the traditional "soloist/accompaniment" demarcation of straight-ahead jazz and featured opportunities for continuous improvisation by every member of the band. That position remained consistent throughout the life of the band. From the point where [Alphonso Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alphonso_Johnson "Alphonso Johnson") joined the band, individual solos became more prominent in concert, but were never allowed to overwhelm the collective approach. Initially, the band's music featured an improvisational method (similar to [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis")'s _[Bitches Brew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew "Bitches Brew")_-period),[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report#cite_note-Larkin-1) but eventually that shifted to a more groove-oriented approach and catchier compositions (as epitomized by their 1977 hit single ["Birdland"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birdland_(composition) "Birdland (composition)")). Joe Zawinul's playing style was often dominated by quirky melodic improvisations (simultaneously [bebop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bebop "Bebop")-, ethnic-, and pop-sounding) combined with sparse but rhythmic big-band chords or bass lines. Having originally made his name as a pioneering [electric piano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_piano "Electric piano") player, he went on to consistently develop the role of the [synthesizer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synthesizer "Synthesizer") in jazz during his time with Weather Report. Working with companies such as [ARP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ARP_Instruments "ARP Instruments") and [Oberheim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oberheim_Electronics "Oberheim Electronics"), Zawinul developed new ways of voicing and patching electronic tones for textures, ensemble roles (including emulations of traditional band instruments) and soloing. In Weather Report, he often employed a [vocoder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vocoder "Vocoder"), as well as recorded sounds played (i.e., filtered and transposed) through a synthesizer, creating a very distinctive, often beautiful, synthesis of [jazz harmonics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_chord "Jazz chord") and "noise" (which he referred to as "using all the sounds the world generates"). On some Weather Report tunes, however, Zawinul was criticized for allowing his synthesized arrangements to dominate the sound. > In the beginning let's say Weather Report was a joint thing. Then, after the second album there's no question about it, it became more and more my group. Wayne wanted it like that, but we were always 'partners in crime'. No Wayne, no Weather Report. —Josef Zawinul on his gradual takeover of Weather Report[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report#cite_note-2) [Wayne Shorter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter "Wayne Shorter") came to the group with a reputation as a dominant role as an instrumentalist,[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report#cite_note-Larkin-1) drawn from both his solo work and his contributions to Miles Davis' "second great quintet" during the 1960s. His choice not to follow the same approach with Weather Report led to some criticism of the group. During his time with Weather Report, Shorter was noted for generally playing saxophone with an economical, "listening" style. Rather than continually taking the lead, he generally added subtle harmonic, melodic, and/or rhythmic complexity by responding to other member's improvisations (although he could and did sometimes exercise a more frenetic style akin to that of [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane") or [Michael Brecker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Brecker "Michael Brecker")). As a composer, he chose a more abstract, sometimes atonal and "free jazz" style of music, opposed to the sometimes flamboyant melodicism of the tunes written by Zawinul or Pastorius. Playing both tenor and soprano saxophones, Shorter continued to develop the role of the latter instrument in jazz, taking his cue from previous work by [Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane"), [Sidney Bechet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidney_Bechet "Sidney Bechet"), [Lucky Thompson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucky_Thompson "Lucky Thompson"), and [Steve Lacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Lacy_(saxophonist) "Steve Lacy (saxophonist)"). Weather Report maintained a consistent interest in a textured sound and developments in music technology and processing. Both Zawinul and original bassist Miroslav Vitouš experimented with electronic effects pedals (as generally used by rock guitarists) with Zawinul using them on electric piano and synthesizers and Vitouš on his [upright bass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upright_bass "Upright bass") (which he frequently bowed through distortion to create a second horn-like voice). The band's third bass player, [Jaco Pastorius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaco_Pastorius "Jaco Pastorius"), popularized the use of fretless bass guitar, melodic bass soloing and extensive use of string harmonics, as well as consolidating the driving R&B pulse in the band's music (which had been brought in by his predecessor [Alphonso Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alphonso_Johnson "Alphonso Johnson")). With the exception of a brief quartet period between 1978 and 1979 (wherein other members could double on various percussion instruments), Weather Report's instrumentation always included both a drummer and a percussionist. For its first eight years of existence, the group had difficulty finding a permanent drummer, moving through about one drummer per year until Jaco Pastorius helped to recruit Peter Erskine in 1978. [Peter Erskine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Erskine "Peter Erskine") and [Omar Hakim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omar_Hakim "Omar Hakim") were the only drummers who played with Weather Report for more than two years. ## History ### 1970: Inception and formation Joe Zawinul and Wayne Shorter had first met and become friends in 1959 while they were playing in [Maynard Ferguson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maynard_Ferguson "Maynard Ferguson")'s [Big Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Band "Big Band"). Zawinul went on to play with [Cannonball Adderley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannonball_Adderley "Cannonball Adderley")'s group in the 1960s, while Shorter joined [Art Blakey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Blakey "Art Blakey")'s Jazz Messengers and then, in 1964, Miles Davis's second great quintet. During this decade, both men made names for themselves as being among the best composers in jazz. Zawinul later joined Shorter in contributing to the initial [fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") music recordings of [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis"), and both men were part of the studio groups that recorded the key Davis albums _[In a Silent Way](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way "In a Silent Way")_ (1969) and _[Bitches Brew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew "Bitches Brew")_ (1970).[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report#cite_note-Larkin-1) Weather Report was initially formed to explore a more impressionistic and individualistic music (or, as Zawinul put it, "away from all that eight bars shit and then you go to the bridge...").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report#cite_note-3) There is some dispute over how Weather Report initially formed. According to Zawinul, it began when he and Shorter recruited another Miles Davis associate, the classically trained Czech-born bass player Miroslav Vitouš, who had previously played with each of them separately (as well as with [Herbie Mann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Mann "Herbie Mann"), [Bob Brookmeyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Brookmeyer "Bob Brookmeyer"), [Stan Getz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Getz "Stan Getz"), and [Chick Corea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chick_Corea "Chick Corea")). According to Vitouš himself, it was he and Shorter who actually founded Weather Report, with Shorter bringing in Zawinul afterwards.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report#cite_note-4) Whichever story is true, it was those three musicians – all composers – who formed the initial core of the project. To complete the band, Zawinul, Shorter and Vitouš brought in [McCoy Tyner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCoy_Tyner "McCoy Tyner")'s former drummer [Alphonse Mouzon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alphonse_Mouzon "Alphonse Mouzon") and began recording their [debut album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report_(1971_album) "Weather Report (1971 album)") while looking for a full-time auxiliary percussionist.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report#cite_note-Larkin-1) The initial recruits were session percussion player [Don Alias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Alias "Don Alias") and symphony orchestra percussionist Barbara Burton. During recording, Alias quarreled with Zawinul (allegedly due to Zawinul being too dictatorial over the percussion approach) and the innovative Brazilian percussionist [Airto Moreira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airto_Moreira "Airto Moreira") (yet another Davis alumnus) was brought in to complete the record. Guitarist [John McLaughlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McLaughlin_(musician) "John McLaughlin (musician)") was also invited to join the group, but decided to pursue his solo career, instead. ### 1971–1972: Avant-garde collective Weather Report's debut album _[Weather Report](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report_(1971_album) "Weather Report (1971 album)")_ featured a softer sound than would be the case in later years, predominantly using acoustic bass, with Shorter exclusively playing soprano saxophone. It built on the avant-garde experiments which Zawinul and Shorter had pioneered with Miles Davis on [_Bitches Brew live_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew_Live "Bitches Brew Live"), including an avoidance of head-and-chorus composition in favor of continuous rhythm and movement.\[ _[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] _[DownBeat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DownBeat "DownBeat")_ magazine described the album as "music beyond category".[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report#cite_note-5) In 1972, Weather Report released its second album, _[I Sing the Body Electric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Sing_the_Body_Electric_(album) "I Sing the Body Electric (album)")_.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report#cite_note-Larkin-1) The first side featured new studio recordings, while the second side was taken from live recordings of a concert in [Tokyo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokyo "Tokyo"), featuring the full-band lineup of Zawinul, Shorter, Vitouš, [Eric Gravatt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Gravatt "Eric Gravatt"), and [Dom Um Romão](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dom_Um_Rom%C3%A3o "Dom Um Romão") (and later available in full as the 1972 Japan-only double album _[Live in Tokyo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live_in_Tokyo_(Weather_Report_album) "Live in Tokyo (Weather Report album)")_).[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report#cite_note-ALLMUSIC-6) The studio side used extended versions of the band including various guest performers, suggesting that Weather Report was not necessarily an integral jazz band, but might possibly work as an expandable project set up to realise the music of its three composers.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report#cite_note-7) The album also featured Zawinul's first use of a [synthesizer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synthesizer "Synthesizer") (an instrument with which he would become synonymous within jazz) and of sound effects. ### 1973: Move towards groove On 1973's _[Sweetnighter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweetnighter "Sweetnighter")_, Weather Report began to abandon the primarily acoustic group improvisation format, and the band started to take a new direction. Primarily at Zawinul's instigation, Weather Report became more [jazz funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_funk "Jazz funk")\- and groove-oriented, drawing more heavily on [R&B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_and_blues "Rhythm and blues") influences and dense electric keyboard work while adding more structure to both the prewritten and the improvisational sections. > \[Miroslav\] loved funk, and he tried to play it, but he wasn't a funk player. It wasn't where he came from. He didn't connect up with how to go there. He could listen to it, talk about it, and he admired it, but that's not what came out of him, so that was something that held back where Joe wanted to go at the time I was with them. Melodically and rhythmically, Miroslav was great; what he did do, in terms of where I was coming from, was very unique. Miroslav was still playing acoustic, and it was an odd kind of a funk. It was very... interesting! —Weather Report touring drummer Greg Errico on [Miroslav Vitouš](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miroslav_Vitou%C5%A1 "Miroslav Vitouš")[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report#cite_note-inasilentway-8) Gravatt took his replacement in the studio sessions badly and quit the band at the end of recording, moving to [Minneapolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minneapolis "Minneapolis") to join the band Natural Life. Many years later, Zawinul paid tribute to Gravatt's skills and stated that he had been the finest of the band's "pure jazz" drummers[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report#cite_note-9) as well as being "from the jazz side... my favorite of them all".[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report#cite_note-10) With Gravatt gone and former drummer Herschel Dwellingham unavailable for touring, former [Sly & the Family Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sly_&_the_Family_Stone "Sly & the Family Stone") drummer [Greg Errico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greg_Errico "Greg Errico") played on the _Sweetnighter_ tour, but did not stay with the band afterwards. At this point, Vitouš and Zawinul found themselves at creative loggerheads, since the former preferred Weather Report's original approach and the latter wished to continue further along the road to funk. Retrospectively, Zawinul accused Vitouš of being unable to play funk convincingly (something which Greg Errico corroborated) and claimed that he had not provided enough music for the band. Vitouš countered that he had in fact brought in compositions, but that Zawinul had been unable to play them. Vitouš has also accused Zawinul of having been "a first-class manipulator" primarily interested in commercial success.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report#cite_note-conversationvitous-11)[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report#cite_note-innerviewsvitous-12) For his part, Zawinul would later recall Vitouš planning to concentrate on more bowed solos and getting the group to hire a second bassist to play the standard basslines, to which Zawinul's response was "why don't we get one bassist who can do all of that?" Zawinul claimed that "there was nothing disrespectful about it... we had to make this move. And history has proved us to have been right."[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report#cite_note-jazztimessportinlife-13) When Shorter sided with Zawinul, the original three-man partnership broke down acrimoniously and Vitouš left Weather Report, moving on to a solo career as composer and band leader. His final contribution to Weather Report was to play bass on a single track, which appeared on the band's 1974 album _[Mysterious Traveller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mysterious_Traveller "Mysterious Traveller")_ ("American Tango", which he had co-written with Zawinul). Vitouš's departure marked the end of the first phase of Weather Report and the shift of overall creative dominance of the band to Josef Zawinul, although Shorter remained an integral, influential, and vital part of the project. Vitouš has subsequently accused both Zawinul and Shorter of having used foul play to edge him out of the band, to deny the scale of his contribution to Weather Report's history and creative approach, and to cheat him out of remuneration.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report#cite_note-conversationvitous-11)[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report#cite_note-innerviewsvitous-12) ### 1974–1975: Further into groove Vitouš's replacement was the Philadelphian electric bass guitarist [Alphonso Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alphonso_Johnson "Alphonso Johnson") (formerly a sideman for the pop-fusion player [Chuck Mangione](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuck_Mangione "Chuck Mangione")). Recruited by Shorter, Alphonso Johnson was a supple player more than capable of providing the funk element which Zawinul desired. He was also an early advocate of the [Chapman Stick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapman_Stick "Chapman Stick"), which he can be heard playing on some of the live Weather Report recordings of the period. According to Zawinul, new drummer Ishmael Wilburn apparently "lost heart" on tour (despite performing well in the studio). To shore up the music, the band hired another drummer, Darryl Brown, to play alongside him. At the end of the tour, both Wilburn and Brown left the band (as did Dom Um Romão) and Weather Report was, once again, drummerless. For the next set of studio sessions, Weather Report added a new Brazilian percussionist (Alyrio Lima) and a new drummer, [Leon "Ndugu" Chancler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leon_%22Ndugu%22_Chancler "Leon \"Ndugu\" Chancler"). The new album, _[Tale Spinnin'](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tale_Spinnin' "Tale Spinnin'")_, was released in 1975. It was the first Weather Report album to feature a consistent rhythm section (rather than a varied set of drummers, percussionists, and bass players) since their debut. The album also made further strides in using technological improvements in synthesizers, even making use of the gigantic studio-based [TONTO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TONTO "TONTO") array. During the same year, Shorter also recorded _[Native Dancer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_Dancer_(album) "Native Dancer (album)")_ under his own name (with the Brazilian composer and vocalist [Milton Nascimento](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milton_Nascimento "Milton Nascimento")). _Tale Spinnin'_ won the _[DownBeat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DownBeat "DownBeat")_ best album award for 1975 (the third Weather Report album to do so) and _Native Dancer_ was the runner-up. ### 1976: In transition [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/89/Weatherreport.jpg/500px-Weatherreport.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Weatherreport.jpg) Weather Report in Argentina. L to R: Shorter, Erskine, Zawinul, and Pastorius 1976's _[Black Market](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Market_(Weather_Report_album) "Black Market (Weather Report album)")_ album was perhaps the most rock-oriented work which the group had produced to date.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report#cite_note-Larkin-1) Weather Report's music had evolved further from open-ended funk jams into more melody-oriented, concise forms, which also offered a greater mass-market appeal. Zawinul further consolidated his use of keyboard synthesizers, while Shorter experimented with an early form of wind synthesizer, the [Lyricon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyricon "Lyricon"). However, the album was recorded during yet another period of change for the group, with multiple personnel shuffles. Although Alyrio Lima played percussion on one track, he was replaced during the sessions by [Don Alias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Alias "Don Alias") (his first appearance with the group since the debut album) and by [Alex Acuña](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Acu%C3%B1a "Alex Acuña") (a Peruvian drummer and conga player based in Las Vegas, who had played with [Elvis Presley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elvis_Presley "Elvis Presley") and [Ike Turner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ike_Turner "Ike Turner"), among others).[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report#cite_note-14) Alphonso Johnson was also worn out from the strain put on the rhythm by the band's frequent changes of drummer. During a break in activity halfway through the recording of _Black Market_, Johnson opted to leave Weather Report to play with the [Billy Cobham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Cobham "Billy Cobham")/ [George Duke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Duke "George Duke") Band (which featured a young [John Scofield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Scofield "John Scofield") on guitar). Prior to his departure, Johnson played on all but two of the new album's tracks. His replacement was [Jaco Pastorius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaco_Pastorius "Jaco Pastorius"), a [virtuoso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virtuoso "Virtuoso") fretless bass guitarist from [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida"), who had been in touch with Zawinul for several years and who came in to play on "Cannonball" and his own composition "Barbary Coast". Zawinul and Shorter had assumed that new drummer [Chester Thompson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chester_Thompson "Chester Thompson") would be departing alongside his friend Johnson, and for the second set of sessions, they replaced him (on Pastorius' recommendation) with the former [Mahavishnu Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahavishnu_Orchestra "Mahavishnu Orchestra") drummer [Narada Michael Walden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Narada_Michael_Walden "Narada Michael Walden"). Although Walden played on several album tracks, he ultimately proved unsuitable. Thompson returned for the final _Black Market_ sessions, but left again after failing to gel as a rhythm section with Pastorius (whose style was much busier than that of Johnson). Thompson subsequently joined [Genesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genesis_(band) "Genesis (band)") as their touring drummer. _Black Market_ continued Weather Report's ongoing run of success,[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report#cite_note-Larkin-1) selling well and being the fourth of the band's albums to win the album of the year award from _[DownBeat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DownBeat "DownBeat")_ magazine. For the subsequent tour, [Alex Acuña](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Acu%C3%B1a "Alex Acuña") moved from percussion to the drum kit, and Don Alias was replaced by the young Puerto Rican percussionist [Manolo Badrena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manolo_Badrena "Manolo Badrena"), who had previously played with various Latin rock bands and with [Art Blakey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Blakey "Art Blakey"). The band made a very well-received appearance in July at the [Montreux Jazz Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montreux_Jazz_Festival "Montreux Jazz Festival") 1976, which was filmed for future release. ### 1977–1979: Jazz-rock stars | | | | --- | --- | | ![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/b/b4/Ambox_important.svg/120px-Ambox_important.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail) | This section **may contain [original research](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:No_original_research "Wikipedia:No original research")**. Statements consisting only of original research should be removed._(March 2023)__([Learn how and when to remove this message](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Maintenance_template_removal "Help:Maintenance template removal"))_ | [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5d/Portrait_of_Tracy_1980.jpg/500px-Portrait_of_Tracy_1980.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Portrait_of_Tracy_1980.jpg) Pastorius, reaching to accentuate his bass guitar sound with harmonics[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8c/Weather_Report1.jpg/500px-Weather_Report1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Weather_Report1.jpg) L-R: Zawinul, Pastorius, Shorter The band's next album was 1977's acclaimed _[Heavy Weather](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heavy_Weather_(album) "Heavy Weather (album)")_, which proved to be the band's most successful recording in terms of sales, while still retaining wide critical acclaim. It included the band's biggest hit, the propulsive and danceable " [Birdland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birdland_(composition) "Birdland (composition)")" (highlighting Pastorius' singing bass lines and Zawinul's synthesized ensemble brass), which became a pop hit and later became a [jazz standard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_standard "Jazz standard"). Weather Report appeared on the [Burt Sugarman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burt_Sugarman "Burt Sugarman")-produced series _[The Midnight Special](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Midnight_Special_(TV_series) "The Midnight Special (TV series)")_, performing both "Birdland" and " [Teen Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teen_Town "Teen Town")". _Heavy Weather_ continued Weather Report's record of awards, including their last _[DownBeat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DownBeat "DownBeat")_ Album of the Year award. During this period, Pastorius' strong professional connection with [Joni Mitchell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joni_Mitchell "Joni Mitchell") (for whom he played bass throughout the latter half of the 1970s) led to another musical connection. Over the next few years, Mitchell hired the Weather Report line-up _en masse_ (although without Zawinul in each case) to play on her studio albums _[Don Juan's Reckless Daughter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Juan's_Reckless_Daughter "Don Juan's Reckless Daughter")_ (1977) and _[Mingus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mingus_(Joni_Mitchell_album) "Mingus (Joni Mitchell album)")_ (1979). [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d7/Weather_Report2_%28Jaco_Pastorius%29.jpg/500px-Weather_Report2_%28Jaco_Pastorius%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Weather_Report2_(Jaco_Pastorius).jpg) Jaco Pastorius, with bass guitar in Toronto, November 1977 During August 1978 the band joined [Maurice White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_White "Maurice White")'s vanity label [ARC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Record_Corporation "American Record Corporation") at [Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Records "Columbia Records").[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report#cite_note-15) At the time they were once again without either a full-time drummer and percussionist, with Alex Acuña having returned to Las Vegas for a career as a studio musician and [Manolo Badrena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manolo_Badrena "Manolo Badrena") having been fired for "non-musical reasons". Shorter had been focusing most of his attention and compositional ideas into his solo work, while Zawinul was sketching out ideas for a solo album of his own, which involved moving away from a raw group sound in favor of constructing a far more orchestrated and experimental studio-based recording with multiple overdubs. However, Weather Report's contract and work schedule required another album, so Zawinul's solo work was absorbed into what became Weather Report's eighth album, _[Mr. Gone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mr._Gone_(album) "Mr. Gone (album)")_ (1978). The studio sessions made use of a variety of drummers – Pastorius played the kit on two tracks and further contributions came from [Tony Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Williams_(drummer) "Tony Williams (drummer)"), [Steve Gadd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Gadd "Steve Gadd"), and [Peter Erskine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Erskine "Peter Erskine") (the latter an ex- [Stan Kenton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Kenton "Stan Kenton")/ [Maynard Ferguson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maynard_Ferguson "Maynard Ferguson") drummer recruited to the project by Pastorius). Erskine became a full member of the band for the next tour and remained with Weather Report until 1982. The album also featured guest appearances from [Deniece Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deniece_Williams "Deniece Williams") and [Earth Wind and Fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth_Wind_and_Fire "Earth Wind and Fire") leader [Maurice White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_White "Maurice White"). The album rose to No. 1 on the [Billboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_(magazine) "Billboard (magazine)") [Jazz Albums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_Albums "Jazz Albums") chart.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report#cite_note-16) Notoriously, _Mr. Gone_ (1978) received only a one-star review rating from _[DownBeat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DownBeat "DownBeat")_ after a string of group releases which had all pulled a five-star rating. The group arranged for a rebuttal interview with the magazine to defend their efforts. Zawinul and Pastorius were uncompromising in their contributions to the interview, Shorter more philosophical, and Erskine the most reticent of the four. [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fe/Weather_Report2_1980.jpg/960px-Weather_Report2_1980.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Weather_Report2_1980.jpg) Weather Report performing in Amsterdam in 1980 By the late '70s, Weather Report was a quartet of Zawinul, Shorter, Pastorius, and Erskine, and (for the first time) had dispensed with the auxiliary percussionist role, which had been integral since the band's inception. Instead, all four members doubled on percussion at various points in live performances. Zawinul commented that this sleeker, less crowded sound provided more listening range and made the music less chaotic now that the band were focusing more on melody and harmony.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report#cite_note-17)[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report#cite_note-18) The larger scale and multimedia staging of the band's tours (complete with stagehands, laser and film projections) began to take on the kind of rock-star proportions mostly unknown in jazz circles. The 1979 double live album _[8:30](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/8:30 "8:30")_ (which won that year's [Best Jazz Fusion Performance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Jazz_Fusion_Performance "Grammy Award for Best Jazz Fusion Performance")) was recorded on the _Mr. Gone_ tour and captured the direct power and energy of this lineup of Weather Report. Zawinul later described this lineup as "one of the greatest bands of all time! That band was a _hummer_!"[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report#cite_note-19) Between March 2 and 4, 1979, Weather Report traveled to [Havana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Havana "Havana"), [Cuba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuba "Cuba"), to participate in the historic [Havana Jam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Havana_Jam "Havana Jam") festival, a break in mutual Cuban/American political hostilities, which had American artists such as [Stephen Stills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Stills "Stephen Stills"), the CBS Jazz All-Stars, [Bonnie Bramlett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bonnie_Bramlett "Bonnie Bramlett"), [Kris Kristofferson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kris_Kristofferson "Kris Kristofferson"), [Rita Coolidge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Coolidge "Rita Coolidge"), and [Billy Joel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Joel "Billy Joel") play alongside Cuban artists such as [Irakere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irakere "Irakere"), [Pacho Alonso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacho_Alonso "Pacho Alonso"), [Tata Güines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tata_G%C3%BCines "Tata Güines"), and [Orquesta Aragón](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orquesta_Arag%C3%B3n "Orquesta Aragón"). Another featured performance was by the [Trio of Doom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trio_of_Doom "Trio of Doom") (a short-lived teaming of Pastorius with [John McLaughlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McLaughlin_(musician) "John McLaughlin (musician)") and [Tony Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Williams_(drummer) "Tony Williams (drummer)")). Weather Report's performance featured in Havana Jam '79, Ernesto Juan Castellanos' documentary celebrating the event. ### 1980–1982: A tighter arrangement [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/62/Bobby_Thomas_jr._and_Wayne_Shorter.jpg/500px-Bobby_Thomas_jr._and_Wayne_Shorter.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bobby_Thomas_jr._and_Wayne_Shorter.jpg) Drummer Thomas, left, and Shorter, performing in Amsterdam, in 1980 At the beginning of 1980, Pastorius recruited hand-drummer [Robert Thomas Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Thomas_Jr. "Robert Thomas Jr.") (a fellow Floridan, with whom he had jammed previously) into the band. Thomas featured on the 1980 album _[Night Passage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Night_Passage_(album) "Night Passage (album)")_. A tighter and more traditional recording than previous releases, the record featured a more prominent role for Shorter, a strong element of [bebop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bebop "Bebop"), and a nod to jazz's golden age via a high-speed cover of [Duke Ellington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_Ellington "Duke Ellington")'s " [Rockin' in Rhythm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rockin'_in_Rhythm "Rockin' in Rhythm")" (showing off Zawinul's pioneering and ever-increasing ability to create synthetic big-band sounds on his synthesizers). By now, Pastorius was displaying signs of the mental instability and substance abuse problems that ultimately wrecked his career; the close relationship he'd previously shared with Zawinul was becoming strained as Zawinul lost patience with Pastorius' showmanship onstage (beginning to feel that it detracted from the music). Towards the end of the year, Pastorius began working on his long-delayed second solo album ( _[Word of Mouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Word_of_Mouth_(Jaco_Pastorius_album) "Word of Mouth (Jaco Pastorius album)")_) (1981) in New York, while Zawinul worked on new Weather Report material in California. Weather Report's next album _[Weather Report](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report_(1982_album) "Weather Report (1982 album)")_ (1982) (their second eponymous release, following their 1971 debut) was recorded in 1981, although it was not released for another year. Zawinul's dominance as instrumentalist and composer (as well as group director) was even more pronounced on this album. Increasingly, the band's music was written out rather than improvised. At the same time, Pastorius was spending more of his creative attention on his _Word of Mouth_ project: his only writing for the Weather Report album was his contribution to a single group-composed piece. Shorter (who only contributed one composition to the 1982 album, beyond group-written work) was already taking a less active approach. He later commented, philosophically, "For a long time in Weather Report, I abstained. I elected not to do things." Erskine's own commitment to _Word of Mouth_ (and his summer commitment to _[Steps Ahead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steps_Ahead "Steps Ahead")_) meant that his part also needed to be replaced; at the same time, Robert Thomas Jr. left the band. Reduced to a duo, and with tour commitments looming, Zawinul and Shorter were obliged to quickly assemble a new band. ### 1982–1985: A new band On the recommendation of [Michał Urbaniak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micha%C5%82_Urbaniak "Michał Urbaniak"),[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report#cite_note-auto-20) Zawinul and Shorter recruited 23-year-old drummer [Omar Hakim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omar_Hakim "Omar Hakim"), a talented session player and multi-instrumentalist, who had played with a variety of musicians including [Mike Mainieri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Mainieri "Mike Mainieri"), [David Bowie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Bowie "David Bowie"), and [Carly Simon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carly_Simon "Carly Simon"). Hakim was immediately entrusted with recruiting the rest of the new lineup. Having failed to secure [Marcus Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcus_Miller "Marcus Miller") as bass guitarist,[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report#cite_note-21) he selected [Victor Bailey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Bailey_(musician) "Victor Bailey (musician)") (a recent graduate from the [Berklee College of Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berklee_College_of_Music "Berklee College of Music"), with whom Hakim had played while backing [Miriam Makeba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miriam_Makeba "Miriam Makeba")). Hakim also recruited percussion/concertina player José Rossy, with whom he had worked in [Labelle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labelle "Labelle"). The new Weather Report went straight onto tour. The music developed on tour was later recorded for the 1983 album _[Procession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Procession_(album) "Procession (album)")_, which showed the band beginning to make something of a return to the "world music" approach which it had pioneered in the mid-1970s, and featured a cameo appearance from [The Manhattan Transfer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Manhattan_Transfer "The Manhattan Transfer").[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report#cite_note-auto-20) Continuing with the same lineup, Weather Report recorded the _[Domino Theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domino_Theory_(album) "Domino Theory (album)")_ album in 1984, with Hakim stepping into Jaco Pastorius' old role as Zawinul's co-producer. The album was Weather Report's first album to employ drum machines and samplers (the Emulator), deepening the band's involvement with cutting-edge music technology, and also featured a guest vocal from [Carl Anderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Anderson_(singer) "Carl Anderson (singer)"). Percussionist and singer [Mino Cinélu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mino_Cin%C3%A9lu "Mino Cinélu") replaced Rossy in the spring of 1984 and appeared on the band's video release _Live in Japan_ (reissued on DVD in 2007). The same lineup played on 1985's _[Sportin' Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportin'_Life_(Weather_Report_album) "Sportin' Life (Weather Report album)")_ album, which included a cover of [Marvin Gaye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marvin_Gaye "Marvin Gaye")'s " [What's Going On](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's_Going_On_(song) "What's Going On (song)")" and appearances by singers [Bobby McFerrin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_McFerrin "Bobby McFerrin") and Carl Anderson. In keeping with Zawinul's technological curiosity, the album heralded the arrival of [MIDI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MIDI "MIDI"), which allowed him to rapidly and inexpensively write, demonstrate, and record music via a set of synthesizers. ### 1986: Final split Both Zawinul and Shorter were beginning to realise that the refreshing nature of other projects was more satisfying than Weather Report work, and both generally felt that the band had run its course.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report#cite_note-Larkin-1) In February 1986, the _[San Diego Union-Tribune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Diego_Union-Tribune "San Diego Union-Tribune")_ announced that Shorter had left the band to concentrate on solo work.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report#cite_note-22) Having reluctantly agreed with Shorter that he would no longer use the band name, Zawinul then ended Weather Report. The final album under the Weather Report name, _[This is This!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/This_is_This! "This is This!")_, was released in June 1986 and fulfilled the band's contract with Columbia Records. Two of its tracks featured guitar work from [Carlos Santana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Santana "Carlos Santana"), and it also marked the return of Peter Erskine on drums, with Hakim only appearing on one track. ### 1986–present: After Weather Report Having split the band, Zawinul promptly attempted to reform it – after a fashion – as Weather Update.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report#cite_note-Larkin-1) For this project, he reunited with recent Weather Report alumni Victor Bailey, Mino Cinélu, and Peter Erskine, but replaced Shorter with guitarist [John Scofield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Scofield "John Scofield"). This lineup was short-lived, with [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles") session guitarist [Steve Khan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Khan "Steve Khan") and former Weather Report percussionist [Robert Thomas Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Thomas_Jr. "Robert Thomas Jr.") replacing Scofield and Cinélu prior to live appearances.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report#cite_note-23) Weather Update toured in 1986 and 1987 before Zawinul dissolved the band. From 1988 onwards, Zawinul went on to enjoy a successful nineteen-year career leading the world music/jazz ensemble [The Zawinul Syndicate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Zawinul_Syndicate "The Zawinul Syndicate") (which has continued, following Zawinul's death, as The Syndicate). Rather than form another collective band, Wayne Shorter concentrated on his solo career and on work as a bandleader, which continued until his death on March 2, 2023. In spite of the band's enduring popularity, a Weather Report reunion never occurred. The nearest that the band ever came to reuniting was when Zawinul and Shorter both played live with Miles Davis on July 10, 1991, in [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris "Paris") (the only time when Zawinul is known to have shared a live stage with Davis).[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report#cite_note-ALLMUSIC-6) A projected mid-1990s reunion CD for Verve never materialized; according to Zawinul, disappointing sales for Shorter's 1995 CD _[High Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Life_(Wayne_Shorter_album) "High Life (Wayne Shorter album)")_ may have played a part in ending the idea.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report#cite_note-innerviewszawinul-24) Six of the band's members have since died. Zawinul himself died on September 11, 2007, in Vienna from [skin cancer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skin_cancer "Skin cancer") ( [Merkel cell carcinoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merkel_cell_cancer "Merkel cell cancer")).[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report#cite_note-25)[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report#cite_note-26) He was predeceased by mid-period bass player Jaco Pastorius, who died on September 21, 1987, following a fatal beating in his hometown of [Fort Lauderdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Lauderdale "Fort Lauderdale"), Florida. Pastorius' successor on bass guitar, Victor Bailey, died on November 11, 2016 (apparently from complications from [Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charcot-Marie-Tooth_disease "Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease") and [amyotrophic lateral sclerosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amyotrophic_lateral_sclerosis "Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis")).[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report#cite_note-27)[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report#cite_note-28) [Alphonse Mouzon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alphonse_Mouzon "Alphonse Mouzon"), the first drummer, died on December 25, 2016, from cardiac arrest after neuroendocrine cancer.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report#cite_note-29)[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report#cite_note-30) Dom Um Romão, the group's percussionist from 1971 to 1974, died in 2005 aged 79.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report#cite_note-31) Wayne Shorter died on March 2, 2023, at the age of 89.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report#cite_note-32) ## Grammy Awards See also: [List of awards and nominations received by Weather Report](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_awards_and_nominations_received_by_Weather_Report "List of awards and nominations received by Weather Report") The [Grammy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Awards "Grammy Awards") are awarded annually by the [National Academy of Recording Arts and Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Recording_Academy "The Recording Academy") of the United States. "This Is This!")_ | ## Releases since the band's breakup A "post band" Weather Report double CD called _[Live and Unreleased](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live_and_Unreleased_(album) "Live and Unreleased (album)")_ was made available in 2002, featuring vintage live recordings made during the late 1970s/early 1980s with various personnel. In September 2006, Columbia/Legacy released a Weather Report boxed set, _[Forecast: Tomorrow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forecast:_Tomorrow "Forecast: Tomorrow")_. It includes three CDs of mostly previously released material (from 1970 to 1985, excluding _This is This!_) and a DVD of the entire September 28, 1978, performance (with Erskine and Pastorius) in Offenbach, Germany, not previously available. A DVD video of the 1976 Montreux Jazz Festival performance (featuring the Heavy Weather lineup of Pastorius, Acuna, and Badrena) has become available, as well. Columbia/Legacy have also re-released the 1984 _Live in Japan_ concert on DVD. In 2011, the Zawinul estate, in conjunction with an independent label, released a 40th-anniversary commemorative trilogy of previously unavailable Weather Report live shows: In March _Live in Berlin 1975_ was released both on vinyl and as a CD/DVD set; in June the _Live in Offenbach 1978_ DVD was re-released together with a previously unavailable double CD of the complete show; in October _Live in Cologne 1983_ was released as both DVD and double CD. ## References 01. [Jean-Luc Ponty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Luc_Ponty "Jean-Luc Ponty") | | | | Website | [return2forever.com](http://return2forever.com/) | **Return to Forever** was an American [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") band that was founded by pianist [Chick Corea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chick_Corea "Chick Corea") in 1972.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Return_to_Forever#cite_note-Larkin-2) The band has had many members, with the only consistent bandmate of Corea's being bassist [Stanley Clarke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_Clarke "Stanley Clarke"). Along with [Weather Report](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report "Weather Report"), [The Headhunters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Headhunters "The Headhunters"), and [Mahavishnu Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahavishnu_Orchestra "Mahavishnu Orchestra"), Return to Forever is often cited as one of the core groups of the jazz-fusion movement of the 1970s. Several musicians, including Clarke, [Flora Purim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flora_Purim "Flora Purim"), [Airto Moreira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airto_Moreira "Airto Moreira") and [Al Di Meola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Di_Meola "Al Di Meola"), came to prominence through their performances on Return to Forever albums. After playing on [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis")'s jazz-fusion albums _[In a Silent Way](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way "In a Silent Way")_ (1969) and _[Bitches Brew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew "Bitches Brew")_ (1970), Corea formed an [avant-garde jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde_jazz "Avant-garde jazz") band called [Circle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circle_(American_band) "Circle (American band)") with [Dave Holland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Holland_(bassist) "Dave Holland (bassist)"), [Anthony Braxton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Braxton "Anthony Braxton") and [Barry Altschul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barry_Altschul "Barry Altschul"). In 1972, after converting to [Scientology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientology "Scientology"), Corea decided he wanted to communicate better with his audience. This meant performing a more accessible style of music than avant-garde jazz. Return to Forever first disbanded in 1977 after five years and seven studio albums. The band never released another studio album, but occasionally reunited for live performances until Corea's death in 2021. ## History \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Return_to_Forever&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: History")\] ### First group (1972–1973) \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Return_to_Forever&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: First group (1972–1973)")\] The first edition of Return to Forever performed primarily [Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_music_(genre) "Latin music (genre)")-oriented music.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Return_to_Forever#cite_note-Larkin-2) This initial band consisted of singer and percussionist [Flora Purim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flora_Purim "Flora Purim"), her husband [Airto Moreira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airto_Moreira "Airto Moreira") (both Brazilians) on [drums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drummer "Drummer") and percussion, Corea's longtime musical co-worker [Joe Farrell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Farrell "Joe Farrell") on [saxophone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxophone "Saxophone") and [flute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flute "Flute"), and the young [Stanley Clarke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_Clarke "Stanley Clarke") on bass.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Return_to_Forever#cite_note-Larkin-2) Within this first line-up in particular, Clarke played acoustic [double bass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_bass "Double bass") in addition to [electric bass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bass_guitar "Bass guitar"). Corea's [Fender Rhodes electric piano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodes_piano "Rhodes piano") formed the basis of this group's sound; he had yet to discover synthesizers, his trademark sound in the group's later years. Clarke and Farrell were given ample solo space themselves. While Purim's vocals lent some commercial appeal to the music, many of their compositions were also instrumental and somewhat experimental in nature. The music was composed by Corea with the exception of the title track of the second album which was written by Stanley Clarke. Lyrics were often written by Corea's friend Neville Potter, and were quite often Scientology-themed. Their first album, titled simply _[Return to Forever](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Return_to_Forever_(album) "Return to Forever (album)")_, was recorded for [ECM Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records "ECM Records") in 1972,[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Return_to_Forever#cite_note-Larkin-2) and was initially released only in [Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europe "Europe"). This album featured Corea's now famous compositions "Crystal Silence" and "La Fiesta". Shortly afterwards, Corea, Airto, Clarke and [Tony Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Williams_(drummer) "Tony Williams (drummer)") formed the band for [Stan Getz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Getz "Stan Getz")'s album _[Captain Marvel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain_Marvel_(album) "Captain Marvel (album)")_ (recorded in 1972 and released in 1975), which featured Corea's compositions, including some from the first and second Return to Forever albums. Their second album, _[Light as a Feather](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light_as_a_Feather "Light as a Feather")_ (1973),[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Return_to_Forever#cite_note-Larkin-2) was released by [Polydor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polydor "Polydor") and included the song " [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain_(composition) "Spain (composition)")", which also became quite well known. ### Jazz rock era (1973–1976) \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Return_to_Forever&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: Jazz rock era (1973–1976)")\] [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/50/Return_to_Forever_1974.jpg/330px-Return_to_Forever_1974.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Return_to_Forever_1974.jpg) L to R: [Stanley Clarke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_Clarke "Stanley Clarke"), [Al Di Meola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Di_Meola "Al Di Meola"), [Chick Corea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chick_Corea "Chick Corea") (drummer [Lenny White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lenny_White "Lenny White") not visible). Return to Forever performing in 1974 at [Onondaga Community College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Onondaga_Community_College "Onondaga Community College") in Syracuse, New York. After the second album, Farrell, Purim and Moreira left the group to form their own bands, and guitarist [Bill Connors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Connors "Bill Connors"), drummer [Steve Gadd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Gadd "Steve Gadd") and percussionist [Mingo Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mingo_Lewis "Mingo Lewis") were added. However, Gadd was unwilling to tour with the band and risk his job as an in-demand session drummer. [Lenny White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lenny_White "Lenny White") (who had played with Corea in [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis")'s band) replaced Gadd and Lewis on drums and percussion, and the group's third album, _[Hymn of the Seventh Galaxy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hymn_of_the_Seventh_Galaxy "Hymn of the Seventh Galaxy")_ (1973), was then re-recorded (the first recording, featuring Gadd on drums, was never released and has since disappeared).[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Return_to_Forever#cite_note-Larkin-2) The nature of the group's music had by now completely changed into jazz-rock, or jazz fusion, and had evolved into a similar vein to that which the [Mahavishnu Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahavishnu_Orchestra "Mahavishnu Orchestra"), [Weather Report](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report "Weather Report"), and some [progressive rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock "Progressive rock") bands were performing at the time. Their music was still melodic and incorporated strong themes. And while the music had a strong, rock oriented approach, it was elevated by the [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") elements of strong, instrumental improvisation and modulating harmonic and rhythmic structures. Over-driven, distorted guitar had also become prominent in the band's new sound, and Clarke had by then switched almost completely to the [electric bass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_bass "Electric bass"). A replacement on vocals was not hired, and all the songs were now instrumentals. This change did not lead to a decrease in the band's commercial fortunes however, Return to Forever's [jazz rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_rock "Jazz rock") albums instead found their way onto [US pop album charts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200"). In the September 1988 _[DownBeat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DownBeat "DownBeat")_ magazine interview with Chick Corea by Josef Woodward, Josef says (page 19), "There is this general view ... that ... Miles \[Davis\] crystallized electric jazz fusion and that he sent his emissaries out." Chick responds, "Nah, that's Disneyland. Miles is definitely a leader ... But there were other things that occurred that I thought were equally as important. What John McLaughlin did with the electric guitar set the world on its ear. No one ever heard an electric guitar played like that before, and it certainly inspired me. ... John's band, more than my experience with Miles, led me to want to turn the volume up and write music that was more dramatic and made your hair move."[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Return_to_Forever#cite_note-3) While their second jazz rock album, _[Where Have I Known You Before](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Where_Have_I_Known_You_Before "Where Have I Known You Before")_ (1974) was similar in style to its immediate predecessor, Corea now played [synthesizers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synthesizer "Synthesizer") in addition to electric [keyboards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keyboard_instrument "Keyboard instrument") (including [piano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano "Piano")), and Clarke's playing had evolved considerably- now using flange and fuzz-tone effects, and with his signature style beginning to emerge. After [Bill Connors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Connors "Bill Connors") left the band to concentrate on his solo career, the group also hired new guitarists. Although [Earl Klugh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_Klugh "Earl Klugh") played guitar for some of the group's live performances, he was soon replaced by the then 19-year-old guitar prodigy [Al Di Meola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Di_Meola "Al Di Meola"), who had also played on the album recording sessions. Their following album, _[No Mystery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No_Mystery "No Mystery")_ (1975), was recorded with the same line-up as _Where Have I Known You Before_, but the style of music had become more varied. The first side of the record consisted primarily of jazz-funk, while the second side featured Corea's acoustic title track and a long composition with a strong [Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_of_Spain "Music of Spain") influence. On this and the following album, each member of the group composed at least one of the tracks. _No Mystery_ went on to win the [Grammy Award for Best Jazz Performance by a Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Jazz_Performance_by_a_Group "Grammy Award for Best Jazz Performance by a Group"). The final album by this longest-lasting "classic" lineup of the group, which had by this time left Polydor for [Columbia Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Records "Columbia Records"), was _[Romantic Warrior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romantic_Warrior "Romantic Warrior")_ (1976), the best selling of all Return to Forever's efforts,[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Return_to_Forever#cite_note-Larkin-2) eventually reaching [gold disc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_recording_sales_certification "Music recording sales certification") status. _Romantic Warrior_ continued their experiments in the realms of jazz-rock and related musical genres, and was lauded by critics for both the technically demanding style of its compositions as well as for its accomplished musicianship. After the release of _Romantic Warrior_ and Return to Forever's subsequent tour in support (as well as having in addition signed a multimillion-dollar contract with [CBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sony_Music "Sony Music")), Corea shocked Clarke by deciding to change the lineup of the group and to not include either White or Di Meola.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Return_to_Forever#cite_note-religio.de-4) ### Final album (1977) \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Return_to_Forever&action=edit§ion=4 "Edit section: Final album (1977)")\] The final incarnation of Return to Forever featured Corea, Clarke and Joe Farrell as well as a four-piece horn section and Corea's wife [Gayle Moran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gayle_Moran "Gayle Moran") on vocals, but recorded only one studio album, _[Musicmagic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musicmagic "Musicmagic")_ (1977). In 1978, after issuing a live album of the tour titled _[Return to Forever Live: The Complete Concert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live_(Return_to_Forever_album) "Live (Return to Forever album)")_[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Return_to_Forever#cite_note-Larkin-2) (a four-LP set, also released in edited form as a single LP and later as a double CD), Chick Corea officially disbanded the group.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Return_to_Forever#cite_note-5) ### Reunions \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Return_to_Forever&action=edit§ion=5 "Edit section: Reunions")\] In 1982, the Corea/Clarke/White/Di Meola lineup reunited to record a ten-minute track, "Compadres", which was issued on Corea's 1982 album _[Touchstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Touchstone_(album) "Touchstone (album)")_. Also, they played at The [Wolf & Rissmiller's Country Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reseda_Country_Club "Reseda Country Club"), Reseda, California, with [Joe Henderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Henderson "Joe Henderson") on April 7, 1982. In 1983, the same Return to Forever lineup played a short reunion tour of the U.S. and Japan, and the live recording in Japan was released in 2021. The repertoire for the tour included some new material by Corea, including one piece titled "Overture" that was later recorded by the [Chick Corea Elektric Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chick_Corea_Elektric_Band "Chick Corea Elektric Band") for the live various artists double album _[GRP Super Live in Concert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GRP_Super_Live_in_Concert?action=edit&redlink=1 "GRP Super Live in Concert (page does not exist)")_ (1992),[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Return_to_Forever#cite_note-6) and another titled "The Phantom" that Di Meola later recorded on his album _[Kiss My Axe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kiss_My_Axe "Kiss My Axe")_ (1991). Twenty-six years later, Corea, Clarke, White, and Di Meola reunited a second time for a tour of the United States and Europe that began in the summer of 2008. A boxed set of remixed and digitally remastered tracks from the albums _Hymn of the Seventh Galaxy_, _Where Have I Known You Before_, _No Mystery_, and _Romantic Warrior_ was released to coincide with the tour.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Return_to_Forever#cite_note-7) Corea, Clarke, and White (minus Di Meola) performed an acoustic tour in 2009 and released a live album in 2011 titled _[Forever](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forever_(Corea,_Clarke_&_White_album) "Forever (Corea, Clarke & White album)")_. It included guest appearances by Bill Connors, [Chaka Khan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chaka_Khan "Chaka Khan"), and [Jean-Luc Ponty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Luc_Ponty "Jean-Luc Ponty"). In February 2011 the group began a world tour in Australia. The lineup for this tour was Corea, Clarke, White, Ponty, and guitarist [Frank Gambale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gambale "Frank Gambale") of the Chick Corea Elektric Band. Many dates included [Dweezil Zappa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dweezil_Zappa "Dweezil Zappa")'s [Zappa Plays Zappa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zappa_Plays_Zappa "Zappa Plays Zappa") band as an opening act with Corea occasionally appearing in Zappa's band on keyboards, as well as Jean-Luc Ponty performing some of the songs that he had performed with [Frank Zappa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa "Frank Zappa").[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Return_to_Forever#cite_note-8) Corea died of cancer on February 9, 2021. ## Discography \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Return_to_Forever&action=edit§ion=6 "Edit section: Discography")\] ### Studio albums \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Return_to_Forever&action=edit§ion=7 "Edit section: Studio albums")\] | Year | Album | Peak chart positions | [Certifications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_music_recording_certifications "List of music recording certifications") | Labels | Note | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | [US Pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200")
