[Mario Cipollina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mario_Cipollina "Mario Cipollina") | **The Tony Williams Lifetime** was a [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") group led by drummer [Tony Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Williams_(drummer) "Tony Williams (drummer)"). The band was pivotal in the development of fusion and featured various noteworthy jazz and rock musicians throughout its history, including guitarists [John McLaughlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McLaughlin_(musician) "John McLaughlin (musician)") and [Allan Holdsworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allan_Holdsworth "Allan Holdsworth"), keyboardists [Larry Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Young_(musician) "Larry Young (musician)") and [Alan Pasqua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Pasqua "Alan Pasqua"), and bassists [Jack Bruce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Bruce "Jack Bruce") and [Ron Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ron_Carter "Ron Carter"). ## Original line-up The Tony Williams Lifetime was founded in 1969 as a [power trio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_trio "Power trio") with John McLaughlin on electric guitar and Larry Young on organ. The band was possibly named for Williams' debut album as a bandleader, _[Life Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_Time_(Tony_Williams_album) "Life Time (Tony Williams album)")_, released on [Blue Note](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records "Blue Note Records") in 1965.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Tony_Williams_Lifetime#cite_note-Larkin-1) Its debut album was _[Emergency!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergency!_(album) "Emergency! (album)")_, a [double album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_album "Double album") released on [Polydor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polydor_Records "Polydor Records")/ [PolyGram Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PolyGram_Records "PolyGram Records") in 1969. It was largely rejected by jazz listeners at the time of its release because of its heavy rock influences, but it is now looked upon as a fusion classic.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Tony_Williams_Lifetime#cite_note-2) [Jack Bruce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Bruce "Jack Bruce") joined the group to provide bass and vocals on its second album, _[Turn It Over](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turn_It_Over "Turn It Over")_, released in 1970.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Tony_Williams_Lifetime#cite_note-3) McLaughlin left the group and was replaced by [Ted Dunbar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Dunbar "Ted Dunbar") on its 1971 album, _[Ego](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ego_(Tony_Williams_Lifetime_album) "Ego (Tony Williams Lifetime album)")_. This album also featured [Ron Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ron_Carter "Ron Carter") on bass and cello, [Warren Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Smith_(jazz_musician) "Warren Smith (jazz musician)") and [Don Alias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Alias "Don Alias") on percussion, and [Larry Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Young_(jazz) "Larry Young (jazz)") on organ. Lifetime gigs around this time featured [Juini Booth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juini_Booth "Juini Booth") on bass. This lineup's performance in France on August 7, 1971 (venue unknown) was filmed in color and broadcast on the French television program Pop2. Following Larry Young's departure from the band sometime after July 1972, Tony Williams was the only original member remaining. Williams performed in August 1972 with a new short-lived trio called Life Time Experience, featuring bassist [Stanley Clarke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_Clarke "Stanley Clarke") and violinist [Jean Luc-Ponty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Luc_Ponty "Jean-Luc Ponty"). Their performance at the Festival de Chateauvallon, Chateauvallon, France, on August 23, 1972, was captured on film in black & white. The fourth and last Lifetime album for Polydor/PolyGram, 1973's _The Old Bum's Rush_, was recorded in Boston and features entirely new personnel consisting of female vocalist and guitarist Linda/Laura 'Tequila' Logan (Williams' love interest at the time), [Webster Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Webster_Lewis "Webster Lewis") on organ & clavinet, David Horowitz on piano, vibes, and ARP synthesizer, and [Herb Bushler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb_Bushler "Herb Bushler") on bass. Tony Williams' father Tillmon Williams makes a guest appearance on saxophone. Prior to recording, this lineup of the Lifetime, augmented by guitarist Bob Cacciola (or possibly Caccicola) performed material from the album on July 7, 1972, at the Newport Jazz Festival, Carnegie Hall, in New York. Marking yet another stylistic departure for the Lifetime and reinvention of the band's musical identity, the record is characterized by a predominantly sprightly and upbeat songwriting approach, electronic keyboard-dominated sound, and soul-jazz female vocals. Notably, keyboardist newcomer Webster Lewis turns in an organ performance which sounds remarkably like his predecessor Larry Young aka Khalid Yasin. Recorded by Williams under the dark cloud of knowing that Polydor would not be renewing his contract, the album received poor reviews and the group was effectively dissolved. In 1974, Williams formed a new Lifetime featuring _Bum's Rush_ holdovers [Webster Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Webster_Lewis "Webster Lewis") on keyboards and Linda/Laura 'Tequila' Logan on vocals, along with former Cream/Lifetime bassist [Jack Bruce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Bruce "Jack Bruce") and British guitarist [Allan Holdsworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allan_Holdsworth "Allan Holdsworth"). This lineup, sometimes referred to as Wildlife, recorded an album's worth of material at Europa Films Studios in Stockholm, Sweden in October 1974. This recording has never been officially released but circulates as a bootleg. ## The New Lifetime In spring 1975, Williams put together a quartet he called The New Tony Williams Lifetime featuring bassist [Tony Newton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Newton_(musician) "Tony Newton (musician)"), pianist [Alan Pasqua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Pasqua "Alan Pasqua"), and guitarist [Allan Holdsworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allan_Holdsworth "Allan Holdsworth").[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Tony_Williams_Lifetime#cite_note-4) Prior to settling on Tony Newton as the choice for bass player, a number of bassists auditioned for the spot including [Jaco Pastorius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaco_Pastorius "Jaco Pastorius").[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Tony_Williams_Lifetime#cite_note-5) This lineup recorded two albums for [Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Records "Columbia Records")/ [CBS Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sony_Music_Entertainment "Sony Music Entertainment"), _[Believe It](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Believe_It_(album) "Believe It (album)")_ in 1975 and _[Million Dollar Legs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Million_Dollar_Legs_(album) "Million Dollar Legs (album)")_ in 1976. These albums were reissued on one CD in 1992 as _[Lifetime: The Collection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lifetime:_The_Collection "Lifetime: The Collection")_. After recording _Million Dollar Legs_, guitarist [Allan Holdsworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allan_Holdsworth "Allan Holdsworth") departed and was replaced first by Larry Herzberg (in the summer of 1976) and then by Marlon Graves for the subsequent tour undertaken to support the album. In 1977, Williams parted ways with Graves, Pasqua, and Newton and formed another Lifetime lineup with entirely new personnel consisting of Mike Hoffmann (lead guitar), Gerry Mule′ (second guitar), Paul Potyen (keyboards), and [Michael Formanek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Formanek "Michael Formanek") (bass). This lineup recorded demos for the Columbia label but had no official releases and played a small number of live gigs performing material from _Ego_ and the two New Lifetime albums _Believe It_ and _Million Dollar Legs_. In July 1978 Williams toured Japan with [Ronnie Montrose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronnie_Montrose "Ronnie Montrose") (guitar), [Brian Auger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Auger "Brian Auger") (keyboards), [Mario Cipollina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mario_Cipollina "Mario Cipollina") (bass) and special guest [Billy Cobham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Cobham "Billy Cobham") also on drums for a series of concerts. They were billed as the Tony Williams All Stars. Later that year he released _[The Joy of Flying](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Joy_of_Flying "The Joy of Flying")_, an eclectic solo album featuring a mix of styles and collaborations with [Herbie Hancock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock "Herbie Hancock"), [Cecil Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor "Cecil Taylor"), [Tom Scott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Scott_(saxophonist) "Tom Scott (saxophonist)"), [Stanley Clarke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_Clarke "Stanley Clarke"), [Michael Brecker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Brecker "Michael Brecker"), [George Benson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Benson "George Benson"), and [Jan Hammer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Hammer "Jan Hammer").[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Tony_Williams_Lifetime#cite_note-6) It also contains " [Open Fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_Fire_(Ronnie_Montrose_album) "Open Fire (Ronnie Montrose album)")" recorded by the All Stars earlier that year. In 1979, Williams formed another all-new Lifetime featuring Tod Carver (guitar), [Bunny Brunel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunny_Brunel "Bunny Brunel") (bass), Bruce Harris (keyboards), and [Tom Grant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Grant_(jazz_musician) "Tom Grant (jazz musician)") (keyboards). The band's sound was a major departure from the former New Lifetime's classic fusion, with the high-energy shredding heard on _Believe It_ and _Million Dollar Legs_ largely abandoned in favor of a cerebral and groove-laden approach that emphasized mood and melody over technical virtuosity. As with the 1977 band the 1979-era Lifetime played a small number of live gigs and no studio recordings are known to exist. Toward the end of this period Williams pared-down the lineup to a trio and played some gigs with [Tom Grant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Grant_(jazz_musician) "Tom Grant (jazz musician)") on keyboards and [Bunny Brunel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunny_Brunel "Bunny Brunel") on bass. In late May 1980, Williams and a new trio incarnation of the Lifetime featuring [Patrick O'Hearn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_O'Hearn "Patrick O'Hearn") on bass (miscredited as Patrick O'Hara) and [Tom Grant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Grant_(jazz_musician) "Tom Grant (jazz musician)") on keyboards recorded the little-known _Play or Die_ album for the Swiss label PS Productions. Stylistically, the recording found Williams returning to high energy keyboard-dominated instrumental fusion reminiscent of the 1975 album _[On the Mountain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Mountain_(album) "On the Mountain (album)")_ by Elvin Jones, Jan Hammer and Gene Perla. At the time of his death Williams was writing and rehearsing with guitarist [Lyle Workman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyle_Workman "Lyle Workman") (who had appeared on Williams' 1996 solo release _Wilderness_) to form yet another incarnation of the Lifetime. ## Legacy and tributes At the time of its release, _Emergency!_ was notably influential on the then-emerging genre of jazz fusion.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Tony_Williams_Lifetime#cite_note-7) It was also one of several albums that the members of [The Allman Brothers Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Allman_Brothers_Band "The Allman Brothers Band") listened to regularly early in their career.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Tony_Williams_Lifetime#cite_note-8) [John Zorn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Zorn "John Zorn") named the Tony Williams Lifetime as a specific musical inspiration in the [liner notes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liner_notes "Liner notes") of the [Naked City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naked_City_(band) "Naked City (band)") album _[Radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_(Naked_City_album) "Radio (Naked City album)")_. British singer-songwriter [Andy Partridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Partridge "Andy Partridge") of [XTC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XTC "XTC") calls _Emergency!_ his all-time favourite album, and says that hearing it in 1969, at the insistence of a friend, was a vital moment in expanding his musical tastes beyond conventional guitar pop and rock.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Tony_Williams_Lifetime#cite_note-9)[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Tony_Williams_Lifetime#cite_note-10) Since the death of Williams in 1997, [Jack DeJohnette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_DeJohnette "Jack DeJohnette") and [John Scofield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Scofield "John Scofield") formed [Trio Beyond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trio_Beyond "Trio Beyond") with [Larry Goldings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Goldings "Larry Goldings") in honour of the Tony Williams Lifetime. They released one album, _[Saudades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudades_(Trio_Beyond_album) "Saudades (Trio Beyond album)")_ (2006), on the German label [ECM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_(record_label) "ECM (record label)"). In 2006, former Lifetime members Allan Holdsworth and Alan Pasqua toured with drummer [Chad Wackerman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chad_Wackerman "Chad Wackerman") and bassist [Jimmy Haslip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Haslip "Jimmy Haslip") performing a set comprising original as well as Lifetime material. _Live at Yoshi's_, a DVD from the U.S. leg of the tour, was released in 2007 and followed by the 2-CD set _[Blues for Tony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blues_for_Tony "Blues for Tony")_ in 2009. In December 2008, guitarist [Vernon Reid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vernon_Reid "Vernon Reid"), organist [John Medeski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Medeski "John Medeski"), drummer [Cindy Blackman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cindy_Blackman "Cindy Blackman"), and former Lifetime member [Jack Bruce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Bruce "Jack Bruce") played a week of shows in Japan as the Tony Williams Lifetime Tribute Band, playing a set of 1969/70 Lifetime material. This was recorded in high-definition and shown on Japanese TV. Cindy Blackman released a Lifetime tribute album titled _[Another Lifetime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Another_Lifetime_(album) "Another Lifetime (album)")_ in 2010.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Tony_Williams_Lifetime#cite_note-11) The Lifetime Tribute Band featuring Jack Bruce reformed in February 2011 to play a further ten shows in high-profile jazz clubs in North America. Unusually the dates have early & evening shows, something most rock musicians stopped doing at the beginning of the 1970s. Reaction to the 2011 U.S. shows was so positive that the band renamed themselves Spectrum Road, after a track on 1969's first Lifetime album. The group released a [self-titled album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectrum_Road "Spectrum Road") in 2012 on the U.S. jazz record label [Palmetto Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palmetto_Records "Palmetto Records").[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Tony_Williams_Lifetime#cite_note-12) ## Discography - 1969: _[Emergency!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergency!_(album) "Emergency! [Jim Beard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Beard "Jim Beard") | The **Mahavishnu Orchestra** was a [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") band formed in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") in 1971, led by English guitarist [John McLaughlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McLaughlin_(musician) "John McLaughlin (musician)").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahavishnu_Orchestra#cite_note-Larkin-1) The group underwent several line-up changes throughout its history across its two periods of activity, from 1971 to 1976 and from 1984 to 1987.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahavishnu_Orchestra#cite_note-2) With its first line-up consisting of McLaughlin, drummer [Billy Cobham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Cobham "Billy Cobham"), keyboardist [Jan Hammer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Hammer "Jan Hammer"), violinist [Jerry Goodman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerry_Goodman "Jerry Goodman") and bassist [Rick Laird](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Laird "Rick Laird"), the band received acclaim for its complex, intense music consisting of a blend of [Indian classical music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_classical_music "Indian classical music"), [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz"), and [psychedelic rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychedelic_rock "Psychedelic rock") as well as its dynamic live performances between 1971 and 1973.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahavishnu_Orchestra#cite_note-harvardcrimson-3)[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahavishnu_Orchestra#cite_note-newyorktimes1-4) Many members of the band have gone on to acclaimed careers of their own in the jazz and jazz-fusion genres. ## History \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mahavishnu_Orchestra&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: History")\] ### 1971–1974: First incarnation \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mahavishnu_Orchestra&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: 1971–1974: First incarnation")\] By mid-1971, McLaughlin had been a member of [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis")' band and [Tony Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Williams_(drummer) "Tony Williams (drummer)")' Lifetime, and released three solo albums. He then set about forming his own [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") group, the first line-up of which featured Panamanian drummer Cobham, Irish bassist Laird, Czech keyboardist Hammer and American violinist Goodman.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahavishnu_Orchestra#cite_note-CD11-73-5) Cobham and Goodman had played on McLaughlin's third solo album _[My Goal's Beyond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My_Goal's_Beyond "My Goal's Beyond")_ (1971). McLaughlin's first choice for violinist was Frenchman [Jean-Luc Ponty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Luc_Ponty "Jean-Luc Ponty"), but he was unable to join due to immigration problems. After listening to various albums he hired Goodman, formerly of [the Flock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Flock_(band) "The Flock (band)"). Though American bassist [Tony Levin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Levin "Tony Levin") was the first person McLaughlin wanted,[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahavishnu_Orchestra#cite_note-6)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahavishnu_Orchestra#cite_note-7) Laird had known McLaughlin for several years and accepted the invitation. Hammer was found through a mutual friendship with [Miroslav Vitouš](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miroslav_Vitou%C5%A1 "Miroslav Vitouš") of the jazz fusion group [Weather Report](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report "Weather Report").[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahavishnu_Orchestra#cite_note-CD11-73-5) The group's name originates from Indian spiritual leader and guru [Sri Chinmoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sri_Chinmoy "Sri Chinmoy"), of whom McLaughlin had become a follower, who gave him the name Mahavishnu, "Maha" meaning "great" in [Sanskrit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanskrit "Sanskrit") and "vishnu" after the Hindu deity [Vishnu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vishnu "Vishnu").[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahavishnu_Orchestra#cite_note-8) With the line-up secured, the five met in New York City in July 1971 and rehearsed for one week. They adopted an instrumental fusion sound characterised by electric rock, funk, complex [time signatures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_signatures "Time signatures"), and arrangements influenced by McLaughlin's interest in [Indian classical music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_classical_music "Indian classical music"). Their debut gigs followed at the [Gaslight at the Au Go Go](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cafe_Au_Go_Go "Cafe Au Go Go") as the opening act for bluesman [John Lee Hooker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Lee_Hooker "John Lee Hooker").[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahavishnu_Orchestra#cite_note-9) McLaughlin recalled: "The first set was shaky but the second set just took off and every night it was great. They wanted to hold us over and a few days after the second week ... we went into the studio".[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahavishnu_Orchestra#cite_note-crawdaddy1973-10) McLaughlin secured a record deal with [Columbia Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Records "Columbia Records"), giving the green light to record an album. [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/75/JohnMcLaughlin.jpg/250px-JohnMcLaughlin.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:JohnMcLaughlin.jpg) McLaughlin in 1973 performing with the band _[The Inner Mounting Flame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Inner_Mounting_Flame "The Inner Mounting Flame")_ was released in November 1971, peaking at No. 11 on the _Billboard_ Jazz Albums and No. 89 on the [_Billboard_ 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200"). This was followed by _[Birds of Fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birds_of_Fire "Birds of Fire")_ (1973) which peaked at No. 15 on the _Billboard 200_. Due to the pressures of sudden fame, exhaustion and a lack of communication, the original band began to tire. The stress was further exacerbated by problematic recording sessions in June 1973 at London's [Trident Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trident_Studios "Trident Studios") that found some of the players not speaking to others. Their project was never fully completed. Cobham was disappointed and felt that the group "were knocking on the door of something really new. Something unique, something that had never been done before in rock and roll."[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahavishnu_Orchestra#cite_note-MM0274-11) This was followed by the release of their first live album _[Between Nothingness & Eternity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Between_Nothingness_&_Eternity "Between Nothingness & Eternity")_, which featured material from the Trident sessions.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahavishnu_Orchestra#cite_note-Larkin-1) Later in 1973, Hammer and Goodman expressed their frustrations with McLaughlin's leadership in an interview for _[Crawdaddy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crawdaddy_(magazine) "Crawdaddy (magazine)")_ magazine. An attempt was made to improve group relations by having each member introduced as they walked on stage, and tunes by Hammer, Laird, and Goodman mixed into the live set.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahavishnu_Orchestra#cite_note-CD11-73-5) It was not enough, however, and the five played their final gig on December 30.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahavishnu_Orchestra#cite_note-MM0174-12) According to Laird, the band did not say goodbye to each other afterward.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahavishnu_Orchestra#cite_note-RS74-13) In January 1974, McLaughlin split the group.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahavishnu_Orchestra#cite_note-MM0174-12) Laird spoke about the group weeks later, claiming that despite McLaughlin's having composed most of the group's tunes, the rest of the band contributed "a great deal" and did not receive credit. He was also critical of Cobham's claim that the group had rejected his musical ideas, and that Hammer, Goodman, and Laird pushed to have their songs performed because of "an ego trip".[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahavishnu_Orchestra#cite_note-RS74-13) ### 1974–1976: Second incarnation \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mahavishnu_Orchestra&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: 1974–1976: Second incarnation")\] After the original group dissolved, it reformed in 1974 with a new cast of musicians behind McLaughlin: [Jean-Luc Ponty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Luc_Ponty "Jean-Luc Ponty") (who had performed with [Frank Zappa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa "Frank Zappa") and the Mothers of Invention) on violin, [Gayle Moran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gayle_Moran "Gayle Moran") on keyboards, Ralphe Armstrong on bass guitar and [Narada Michael Walden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Narada_Michael_Walden "Narada Michael Walden") on drums, Steve Kindler and Carol Shive on violins, Marcia Westbrook on viola, Phil Hirschi on cello, Steve Frankevich, [Premik Russell Tubbs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premik_Russell_Tubbs "Premik Russell Tubbs") on alto, tenor and soprano saxophones, and Bob Knapp on brass.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahavishnu_Orchestra#cite_note-Larkin-1) This "new", expanded Mahavishnu Orchestra (which McLaughlin has reportedly called the "real" Mahavishnu Orchestra) changed personnel slightly between 1974's _[Apocalypse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apocalypse_(Mahavishnu_Orchestra_album) "Apocalypse (Mahavishnu Orchestra album)")_ and _[Visions of the Emerald Beyond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visions_of_the_Emerald_Beyond "Visions of the Emerald Beyond")_ in 1975. _Apocalypse_ was recorded in London with the [London Symphony Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Symphony_Orchestra "London Symphony Orchestra") under the direction of [Michael Tilson Thomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Tilson_Thomas "Michael Tilson Thomas"), with [George Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Martin "George Martin") producing and [Geoff Emerick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geoff_Emerick "Geoff Emerick") engineering the sessions.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahavishnu_Orchestra#cite_note-Larkin-1) The band was then reduced to a four-piece for 1976's _[Inner Worlds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_Worlds "Inner Worlds")_, with Jean-Luc Ponty leaving after a heated disagreement about writing credits on the _Visions_ album (one of Ponty's compositions, Pegasus, was mistakenly credited to John McLaughlin),[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahavishnu_Orchestra#cite_note-14) and Gayle Moran being replaced with [Stu Goldberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stu_Goldberg "Stu Goldberg"). Ponty would later settle over the royalties for the tracks _Pegasus_ and _Opus 1_ for an undisclosed amount of money. ### 1984–1987: Third incarnation \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mahavishnu_Orchestra&action=edit§ion=4 "Edit section: 1984–1987: Third incarnation")\] After the dissolution of this version of the Orchestra, McLaughlin formed another group called [Shakti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakti_(band) "Shakti (band)") to explore his interest in Indian music;[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahavishnu_Orchestra#cite_note-Larkin-1) following that, he went on to form other bands including the [One Truth Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_Dreams_(John_McLaughlin_album) "Electric Dreams (John McLaughlin album)") and [the Translators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belo_Horizonte_(album) "Belo Horizonte (album)"), and a guitar trio with [Al Di Meola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Di_Meola "Al Di Meola") and flamenco guitarist [Paco de Lucía](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paco_de_Luc%C3%ADa "Paco de Lucía"). In 1984, McLaughlin reformed the Mahavishnu Orchestra with [Bill Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans_(saxophonist) "Bill Evans (saxophonist)") on saxophones, [Jonas Hellborg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonas_Hellborg "Jonas Hellborg") on bass, [Mitchel Forman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitchel_Forman "Mitchel Forman") on keyboards, and original member [Billy Cobham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Cobham "Billy Cobham") on drums. Cobham participated in the sessions for their self-titled 1984 album, but was replaced by [Danny Gottlieb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danny_Gottlieb "Danny Gottlieb") for live work, and [Jim Beard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Beard "Jim Beard") replaced [Mitchel Forman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitchel_Forman "Mitchel Forman") for the latter period of this band's life. This band's overall sound was different from the original Mahavishnu Orchestra, in particular because of McLaughlin's extensive use of the [Synclavier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synclavier "Synclavier") synthesizer system. ### Post-Mahavishnu Orchestra \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mahavishnu_Orchestra&action=edit§ion=5 "Edit section: Post-Mahavishnu Orchestra")\] McLaughlin then worked with a number of incarnations of the John McLaughlin Guitar Trio, all of which featured [Trilok Gurtu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trilok_Gurtu "Trilok Gurtu") on percussion, and, at various times, [Jeff Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Berlin "Jeff Berlin"), [Kai Eckhardt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kai_Eckhardt "Kai Eckhardt"), and [Dominique Di Piazza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominique_Di_Piazza "Dominique Di Piazza") on bass. He then formed the Free Spirits, a guitar, organ and drums trio, with [Joey DeFrancesco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joey_DeFrancesco "Joey DeFrancesco") on Hammond organ and trumpet, and [Dennis Chambers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dennis_Chambers "Dennis Chambers") on drums, as well as touring and recording again with [Al Di Meola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Di_Meola "Al Di Meola") and [Paco de Lucía](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paco_de_Luc%C3%ADa "Paco de Lucía"). [Billy Cobham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Cobham "Billy Cobham") went on to perform as a solo artist, recording many albums including _[Total Eclipse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_Eclipse_(Billy_Cobham_album) "Total Eclipse (Billy Cobham album)")_, _[Crosswinds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crosswinds_(Billy_Cobham_album) "Crosswinds (Billy Cobham album)")_ and _[Spectrum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectrum_(Billy_Cobham_album) "Spectrum (Billy Cobham album)")_, and toured with the "Billy Cobham & [George Duke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Duke "George Duke") Band" for many years. [Jan Hammer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Hammer "Jan Hammer") went on to collaborate with [Jeff Beck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Beck "Jeff Beck") (together with [Narada Michael Walden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Narada_Michael_Walden "Narada Michael Walden")) in Beck's acclaimed album _[Wired](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wired_(Jeff_Beck_album) "Wired (Jeff Beck album)")_ and also recorded a [live album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Beck_with_the_Jan_Hammer_Group_Live "Jeff Beck with the Jan Hammer Group Live") with Beck. He released several solo albums and composed the theme and incidental music for the hit 1980s TV show _[Miami Vice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miami_Vice "Miami Vice")_. [Jerry Goodman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerry_Goodman "Jerry Goodman") recorded the album _[Like Children](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Like_Children "Like Children")_ with Mahavishnu keyboard alumnus Jan Hammer. Starting in 1985 he recorded three solo albums for [Private Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Private_Music_(record_label) "Private Music (record label)") and went on tour with his own band, as well as with [Shadowfax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadowfax_(band) "Shadowfax (band)") and the [Dixie Dregs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dixie_Dregs "Dixie Dregs"). [Rick Laird](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Laird "Rick Laird") played with [Stan Getz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Getz "Stan Getz") and [Chick Corea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chick_Corea "Chick Corea") as well as releasing one solo LP, _Soft Focus_, but retired from the music business in 1982. He worked both as a bass teacher and photographer since then. He died on July 4, 2021, at the age of 80. ## Legacy \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mahavishnu_Orchestra&action=edit§ion=6 "Edit section: Legacy")\] Mahavishnu Orchestra has been cited as an influence on many bands of different genres. [Greg Ginn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greg_Ginn "Greg Ginn"), guitarist and main composer of [hardcore punk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardcore_punk "Hardcore punk") band [Black Flag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Flag_(band) "Black Flag (band)"), cited their early records which inspired him to record more progressive guitar work and even record instrumental albums.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahavishnu_Orchestra#cite_note-15) There has been a resurgence of interest in the Mahavishnu Orchestra in recent years, with bands like [The Mars Volta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Mars_Volta "The Mars Volta"),[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahavishnu_Orchestra#cite_note-16) [Opeth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opeth "Opeth"),[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahavishnu_Orchestra#cite_note-17) [Black Midi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Midi "Black Midi"),[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahavishnu_Orchestra#cite_note-18) [The Fierce and the Dead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fierce_and_the_Dead "The Fierce and the Dead"),[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahavishnu_Orchestra#cite_note-19) and [the Dillinger Escape Plan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Dillinger_Escape_Plan "The Dillinger Escape Plan"),[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahavishnu_Orchestra#cite_note-20) naming them as an influence. Jon Fishman, drummer for Phish, has also cited them as an influence.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahavishnu_Orchestra#cite_note-21) There have been no fewer than five major tribute recordings released. In addition, a book _Power, Passion and Beauty: The Story of the Legendary Mahavishnu Orchestra_ by Walter Kolosky (AbstractLogix Books) has been published. It contains interviews with all of the band's members and quotes obtained specifically for the book from many famous admirers such as [Jeff Beck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Beck "Jeff Beck"), [Pat Metheny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pat_Metheny "Pat Metheny"), the artist [Peter Max](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Max "Peter Max"), [Bill Bruford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Bruford "Bill Bruford") and many more. The Mahavishnu Orchestra have also been sampled in contemporary music, most notably by [Massive Attack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massive_Attack "Massive Attack") on their track " [Unfinished Sympathy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unfinished_Sympathy "Unfinished Sympathy")", which sampled "Planetary Citizen", resulting in the band's being sued by Ralphe Armstrong, who received a healthy out-of-court settlement.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahavishnu_Orchestra#cite_note-22) "You Know, You Know" was sampled on Massive Attack's "One Love" and Mos Def's "Kalifornia." ## Band members \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mahavishnu_Orchestra&action=edit§ion=7 "Edit section: Band members")\] | Image | Name | Years active | Instruments | Release contributions | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cc/John_McLaughlin_Blue_Note_2016.JPG/250px-John_McLaughlin_Blue_Note_2016.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:John_McLaughlin_Blue_Note_2016.JPG) | [John McLaughlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McLaughlin_(musician) "John McLaughlin (musician)") | - 1971–1976

If Wikipedia has given you at least $2.75 worth of knowledge, please give today. Wikipedia is free to use, but not free to provide. An unprecedented rise in hardware costs is making the essential equipment needed to keep Wikipedia available to everyone much more expensive. Your donation helps our nonprofit meet those costs while keeping Wikipedia free and independent. Thank you. - [Dinner Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinner_Party_(Jazz/hip-hop_supergroup) "Dinner Party (Jazz/hip-hop supergroup)") | | | | Website | [kamasiwashington.com](http://kamasiwashington.com/) | Musical artist **Kamasi Tii Washington** (born February 18, 1981) is an American [arranger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arranger "Arranger"), [composer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Composer "Composer") and [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") [saxophonist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxophonist "Saxophonist").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamasi_Washington#cite_note-serrano1-1) He is a founding member of the jazz [collective](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_collective "Musical collective") [West Coast Get Down](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Coast_Get_Down "West Coast Get Down").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamasi_Washington#cite_note-nyt-giant-step-2) ## Career \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kamasi_Washington&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Career")\] Washington was born in 1981 and raised in [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles"), California.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamasi_Washington#cite_note-nyt-giant-step-2)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamasi_Washington#cite_note-3) He is a graduate of the Academy of Music of [Alexander Hamilton High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Hamilton_High_School_(Los_Angeles) "Alexander Hamilton High School (Los Angeles)") in [Beverlywood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beverlywood "Beverlywood"), Los Angeles.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamasi_Washington#cite_note-serrano1-1) Washington next enrolled in [UCLA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UCLA "UCLA")'s Department of [Ethnomusicology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethnomusicology "Ethnomusicology"), where he began playing with faculty members such as [Kenny Burrell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenny_Burrell "Kenny Burrell"), [Gerald Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerald_Wilson "Gerald Wilson"), and [Billy Higgins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Higgins "Billy Higgins"), who mentored a quartet with Washington, pianist Cameron Graves, and the brothers [Stephen ("Thundercat")](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Bruner "Stephen Bruner") and [Ronald Bruner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Bruner_Jr. "Ronald Bruner Jr."). They released their debut album _Young Jazz Giants_ in 2004 on [Birdman Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birdman_Records "Birdman Records").[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamasi_Washington#cite_note-4)[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamasi_Washington#cite_note-allmusic_bio-5) Washington joined the [Gerald Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerald_Wilson "Gerald Wilson") Orchestra for its 2005 album _[In My Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_My_Time_(Gerald_Wilson_album) "In My Time (Gerald Wilson album)")_.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamasi_Washington#cite_note-gerald-6) In 2008 and 2009 "The Kamasi Washington Band" played the outdoor Labor Day Jazz Concert on the Main Green at [Village Green, Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Village_Green,_Los_Angeles "Village Green, Los Angeles").[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamasi_Washington#cite_note-7)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamasi_Washington#cite_note-8) Washington played saxophone on [Kendrick Lamar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kendrick_Lamar "Kendrick Lamar")'s album _[To Pimp a Butterfly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/To_Pimp_a_Butterfly "To Pimp a Butterfly")_,[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamasi_Washington#cite_note-billboard-9) released on March 15, 2015. Washington's debut solo recording, _[The Epic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Epic_(album) "The Epic (album)")_, was released in May 2015.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamasi_Washington#cite_note-pitchfork-10) Washington contributed saxophone on the Thundercat song " [Them Changes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Them_Changes_(Thundercat_song) "Them Changes (Thundercat song)")", which was released on June 18, 2015, as a single from the EP _[The Beyond / Where the Giants Roam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Beyond_/_Where_the_Giants_Roam "The Beyond / Where the Giants Roam")_;[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamasi_Washington#cite_note-11)[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamasi_Washington#cite_note-12) the track was later included on Thundercat's full-length album _[Drunk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drunk_(album) "Drunk (album)")_ (2017). Washington released the mini-album/EP _[Harmony of Difference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmony_of_Difference "Harmony of Difference")_ in September 2017. This was followed by his second full-length studio album, _[Heaven and Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heaven_and_Earth_(Kamasi_Washington_album) "Heaven and Earth (Kamasi Washington album)")_, which was released in June 2018, with a companion EP titled _[The Choice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Choice_(EP) "The Choice (EP)")_ released a week later. [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/24/Kamasi_Washington_Coachella.jpg/250px-Kamasi_Washington_Coachella.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kamasi_Washington_Coachella.jpg) Washington at [Coachella Valley Music and Arts Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coachella_Valley_Music_and_Arts_Festival "Coachella Valley Music and Arts Festival") in 2016 Washington has played along with a diverse group of musicians including [Wayne Shorter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter "Wayne Shorter"), [Herbie Hancock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock "Herbie Hancock"), [Horace Tapscott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Tapscott "Horace Tapscott"), [Lauryn Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lauryn_Hill "Lauryn Hill"), [Nas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nas "Nas"), [Snoop Dogg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snoop_Dogg "Snoop Dogg"),[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamasi_Washington#cite_note-13) [George Duke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Duke "George Duke"), [Chaka Khan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chaka_Khan "Chaka Khan"), [Flying Lotus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flying_Lotus "Flying Lotus"), [Mike Muir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Muir "Mike Muir"), [Francisco Aguabella](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francisco_Aguabella "Francisco Aguabella"), [St. Vincent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Vincent_(musician) "St. Vincent (musician)"), the Pan Afrikaan People's Orchestra, [Run the Jewels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Run_the_Jewels "Run the Jewels") and [Raphael Saadiq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raphael_Saadiq "Raphael Saadiq"). On June 25, 2020, Washington, [Terrace Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terrace_Martin "Terrace Martin"), [Robert Glasper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Glasper "Robert Glasper"), and [9th Wonder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/9th_Wonder "9th Wonder") announced the formation of the supergroup Dinner Party. They released a single, "Freeze Tag", and their debut extended play, _[Dinner Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinner_Party_(EP) "Dinner Party (EP)")_, was released on July 10, 2020.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamasi_Washington#cite_note-14) Washington and members of West Coast Get Down were featured in the final episode of the television series _[Homeland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homeland_(TV_series) "Homeland (TV series)")_ in 2020.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamasi_Washington#cite_note-15) On June 18, 2021, Washington released a new song "Sun Kissed Child" as part of _[The Undefeated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Undefeated_(website) "The Undefeated (website)")_'s _Music for the Movement_ series.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamasi_Washington#cite_note-16) Also in 2021, Washington and his band contributed a cover of the Metallica song "My Friend of Misery" to the charity tribute album _[The Metallica Blacklist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Metallica_Blacklist "The Metallica Blacklist")_.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamasi_Washington#cite_note-17) On July 4, 2024, Kendrick Lamar released the music video for " [Not Like Us](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Not_Like_Us "Not Like Us")". In the video, there was a snippet that played in the beginning of the video (later revealed to be " [Squabble Up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Squabble_Up "Squabble Up")"). In the song, Kendrick mentions Washington in the line "High key; keep a horn on me, that Kamasi". Watanabe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shinichir%C5%8D_Watanabe "Shinichirō Watanabe").[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamasi_Washington#cite_note-auto-18) In 2026, all three collectively won
