(1966) | | _**Ascension**_ is a studio album by the [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") composer and musician [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane"). It was released through [Impulse! Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impulse!_Records "Impulse! Records") in February 1966. It is considered a watershed in Coltrane's work, with the albums recorded before it being more conventional in structure and the albums recorded after it being looser, [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz") inspired works. In addition, it signaled Coltrane's interest in moving away from the quartet format. [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic") called it "the single recording that placed John Coltrane firmly into the avant-garde".[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-allmusic-2) It was recorded at the [Van Gelder Studio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Gelder_Studio "Van Gelder Studio") in June 1965. ## Background At the time of the _Ascension_ recording session, Coltrane was one of the world's most successful jazz artists in both the artistic and commercial sense. His best-selling album _[A Love Supreme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme "A Love Supreme")_[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-3) was nominated for a Grammy Award,[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-4) and was voted "album of the year" by both _[DownBeat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DownBeat "DownBeat")_ and _[Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_Magazine "Jazz Magazine")_ magazines.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-porter262-5) In addition, Coltrane was elected to DownBeat's Hall of Fame, putting him in the company of [Coleman Hawkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coleman_Hawkins "Coleman Hawkins") and [Lester Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lester_Young "Lester Young").[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-porter262-5) At the same time, in the months since _A Love Supreme_ was recorded, Coltrane's music had become increasingly turbulent, moving further in the direction of free jazz.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-6) Coltrane had befriended saxophonist [Albert Ayler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler "Albert Ayler"), and was heavily influenced by his music;[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-7) meanwhile, he had also become somewhat of a father figure for a number of younger avant-garde players, some of whom would appear on _Ascension_.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-8) According to writer Bernard Gendron, "At the height of his career, riding on the momentum of the critical and popular triumph of _A Love Supreme_, Coltrane was the modern jazz star of the 1960s, with a large following of serious jazz fans and great respect from his musician peers. He was in an ideal position to bring into the orbit of the avant-garde fans and musicians who had previously hesitated, been puzzled or mildly hostile."[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-9) ## Additional musicians The musicians that Coltrane chose to supplement the members of the classic quartet were a mix of players ranging from established to relatively unknown, all of whom were younger than Coltrane, and many of whom had played with Coltrane in the years preceding the recording of _Ascension._[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-10) Trumpeter [Freddie Hubbard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freddie_Hubbard "Freddie Hubbard") and bassist [Art Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Davis_(bassist) "Art Davis (bassist)") were well-known and well-recorded by that point, and both had recorded with Coltrane on _[Africa/Brass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africa/Brass "Africa/Brass")_ and _[Olé Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ol%C3%A9_Coltrane "Olé Coltrane")_. (Davis also appeared on _[The John Coltrane Quartet Plays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_John_Coltrane_Quartet_Plays "The John Coltrane Quartet Plays")_, recorded earlier in 1965.) Saxophonist [Archie Shepp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Shepp "Archie Shepp") recorded his first [Impulse!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impulse!_Records "Impulse! Records") album, _[Four for Trane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four_for_Trane "Four for Trane")_, in 1964 after Coltrane recommended him to producer [Bob Thiele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Thiele "Bob Thiele"),[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-house-11)[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-giddins_first_century-12) and went on to release over a dozen albums on the label. Shepp, along with Art Davis, also appeared on an alternate take of the "Acknowledgement" section of _[A Love Supreme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme "A Love Supreme")_, which was released more than thirty years after the appearance of the original recording.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-13)[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-14) Shortly after the recording of _Ascension_, Shepp appeared on _[New Thing at Newport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Thing_at_Newport "New Thing at Newport")_, a split LP with Coltrane's quartet appearing on side one and Shepp's quartet on side two. Shepp also introduced Coltrane to saxophonist [Marion Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marion_Brown "Marion Brown"),[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-15) and Coltrane soon used his influence at [Impulse!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impulse!_Records "Impulse! Records") to help Brown secure the recording date for _[Three for Shepp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_for_Shepp "Three for Shepp")_.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-giddins_first_century-12) Saxophonist [John Tchicai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Tchicai "John Tchicai") had previously recorded with Shepp as part of the [New York Contemporary Five](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Contemporary_Five "New York Contemporary Five") and on _Four for Trane_, and also sat in with Coltrane during one or more performances at the [Half Note](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_Note_Club "Half Note Club").[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-16) Trumpeter [Dewey Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dewey_Johnson_(musician) "Dewey Johnson (musician)") had played with Marion Brown[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-jones-17) and repeatedly sat in with Coltrane's group before being asked to participate in the recording of _Ascension._[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-18) Saxophonist [Pharoah Sanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pharoah_Sanders "Pharoah Sanders") had performed with [Sun Ra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_Ra "Sun Ra"), whose music Coltrane admired, and had also played and practiced yogic breathing exercises with Marion Brown.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-jones-17) In 1964, Coltrane invited Sanders to sit in with his group after hearing his debut recording on the [ESP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESP-Disk "ESP-Disk") label and attending a concert by Sanders's band, which featured [John Hicks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hicks_(pianist) "John Hicks (pianist)"), [Wilbur Ware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilbur_Ware "Wilbur Ware"), and [Billy Higgins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Higgins "Billy Higgins"), at the [Village Gate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Village_Gate "Village Gate").[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-19)[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-20) (Ware and Higgins had both previously recorded with Coltrane.) Sanders was invited to join Coltrane's band in September 1965 and went on to play and record on many of Coltrane's later recordings.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-21)[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-22) In addition, drummer [Rashied Ali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rashied_Ali "Rashied Ali"), who would eventually join Coltrane's group, was invited to participate in the recording of _Ascension,_ but passed up the opportunity, a decision he would soon come to regret.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-23)[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-24) Saxophonist [Frank Wright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Wright_(jazz_musician) "Frank Wright (jazz musician)") was also invited, but reportedly felt that his skills were not up to the demands of the music.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-25) ## Recording session The recording took place, unrehearsed, at [Van Gelder Studio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Gelder_Studio "Van Gelder Studio") in [Englewood Cliffs, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Englewood_Cliffs,_New_Jersey "Englewood Cliffs, New Jersey"), on June 28, 1965.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-house-11) At the start of the session, Coltrane handed out lead sheets.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-26) According to Archie Shepp, "The ensemble passages were based on chords, but these chords were optional... In the solo plus quartet parts there are no specified chords. These sections were to be dialogues between the soloists and the rhythm section."[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-orig_liner-27) Marion Brown added: "Trane had obviously thought a lot about what he wanted to do, but he wrote most of it out in the studio. Then he told everybody what he wanted: He played this line and he said that everybody would play that line in the ensembles. Then he said he wanted crescendi and decrescendi after every solo. We ran through some things together, until we were together, and then we got into it."[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-orig_liner-27) The group recorded two takes of roughly equal duration. These would become known as Edition I and Edition II. At the end of the second take, Elvin Jones "flung his snare at the studio wall, signaling his decision that for him, the date was over."[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-house-11) Marion Brown was more enthusiastic; later he described the session as "wildly exciting", the kind of record "you could use... to heat up the apartment on those cold winter days,"[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-orig_liner-27) and stated that both takes "had that kind of thing in them that makes people scream. The people who were in the studio were screaming. I don't know how the engineers kept the screams out of the record."[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-orig_liner-27) John Tchicai recalled: "It was a feast, incomparable. On the day of the recording, ecstasy and excitement were the prime movers. All of us did our very best to contribute and to carry out the few instructions the Master had given us. It was very African! Our Ancestors were definitely among us more than usual!"[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-penguin-28) Coltrane later stated that, during the session, "I was so doggone busy; I was worried to death... I couldn't really enjoy the \[recording\] date. If it hadn't been a date, then I would have really enjoyed it."[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-ratliff98-29) At some point, he called Albert Ayler and explained: "I recorded an album and found that I was playing just like you", to which Ayler replied: "No, man, don't you see, you were playing like yourself. You were just feeling what I feel and were just crying out for spiritual unity."[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-30) On July28, 1965, Coltrane and his quartet performed a version of _Ascension_ on a concert at the [Salle Pleyel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salle_Pleyel "Salle Pleyel") in Paris. A recording of the performance appears on _[Live in Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live_in_Paris_(John_Coltrane_album) "Live in Paris (John Coltrane album)")_, incorrectly titled "Blue Valse".[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-31) ## Music Coltrane described _Ascension_ in a radio interview as a " [big band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_band "Big band") thing",[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-house-11) although it resembles no big band recording made before it. The most obvious antecedent is [Ornette Coleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman "Ornette Coleman")'s octet (or "double quartet") recording, _[Free Jazz: A Collective Improvisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Jazz:_A_Collective_Improvisation "Free Jazz: A Collective Improvisation")_, which—like _Ascension_—is a continuous 40-minute performance with [ensemble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_ensemble "Musical ensemble") passages and without breaks. However, on _Ascension_ (and unlike on _Free Jazz_), ensemble sections alternate with solos, which take up about equal space. According to Shepp, " _Free Jazz_ created a new form, and _Ascension_ is a further step in the development of that form."[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-orig_liner-27) Shepp also noted the influence of [Sun Ra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_Ra "Sun Ra") and [Cecil Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor "Cecil Taylor") on the recording, and concluded: "The precedent for what John did here goes all the way back to New Orleans... This is like a New Orleans concept, but with 1965 people".[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-orig_liner-27) (Sun Ra's influence on _Ascension_ was also suggested by Coltrane biographer J. C. Thomas,[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-Thomas-32) and by [Val Wilmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Val_Wilmer "Val Wilmer"), who pointed out that Coltrane was exposed to Sun Ra's music through his friendship with [John Gilmore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Gilmore_(musician) "John Gilmore (musician)").[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-33)) Structurally, _Ascension_ is organized around a succession of modes that serve as starting points for the musicians. Ekkehard Jost identified three modes: B♭ Aeolian, D Phrygian, and F Phrygian,[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-34) while David Such added a fourth, G♭ Lydian.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-35) Changes of mode were signalled by Coltrane, Hubbard, and Tyner.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-36) The melodic germ of _Ascension_ is a short motif that resembles the main theme of _A Love Supreme'_ s "Acknowledgment" section; however, this motif is secondary in importance to the presence of descending lines that serve to define and articulate the modes.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-jost89-37) Jost noted that, in contrast with _Free Jazz_, "the central idea is not to produce a network of interwoven independent melodic lines, but dense sound complexes."[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-jost89-37) He explained: "a large number of rhythmically independent lines are set against one another by seven wind instruments, with the resultant overlappings. This superimposition produces rapidly moving sound-fields whose rhythmic differentiation is provided as a rule by the rhythm section, rather than coming from within. When seven independent melodic-rhythmic lines coincide, the relationships between them lose clarity, fusing into a field of sound enlivened by irregular accentuations."[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-jost89-37) Jost summarized this as follows: "A new type of group improvisation emerges in which melodic-motivic evolution gives way to the moulding of a total sound.… the macro-structures of the total sound are more important than the micro-structure of the parts."[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-38) Similarly, Such wrote: "The overall texture in the collectively improvised sections of _Ascension_ is extremely dense. As a result, the listener has difficulty separating the individual lines of the seven improvisers. In comparison, the three lead soloists in Coleman's _Free Jazz_ remain distinguishable."[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-39) Shepp's comments are in agreement: "The emphasis was on textures rather than the making of an organizational entity. There was unity, but it was a unity of sounds and textures rather than like an ABA approach. You can hear...a reaching for sound and an exploration of the possibilities of sound."[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-orig_liner-27) [Ben Ratliff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Ratliff "Ben Ratliff") called _Ascension_ "the first major piece of work from the jazz avant-garde to valorize the idea not only of sheer volume but of _texture_ in jazz-group interaction",[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-ratliff98-29) and noted that "immediately thereafter, the idea of texture would become very basic to experimental jazz."[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-ratliff98-29) With regard to the solo sections, Jost also differentiated between players like Tchicai, who tended to organize their solos motivically, as opposed to "sound" players like Sanders and Shepp, who tended to use extended techniques in an expressive way.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-40) According to Jost, Coltrane's solo is a synthesis of the two approaches: "Into a context that is melodic-motivic, all possibilities of tone coloration are incorporated, partly as a constructive device—when they serve as a means of formal articulation—and partly to provide for emotional intensification".[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-41) Shepp pointed out that Coltrane "didn't want any stars on this record" and noted that "he took no more solo time than anybody else".[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-orig_liner-27) Such also commented that "the roles among performers in _Ascension_ are minimally differentiated",[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-such123-42) and wrote that this approach "enables soloists and improvisers to fuse their emotions and personalities more effectively".[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-such123-42) Similarly, writer Tony Whyton stated that "Although this type of nonhierarchical experiment is typical of several collective practices in the 1960s, the role that Coltrane fulfils within the sound world of _Ascension_ is diametrically opposed to canonical aesthetics, where the iconic genius is presented as the center of creativity and performance practice,"[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-whyton79-43) and noted that "Coltrane's involvement in the creation of an ensemble sound is somewhat antithetical to the album's cover design, which shows the artist seated alone in quiet contemplation".[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-whyton79-43) Ben Ratliff wrote that the album suggested "the notion of the jazz band as community, a collective effort to make large-scale textural music rather than an exclusive, carefully structured machine",[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-ratliff97-44) and offered these comments: "Within the individual group, the leader-with-sidemen idea seemed suddenly old; a freer and more simultaneous notion of group playing was moving in. Jazz had never been less hierarchical. The spirit of musicians' collectives was making obsolete the old story of band-versus-band competition... If there is any truth to the rumors that Coltrane was taking acid between '64 and '67, it would only amount to more similar evidence. | Professional ratings Reaction to _Ascension_ was swift and generally intense. ABC executive Alan Bergman recalled receiving an advance copy of the album prior to its release; he stated: "I listened to about five minutes... I walked into Bob Thiele's office and I can see myself holding this thing up with my mouth open. He says, 'I know, I know'... He says, 'It's going to be a classic!'"[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-house-11) Since its release, the album has been portrayed as a turning point in the history of jazz. According to [Dave Liebman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Liebman "Dave Liebman"), the album "blew everybody out of the water",[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-kahnals-51) and was "the torch that lit the free-jazz thing. I mean, it really begins with Cecil \[Taylor\] and Ornette \[Coleman\] in '59, but _Ascension_ was like the patron saint saying, 'It's OK—this is valid.' I think that even had much more of an effect on everybody than _A Love Supreme_."[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-kahnals-51) [George Russell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Russell_(composer) "George Russell (composer)") stated that the recording of _Ascension_ was "when Coltrane turned his back on the money."[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-nis-52) Coltrane biographer [Eric Nisenson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Nisenson "Eric Nisenson") wrote that the album "signaled Coltrane's full embrace of the New Thing and its players", and that, with the album, "he finally became a full-fledged member of the free jazz avant-garde, with no turning back."[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-nis-52) A review by [Wilfrid Mellers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilfrid_Mellers "Wilfrid Mellers") shortly after the album's release called the album "the most impressive example of 'free jazz' that has come my way. Its relationship both to jazz tradition and also to developments in avant-garde music from [Varèse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edgard_Var%C3%A8se "Edgard Varèse") to [Cage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Cage "John Cage")'s wilder disciples is clear..."[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-53) In a review for DownBeat, Bill Mathieu called _Ascension_ "possibly the most powerful human sound ever recorded".[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-54) Others were less positive. Saxophonist [Frank Foster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Foster_(jazz_musician) "Frank Foster (jazz musician)") stated: "The main complaint came after the album _Ascension_. That was the turning point for some musicians who had been Coltrane enthusiasts up to that time; after that they turned off. I thought it was a little extreme, but he was always my man."[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-kahnals-51) Violinist [Leroy Jenkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leroy_Jenkins_(jazz_musician) "Leroy Jenkins (jazz musician)") recalled having heard Coltrane's group at around the time _Ascension_ was recorded, and recalled: "They were playing this music, screaming and ranting and raving, and, Lord - I was so _drug_. I said 'What?'... I _dug_ Coltrane but I didn't know what was happening."[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-55) Audiences began walking out of his concerts, as they did in August 1965, at Soldier Field in Chicago following the album's recording but prior to its release.[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-56) More recent reviews have been positive overall. In 1998, [Gary Giddins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Giddins "Gary Giddins") wrote: "After nearly thirty-five years, it is still impossible to speak of _Ascension_ without a word of caution. It is the single most vexatious work in jazz history. So, a word of caution: It can't hurt you. In fact, contrary to its reputation as the apogee in '60s free-jazz rants, the piece goes down as smooth as bourbon, at least after you've heard it a few times and can no longer be intimidated by its shock tactics... Coming to the end of the music's long night, you may blink at the silence in stunned relief and inscrutable rapture. Or you may not. In any case, return visits to _Ascension_ reveal it as decreasingly monolithic. Fake notes—cackles and hollers and shrieks and squawks—are still notes, and fortuitous harmonies and melodies, forged in the cauldron of chance, will on repeated exposure seem as preordained as composed music."[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-57) In a review for [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic"), Sam Samuelson awarded the album five stars, and wrote: "this can be a difficult listen at first, but with a patient ear and an appreciation for the finer things in life, the reward is a greater understanding of the personal path that the artist was on at that particular time in his development."[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-allmusic-2) Writing for _[All About Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_About_Jazz "All About Jazz")_, Derek Taylor admitted that his initial encounters with _Ascension_ were difficult, but "like anything worth investigating the logic and effulgence of this work eventually started to reveal itself with repeated listenings. In the intervening years the elements I first mistook for anger and discord have exposed themselves as those of spirituality and unification. This is music that emancipates both players and listeners- it challenges at the same time it educates."[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-58) Chris Baber, in a review for Jazz Views, called the album "one of the most significant recordings in the canon of what people might call 'free-jazz'", and wrote: "it begins by shaking any preconceptions from you and pinning you back so that you are ready to follow the logic and coherence of the piece as it unfolds. After a total immersion in the piece, you emerge, perhaps cleansed, perhaps relaxed, but definitely changed to the way you were before the piece began." He concluded: "there is a strong case to be made that _Ascension_ is Coltrane’s best, most coherent and clearest statement of what he felt music should be for and what it could achieve."[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-59) The authors of the Penguin Jazz Guide wrote: "There is nothing else like _Ascension_ in Coltrane's work; indeed, there is nothing quite like _Ascension_ in the history of jazz... It is a work that synthesizes the rules of classic jazz with the freedoms of the New Thing. Its success is difficult to gauge; its impact is total, overwhelming. Only slowly has it been recognized, not just as an iconic record, but a great composition." Regarding the two Editions, they commented: "After a time, they resemble a rock formation seen from a subtly different angle, but still unmistakably the same grand and forbidding outcrop."[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-penguin-28) ## Influence and legacy A number of younger musicians found inspiration in _Ascension_. [Peter Brötzmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Br%C3%B6tzmann "Peter Brötzmann")'s _[Machine Gun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machine_Gun_(Peter_Br%C3%B6tzmann_album) "Machine Gun (Peter Brötzmann album)")_, recorded in 1968, was heavily influenced by the album.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-ratliff97-44) [Glenn Branca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenn_Branca "Glenn Branca") intended his 1981 album _[The Ascension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ascension_(Glenn_Branca_album) "The Ascension (Glenn Branca album)")_ to be a continuation of Coltrane's album, as well as [Olivier Messiaen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olivier_Messiaen "Olivier Messiaen")'s _[L'ascension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L'ascension "L'ascension")._[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-60) The music produced by the members of the [Association for the Advancement of Creative Musicians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Creative_Musicians "Association for the Advancement of Creative Musicians") was frequently the result of an emphasis on a collective approach to the creation of unique textures, often using non-traditional instruments.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-ratliff98-29) The [Rova Saxophone Quartet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rova_Saxophone_Quartet "Rova Saxophone Quartet") has repeatedly explored _Ascension_, recording interpretations of the work on _John Coltrane's Ascension_ (Black Saint, 1997), _[Electric Ascension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_Ascension "Electric Ascension")_ (Atavistic, 2005), and _Rova Channeling Coltrane Electric Ascension_ ( [RogueArt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RogueArt "RogueArt"), 2016). In 2007, 2008, 2010, and 2012, saxophonist Jeremy Strachan organized performances of the work, and documented the experience in an essay.[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-61) In 2018, the new music group wild Up presented a concert titled "Of Ascension" featuring a set of compositions inspired by _Ascension_.[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-62) During their 1985 United States tour, the band [Minutemen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minutemen_(band) "Minutemen (band)") played a tape of _Ascension_ in its entirety for their audiences prior to their live sets.[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-63) ## Track listing / order of soloists and ensembles Two takes were made of "Ascension" during the recording session on June 28, 1965. The second take was released on the album that is now known as _Ascension (Edition I)_. Some months after its release, Coltrane expressed a preference for the first take, so _Ascension (Edition II)_ was created using the first take. Impulse! used the same artwork and catalog number A-95 for both editions, but inscribed "EDITION II" on the vinyl runout circle of that edition.[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-64) Both editions are available on the single-CD version released by Impulse!/Verve/Universal in 2000, and were previously available on the 1992 double-disc collection _[The Major Works of John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Major_Works_of_John_Coltrane "The Major Works of John Coltrane")_ on Impulse!/GRP/MCA.[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-65) The [solo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solo_(music) "Solo (music)") order differs slightly between the takes; [Elvin Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elvin_Jones "Elvin Jones") does not solo in Edition II. | | | | --- | --- | | Ascension (Edition II) (John Coltrane)

| Professional ratings _**Meditations**_ is a 1966 album by [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane"). The album was considered the "spiritual follow-up to _[A Love Supreme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme "A Love Supreme")_."[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meditations_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-7) It features Coltrane and [Pharoah Sanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pharoah_Sanders "Pharoah Sanders") as [soloists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solo_(music) "Solo (music)"), both playing [tenor saxophones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenor_saxophone "Tenor saxophone"). This was the last Coltrane recording to feature his classic quartet lineup of himself, bassist [Jimmy Garrison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Garrison "Jimmy Garrison"), drummer [Elvin Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elvin_Jones "Elvin Jones") and pianist [McCoy Tyner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCoy_Tyner "McCoy Tyner") (augmented here as a sextet with Sanders and second drummer [Rashied Ali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rashied_Ali "Rashied Ali")), as both Jones and Tyner would quit the band by early 1966. Sanders, Ali, Garrison and Coltrane's wife [Alice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alice_Coltrane "Alice Coltrane") would comprise his next group. Alternative versions of tracks 2–5 had been recorded in September 1965 by the same musicians minus [Rashied Ali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rashied_Ali "Rashied Ali") and Sanders. (1965) | | _**A Love Supreme**_ is an album by the American [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") saxophonist and composer [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane"). It was recorded in one session on December 9, 1964, at [Van Gelder Studio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Gelder_Studio "Van Gelder Studio") in [Englewood Cliffs, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Englewood_Cliffs,_New_Jersey "Englewood Cliffs, New Jersey"), with a quartet featuring pianist [McCoy Tyner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCoy_Tyner "McCoy Tyner"), bassist [Jimmy Garrison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Garrison "Jimmy Garrison"), and drummer [Elvin Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elvin_Jones "Elvin Jones"). _A Love Supreme_ was released by [Impulse! Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impulse!_Records "Impulse! Records") in January 1965. Referred to as the saxophonist's "definitive tone poem", it ranks among Coltrane's best-selling albums and is widely considered one of the greatest masterpieces in the history of jazz and one of the greatest albums ever made.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme#cite_note-:0-2) It was nominated for the 1966 [Grammy Award for Best Jazz Instrumental Album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Jazz_Instrumental_Album "Grammy Award for Best Jazz Instrumental Album"). ## Composition _A Love Supreme_ is a [through-composed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Through-composed_music "Through-composed music")[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme#cite_note-xgau-3) [suite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suite_(music) "Suite (music)")[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme#cite_note-nyt-4) in four parts: "Acknowledgement" (which includes the oral chant that gives the album its name), "Resolution", "Pursuance", and "Psalm". Coltrane plays [tenor saxophone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenor_saxophone "Tenor saxophone") on all parts. One critic has written that the album was intended to represent a struggle for purity, an expression of gratitude, and an acknowledgement that the musician's talent comes from a higher power.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme#cite_note-kahn-5) The album's improvisational and spiritual intensity has led some to liken it to [glossolalia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speaking_in_tongues "Speaking in tongues"), or speaking in tongues, as it conveys a profound sense of ecstatic devotion.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme#cite_note-6) This sacred quality has led it to become the "central text" of the [Saint John Coltrane African Orthodox Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_John_Coltrane_African_Orthodox_Church "Saint John Coltrane African Orthodox Church") in San Francisco.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme#cite_note-7) [Coltrane's home](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane_Home "John Coltrane Home") in [Dix Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dix_Hills,_New_York "Dix Hills, New York"), Long Island, may have inspired the album.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme#cite_note-kahn-5) Another influence may have been [Ahmadiyya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmadiyya "Ahmadiyya") Islam.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme#cite_note-HammerSafi2013-8) [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/97/A_Love_Supreme.jpg/500px-A_Love_Supreme.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:A_Love_Supreme.jpg) Coltrane's handwritten notes for _A Love Supreme_ According to assistant music editor at _[Time Out](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_Out_(magazine) "Time Out (magazine)")_ John Lewis, the album "pulls off the rare trick of being utterly uncompromising yet completely accessible."[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme#cite_note-:0-2) [![Elvin Jones in a black suit performing behind a drum kit](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/50/Elvin_Jones_3.jpg/500px-Elvin_Jones_3.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Elvin_Jones_3.jpg) [Elvin Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elvin_Jones "Elvin Jones") (pictured in 1976) The album begins with the bang of a gong ( [tam-tam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tam-tam "Tam-tam")) and cymbal washes on the first track, "Acknowledgement". [Jimmy Garrison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Garrison "Jimmy Garrison") enters on double bass with the four-note motif that lays the foundation of the movement. Coltrane begins a solo. He plays variations on the motif until he repeats the four notes thirty-six times. The motif then becomes the vocal chant "a love supreme", sung by Coltrane accompanying himself through overdubs nineteen times.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme#cite_note-9) According to _[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone "Rolling Stone")_, this movement's four-note theme is "the humble foundation of the suite".[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme#cite_note-RS500-10) ![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cb/Gnome-mime-audio-openclipart.svg/120px-Gnome-mime-audio-openclipart.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail) ["Part 1: Acknowledgement"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:John_Coltrane_-_Acknowledgement.ogg "File:John Coltrane - Acknowledgement.ogg") The first 30 seconds of "Part 1: Acknowledgement", the first track on _A Love Supreme_ * * * _Problems playing this file? See [media help](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Media "Help:Media")._ In the fourth and final movement, "Psalm", Coltrane performs what he calls a "musical narration". [Lewis Porter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewis_Porter "Lewis Porter") calls it a "wordless recitation".[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme#cite_note-11) The devotional is included in the [liner notes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liner_notes "Liner notes"). Coltrane "plays" the words of the poem on saxophone but doesn't speak them. Some scholars have suggested that this performance is an homage to the [sermons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sermon "Sermon") of [African-American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Americans "African Americans") preachers.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme#cite_note-12) The poem (and, in his own way, Coltrane's solo) ends with the cry, "Elation. Elegance. Exaltation. All from God. Thank you God. Amen."[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme#cite_note-13) _A Love Supreme_ was categorized by _[Rockdelux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rockdelux "Rockdelux")_ as [modal jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz "Modal jazz"), [avant-garde jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde_jazz "Avant-garde jazz"), [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz"), [hard bop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop "Hard bop"), and [post-bop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-bop "Post-bop").[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme#cite_note-14) ## Other performances Two alternative versions of "Acknowledgement" were recorded the next day, on December 10, with tenor saxophonist [Archie Shepp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Shepp "Archie Shepp") and a second bassist, [Art Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Davis_(bassist) "Art Davis (bassist)"). These versions omit Coltrane chanting "a love supreme"; he preferred the quartet version with the chant, placing that on the issued album. There are two known live recordings of the "Love Supreme" suite. For years the only known live recording of the "Love Supreme" suite was of a performance at the Festival Mondial du Jazz Antibes in [Juan-les-Pins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan-les-Pins "Juan-les-Pins"), France, on July 26, 1965. On October 29, 2002, the album was reissued as a remastered deluxe edition by [Impulse! Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impulse!_Records "Impulse! Records") with this live performance and the alternate takes on a [bonus disc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bonus_disc "Bonus disc").[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme#cite_note-15) A further iteration with more studio breakdowns and overdubs was issued as a three-disc complete masters edition released by Impulse! on November 20, 2015.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme#cite_note-16) The other known live recording of the suite was recorded October 2, 1965, at [The Penthouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Penthouse_(Seattle) "The Penthouse (Seattle)") in Seattle. The set was recorded by saxophonist [Joe Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Brazil "Joe Brazil"). This live performance was released on October 22, 2021, by Impulse! as _[A Love Supreme: Live in Seattle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme:_Live_in_Seattle "A Love Supreme: Live in professional ratings _A Love Supreme_ was widely recognized as a work of deep spirituality and analyzed with religious subtext, although cultural studies scholars Richard W. Santana and Gregory Erickson argued that the "avant-garde jazz suite" could be interpreted otherwise.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme#cite_note-34) According to music professor [Ingrid Monson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ingrid_Monson "Ingrid Monson") of [Harvard University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_University "Harvard University"), the album was an exemplary recording of [modal jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz "Modal jazz").[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme#cite_note-35) Nick Dedina wrote on the [Rhapsody](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhapsody_(online_music_service) "Rhapsody (online music service)") website that the music ranged from [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz") and [hard bop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop "Hard bop") to _sui generis_ [gospel music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gospel_music "Gospel music") in "an epic aural poem to man's place in God's plan".[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme#cite_note-36) Calling it a "legendary album-long hymn of praise", _[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone "Rolling Stone")_ said that "Coltrane's majestic, often violent blowing (famously described as 'sheets of sound') is never self-aggrandizing" and that he is "aloft with his classic quartet", "soar\[ing\] with nothing but gratitude and joy" on a compelling journey for listeners.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme#cite_note-RS500-10) _[The Rolling Stone Jazz Record Guide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rolling_Stone_Jazz_Record_Guide "The Rolling Stone Jazz Record Guide")_ (1985) said that "each man performs with eloquence and economy", while calling the album "the masterpiece from the quartet's studio work", "the first comprehensive statement of Coltrane's spiritual concerns", and "the cornerstone of many Coltrane collections".[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme#cite_note-RSJRG-37) On the other hand, jazz critic [Tom Hull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Hull_(critic) "Tom Hull (critic)") said that he has not much considered the album "spiritual" but rather "the most perfectly plotted single piece of jazz ever recorded".[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme#cite_note-Hull-33) _A Love Supreme_ has appeared on professional listings of the greatest albums. In 2003, it was ranked number 47 on _[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone "Rolling Stone")_'s list of [the 500 greatest albums of all time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone's_500_Greatest_Albums_of_All_Time "Rolling Stone's 500 Greatest Albums of All Time");[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme#cite_note-RS500-10) maintaining the rating in a 2012 revised list,[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme#cite_note-38) it was re-ranked at number 66 in a 2020 reboot of the list.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme#cite_note-39) _[NME](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NME "NME")_ ranked it number 188 on [a similar list](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NME's_The_500_Greatest_Albums_of_All_Time "NME's The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time") in 2013.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme#cite_note-40) It was included in Robert Dimery's _[1001 Albums You Must Hear Before You Die](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1001_Albums_You_Must_Hear_Before_You_Die "1001 Albums You Must Hear Before You Die")_.[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme#cite_note-Dimery-41) It was voted number 85 in the third edition of [Colin Larkin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colin_Larkin "Colin Larkin")'s _[All Time Top 1000 Albums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_Time_Top_1000_Albums "All Time Top 1000 Albums")_ (2000).[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme#cite_note-Larkin-42) According to [Joachim-Ernst Berendt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joachim-Ernst_Berendt "Joachim-Ernst Berendt"), the album's hymn-like quality permeated modern jazz and rock music.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme#cite_note-43) As Christgau explains, the record was "adored by American hippies from [the Byrds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Byrds "The Byrds") and [Carlos Santana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Santana "Carlos Santana") on down, and served as theme music to [Lester Bangs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lester_Bangs "Lester Bangs")'s wake at [CBGB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBGB "CBGB")".[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme#cite_note-xgau-3) In _[The Penguin Guide to Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Penguin_Guide_to_Jazz "The Penguin Guide to Jazz")_, [Richard Cook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Cook_(journalist) "Richard Cook (journalist)") and [Brian Morton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Morton_(Scottish_writer) "Brian Morton (Scottish writer)") gave _A Love Supreme_ a rare "crown" rating but asked whether it was "the greatest jazz album of the modern period... or the most overrated?" [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis"), Coltrane's former bandleader, said the record "reached out and influenced those people who were into peace. Hippies and people like that". Christgau, writing in 2020, said, "it's meditative rather than freewheeling, with each member of his classic quartet instructed to embark on his own harmonically mapped excursion and the title set to a chanted four-note melody you could hum in your sleep. I'm on my fourth consecutive play with no signs of tune fatigue as I write, plus my wife loves it. All true, all remarkable. But how much you value it, I expect, depends on how much faith you place in your own spirituality." He concluded that the next time he will listen to the album "may well depend on who dies when".[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme#cite_note-xgau-3) In June 2026, [CBS News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBS_News "CBS News") included _A Love Supreme, Pt. I – Acknowledgement_ in its list of the 250 essential American songs of the past 250 years.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme#cite_note-44) ## Legacy [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0a/Carlos_Santana-2_1978_by_Chris_Hakkens.jpg/500px-Carlos_Santana-2_1978_by_Chris_Hakkens.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Carlos_Santana-2_1978_by_Chris_Hakkens.jpg) [Carlos Santana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Santana "Carlos Santana") (1978), one of many rock musicians to have been deeply influenced by the album Musicians such as [Joshua Redman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Redman "Joshua Redman")[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme#cite_note-45) and [U2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U2 "U2"),[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme#cite_note-46) who mention the album in their song " [Angel of Harlem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angel_of_Harlem "Angel of Harlem")",[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme#cite_note-47) have mentioned the influence of the album on their own work. Guitarists [Carlos Santana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Santana "Carlos Santana") and [John McLaughlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McLaughlin_(musician) "John McLaughlin (musician)") called the album one of their biggest early influences, and they teamed up to record _[Love Devotion Surrender](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love_Devotion_Surrender "Love Devotion Surrender")_ in 1973 as a tribute.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme#cite_note-48) "Every so often this ceases to be a jazz record and is more avant-garde contemporary classical", said [Neil Hannon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Hannon "Neil Hannon") of the band [the Divine Comedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Divine_Comedy_(band) "The Divine Comedy (band)"). "I love the combination of abstract piano that's all sort of 'clang', and weird chords with wailing saxophone over the top."[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme#cite_note-Thornton-49) The American singer [Will Downing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Will_Downing "Will Downing")'s debut single, "A Love Supreme", (1988) was inspired by the vocal section at the end of "A Love Supreme, Pt. I - Acknowledgement". The single reached number 4 on the US Dance chart, number 77 on the US R&B chart, and number 14 in the UK.[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme#cite_note-50) The manuscript for the album was included in the [National Museum of American History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_American_History "National Museum of American History")'s "Treasures of American History" collection at the [Smithsonian Institution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_Institution "Smithsonian Institution").[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme#cite_note-NMAH-51) In 2015, the album was selected for preservation in the [National Recording Registry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Recording_Registry "National Recording Registry") due to its "cultural, historic, or artistic significance."[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme#cite_note-52) It is Coltrane's second album to be included after _[Giant Steps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giant_Steps "Giant Steps")_ in 2005.[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme#cite_note-2nd-53) ## Track listing All tracks are composed by John Coltrane and published by Jowcol Music ( [BMI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadcast_Music,_Inc. - Elliot Ngubone | | | | Website | [www.artensembleofchicago.com](http://www.artensembleofchicago.com/) | The **Art Ensemble of Chicago** is an [avant-garde jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde_jazz "Avant-garde jazz") group that grew out of the Association for the Advancement of Creative Musicians ( [AACM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Creative_Musicians "Association for the Advancement of Creative Musicians")) in the late 1960s.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Ensemble_of_Chicago#cite_note-RCJE-1) The ensemble integrates many jazz styles and plays many instruments, including "little instruments": bells, bicycle horns, birthday party noisemakers, wind chimes, and various forms of percussion. The musicians would wear costumes and face paint while performing. These characteristics combined to make the ensemble's performances both aural and visual. While playing in Europe in 1969, five hundred instruments were used.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Ensemble_of_Chicago#cite_note-2) ## History Members of what was to become the Art Ensemble performed together under various band names in the mid-sixties, as members of the [Association for the Advancement of Creative Musicians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Creative_Musicians "Association for the Advancement of Creative Musicians") (AACM). They performed on the 1966 album _[Sound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sound_(Roscoe_Mitchell_album) "Sound (Roscoe Mitchell album)"),_ as the [Roscoe Mitchell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roscoe_Mitchell "Roscoe Mitchell") Sextet. The Sextet included saxophonist Roscoe Mitchell, trumpeter [Lester Bowie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lester_Bowie "Lester Bowie"), and bassist [Malachi Favors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malachi_Favors "Malachi Favors"). For the next year, they played as the Roscoe Mitchell Art Ensemble. In 1967, they were joined by fellow AACM members [Joseph Jarman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Jarman "Joseph Jarman") (saxophone) and [Phillip Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phillip_Wilson_(drummer) "Phillip Wilson (drummer)") (drums) and recorded for [Nessa Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nessa_Records "Nessa Records"). All of the musicians were multi-instrumentalists. Jarman and Mitchell's primary instruments were [alto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alto_saxophone "Alto saxophone") and [tenor saxophone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenor_saxophone "Tenor saxophone"), respectively. Additionally, they both played other saxophones ranging from the small [sopranino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sopranino_saxophone "Sopranino saxophone") to the large [bass saxophone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bass_saxophone "Bass saxophone"), as well as the flute and clarinet. In addition to trumpet, Bowie played [flugelhorn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flugelhorn "Flugelhorn"), [cornet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornet "Cornet"), [shofar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shofar "Shofar"), and [conch shells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conch_shell "Conch shell"). Favors added touches of banjo and bass guitar. Most of them dabbled in piano, [synthesizer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synthesizer "Synthesizer"), and other keyboards, and they all played percussion instruments. They were known for wearing costumes and makeup on stage. Member [Joseph Jarman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Jarman "Joseph Jarman") described part of their style: > So what we were doing with that face painting was representing everyone throughout the universe, and that was expressed in the music as well. That's why the music was so interesting. It wasn't limited to Western instruments, African instruments, or Asian instruments, or South American instruments, or anybody's instruments.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Ensemble_of_Chicago#cite_note-3) In 1967, Wilson left the group to join [Paul Butterfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Butterfield "Paul Butterfield")'s band, and for a period the group was a quartet without a full-time drummer. [Jarman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jarman "Jarman") and [Mitchell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roscoe_Mitchell "Roscoe Mitchell") served as artistic directors at the [cooperative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooperative "Cooperative") summer camp [Circle Pines Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circle_Pines_Center?action=edit&redlink=1 "Circle Pines Center") in [Delton, Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delton,_Michigan "Delton, Michigan"), in August 1968, during the same week that the Democratic Convention was in Chicago. After a farewell concert at the Unitarian Church in [Evanston, Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evanston,_Illinois "Evanston, Illinois"), in fall, 1968, the remaining group traveled to Paris.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Ensemble_of_Chicago#cite_note-Wilmer,_Valerie_1977_122%E2%80%93123-4) In Paris, the ensemble was based at the Théâtre du Vieux Colombier.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Ensemble_of_Chicago#cite_note-Jost,_Ekkehard_1975_167-5)[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Ensemble_of_Chicago#cite_note-Wilmer,_Valerie_1977_122%E2%80%93123-4) In France, they became known as the Art Ensemble of Chicago. The impetus for the name change came from a French promoter who added "of Chicago" to their name for descriptive purposes. The new name stuck because band members felt that it better reflected the cooperative nature of the group. In Paris, the ensemble was based at the Théâtre du Vieux Colombier [\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Ensemble_of_Chicago#cite_note-Jost,_Ekkehard_1975_167-5) and they recorded for the [Freedom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_Records_(jazz_label) "Freedom Records (jazz label)") and [BYG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BYG_Actuel "BYG Actuel") labels. They also recorded _[Comme à la radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comme_%C3%A0_la_radio "Comme à la radio")_ with [Brigitte Fontaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigitte_Fontaine "Brigitte Fontaine") and [Areski Belkacem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Areski_Belkacem "Areski Belkacem") but without a drummer until percussionist [Don Moye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Moye "Don Moye") became a member of the group in 1970. During that year, they recorded the albums _[Art Ensemble of Chicago with Fontella Bass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Ensemble_of_Chicago_with_Fontella_Bass "Art Ensemble of Chicago with Fontella Bass")_ and _[Les Stances a Sophie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Les_Stances_a_Sophie "Les Stances a Sophie")_ with singer [Fontella Bass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fontella_Bass "Fontella Bass"), who was Lester Bowie's wife. The latter was the soundtrack to the French movie of the same title.
