- Uruguay | **Latin jazz** is a genre of [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") with [Latin American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_America "Latin America") rhythms. The two main categories are [Afro-Cuban jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afro-Cuban_jazz "Afro-Cuban jazz"), rhythmically based on Cuban popular dance music, with a rhythm section employing [ostinato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ostinato "Ostinato") patterns or a [clave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clave_(rhythm) "Clave (rhythm)"), and Afro-Brazilian jazz, which includes [samba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samba "Samba") and [bossa nova](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bossa_nova "Bossa nova"). ## Afro-Cuban jazz \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Latin_jazz&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Afro-Cuban jazz")\] Main article: [Afro-Cuban jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afro-Cuban_jazz "Afro-Cuban jazz") ### "Spanish tinge"—The Cuban influence in early jazz and proto-Latin jazz \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Latin_jazz&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: \"Spanish tinge\"—The Cuban influence in early jazz and proto-Latin jazz")\] [African American music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_American_music "African American music") began incorporating [Afro-Cuban](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afro-Cuban "Afro-Cuban") musical motifs in the 19th century, when the [habanera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habanera_(music) "Habanera (music)") (Cuban [contradanza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contradanza "Contradanza")) gained international popularity. The habanera was the first written music to be rhythmically based on an African motif. The _habanera rhythm_ (also known as _congo_,[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_jazz#cite_note-1) _tango-congo_,[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_jazz#cite_note-2) or _[tango](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tango_(music) "Tango (music)")_[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_jazz#cite_note-3)) can be thought of as a combination of [tresillo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tresillo_(rhythm) "Tresillo (rhythm)") and the [backbeat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#Backbeat "Beat (music)"). [Wynton Marsalis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wynton_Marsalis "Wynton Marsalis") considers [tresillo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tresillo_(rhythm) "Tresillo (rhythm)") to be the New Orleans "clave," although technically, the pattern is only half a [clave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clave_(rhythm) "Clave (rhythm)").[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_jazz#cite_note-4) [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/26/Tresillo_divisive.png/250px-Tresillo_divisive.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tresillo_divisive.png) Tresillo [Play](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/8/8c/Tresillo_divisive.mid/Tresillo_divisive.mid.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tresillo_divisive.mid "File:Tresillo divisive.mid")[![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/f2/Basic_habanera_rhythm%2C_Orovio_1981_237.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Basic_habanera_rhythm,_Orovio_1981_237.png) Habanera rhythm[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_jazz#cite_note-5) " [St. Louis Blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Louis_Blues_(song) "St. Louis Blues (song)")" (1914) by [W. C. Handy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W._C._Handy "W. C. Handy") has a habanera-tresillo bass line. Handy noted a reaction to the habanera rhythm included in Will H. Tyler's "Maori": "I observed that there was a sudden, proud and graceful reaction to the rhythm...White dancers, as I had observed them, took the number in stride. I began to suspect that there was something Negroid in that beat." After noting a similar reaction to the same rhythm in "La Paloma", Handy included this rhythm in his "St. Louis Blues", the instrumental copy of "Memphis Blues", the chorus of "Beale Street Blues", and other compositions.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_jazz#cite_note-autogenerated2-6) [Jelly Roll Morton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jelly_Roll_Morton "Jelly Roll Morton") considered the tresillo-habanera (which he called the [Spanish tinge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_tinge "Spanish tinge")) to be an essential ingredient of jazz.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_jazz#cite_note-7) The habanera rhythm can be heard in his left hand on songs like "The Crave" (1910, recorded 1938). > Now in one of my earliest tunes, "New Orleans Blues," you can notice the Spanish tinge. In fact, if you can't manage to put tinges of Spanish in your tunes, you will never be able to get the right seasoning, I call it, for jazz—Morton (1938: Library of Congress Recording).[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_jazz#cite_note-8) [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/35/MortonBricktopRowCropMortonFace.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:MortonBricktopRowCropMortonFace.jpg) Jelly Roll Morton Although the exact origins of jazz syncopation may never be known, there is evidence that the habanera-tresillo was there at its conception. [Buddy Bolden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddy_Bolden "Buddy Bolden"), the first _known_ jazz musician, is credited with creating the _big four_, a habanera-based pattern. The big four (below) was the first syncopated bass drum pattern to deviate from the standard on-the-beat march.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_jazz#cite_note-9) As the example below shows, the second half of the big four pattern is the habanera rhythm. [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c8/Big_four_Buddy_Bolden.png/330px-Big_four_Buddy_Bolden.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Big_four_Buddy_Bolden.png) Buddy Bolden's "big four" pattern > It is probably safe to say that by and large the simpler African rhythmic patterns survived in jazz... because they could be adapted more readily to European rhythmic conceptions. Some survived, others were discarded as the Europeanization progressed. It may also account for the fact that patterns such as \[tresillo have\] . . . remained one of the most useful and common syncopated patterns in jazz—Schuller (1968).[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_jazz#cite_note-10) The Cuban influence is evident in many pre-1940s jazz tunes, but rhythmically, they are all based on single-celled motifs such as [tresillo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tresillo_(rhythm) "Tresillo (rhythm)"), and not do not contain an overt two-celled, [clave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clave_(rhythm) "Clave (rhythm)")-based structure. " [Caravan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caravan_(1937_song) "Caravan (1937 song)")", written by [Juan Tizol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_Tizol "Juan Tizol") and [Duke Ellington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_Ellington "Duke Ellington") and first performed in 1936, is an early proto-Latin jazz composition. [Mongo Santamaría](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongo_Santamar%C3%ADa "Mongo Santamaría") recorded ever green "Watermelon Man" in 1962. [Hank Mobley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hank_Mobley "Hank Mobley"), [Kenny Dorham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenny_Dorham "Kenny Dorham"), and [Willie Bobo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Bobo "Willie Bobo") released latin jazz albums. [Willie Bobo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Bobo "Willie Bobo") fused [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz"), latin, and R&B music.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_jazz#cite_note-11) ### Jazz in-clave \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Latin_jazz&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: Jazz in-clave")\] [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2a/Machito_and_his_sister_Graciella_Grillo.jpg/250px-Machito_and_his_sister_Graciella_Grillo.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Machito_and_his_sister_Graciella_Grillo.jpg) [Machito](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machito "Machito") and his sister [Graciela](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graciela "Graciela") The first [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") piece to be overtly based _in-clave_, and therefore, the first true Latin jazz piece, was "Tanga" (1943) composed by [Mario Bauza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mario_Bauza "Mario Bauza") and recorded by [Machito](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machito "Machito") and his Afro-Cubans the same year, 1943. The tune was initially a descarga (Cuban jam) with jazz solos superimposed, spontaneously composed by Bauzá. The right hand of the "Tanga" piano [guajeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guajeo "Guajeo") is in the style known as ponchando, a type of non-arpeggiated guajeo using block chords. The sequence of attack-points is emphasized, rather than a sequence of different pitches. As a form of accompaniment it can be played in a strictly repetitive fashion or as a varied motif akin to jazz comping.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_jazz#cite_note-12) The following example is in the style of a 1949 recording by Machito. 2‐3 clave, piano by René Hernández.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_jazz#cite_note-13) [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/52/Tanga_piano_guajeo.jpg/500px-Tanga_piano_guajeo.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tanga_piano_guajeo.jpg)"Tanga" in the style of Machito and His Afro‐Cubans (recorded 1949). 2‐3 clave, piano: René Hernández. > The first descarga that made the world take notice is traced to a [Machito](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machito "Machito") rehearsal on May 29, 1943, at the Park Palace Ballroom, at 110th Street and 5th Avenue. At this time, Machito was at Fort Dix (New Jersey) in his fourth week of basic training. The day before at [La Conga Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Conga_(nightclub) "La Conga (nightclub)"), [Mario Bauza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mario_Bauza "Mario Bauza"), Machito's [trumpeter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trumpet "Trumpet") and [music director](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_director "Music director"), heard pianist Luis Varona and bassist Julio Andino play El Botellero composition and arrangements of the Cuban-born Gilberto Valdez which would serve as a permanent sign off (end the dance) tune. > > On this Monday evening, Dr. Bauza leaned over the piano and instructed Varona to play the same piano vamp he did the night before. Varona's left hand began the introduction of Gilberto Valdes' El Botellero. Bauza then instructed Julio Andino what to play; then the saxes; then the trumpets. The broken chord sounds soon began to take shape into an Afro-Cuban jazzed up melody. Gene Johnson's alto sax then emitted oriental-like jazz phrases. [Afro-Cuban jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afro-Cuban_jazz "Afro-Cuban jazz") was invented when Bauza composed "Tanga" (African word for marijuana) that evening of 1943. > > Thereafter, whenever "Tanga" was played, it sounded different, depending on a soloist's individuality. In August 1948, when trumpeter Howard McGhee soloed with Machito's orchestra at the Apollo Theatre, his ad-libs to "Tanga" resulted in "Cu-Bop City," a tune which was recorded by Roost Records months later. The jams which took place at the Royal Roots, [Bop City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bop_City "Bop City") and Birdland between 1948 and 1949, when Howard McGhee, tenor saxophonist Brew Moore, Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie sat in with the Machito orchestra, were unrehearsed, uninhibited, unheard-of-before jam sessions which at the time, master of ceremonies Symphony Sid called [Afro-Cuban jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afro-Cuban_jazz "Afro-Cuban jazz"). > > The Machito orchestra's ten- or fifteen-minute jams were the first in Latin music to break away from the traditional under-four-minute recordings. In February 1949, the Machito orchestra became the first to set a precedent in Latin music when it featured tenor saxophonist Flip Phillips in a five-minute recording of "Tanga." The twelve-inch 78 RPM, part of _The Jazz Scene_ album, sold for $25—Salazar (1997).[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_jazz#cite_note-14) [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5f/Son_clave_cut-time_3-2_%26_2-3.png/330px-Son_clave_cut-time_3-2_%26_2-3.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Son_clave_cut-time_3-2_&_2-3.png) 3-2 clave ([Play](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/0/07/Son_Clave_Pattern_duple.mid/Son_Clave_Pattern_duple.mid.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Son_Clave_Pattern_duple.mid "File:Son Clave Pattern duple.mid")) and 2-3 clave ([Play](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/d/d2/2-3_Son_Clave.MID/2-3_Son_Clave.MID.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:2-3_Son_Clave.MID "File:2-3 Son Clave.MID")) written in cut-time Mario Bauzá developed the 3-2 / 2-3 [clave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clave_(rhythm) "Clave (rhythm)") concept and terminology. A chord progression can begin on either side of clave. When the progression begins on the three-side, the song or song section is said to be in 3–2 clave. When the chord progression begins on the two-side, it is in 2–3 clave. In North America, salsa and Latin jazz charts commonly represent clave in two measures of [cut-time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alla_breve "Alla breve") (2/2); this is most likely the influence of jazz conventions.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_jazz#cite_note-15) When clave is written in two measures (above) changing from one clave sequence to the other is a matter of reversing the order of the measures. [Bobby Sanabria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Sanabria "Bobby Sanabria"), who was Bauzá's drummer, cites several important innovations of Machito's band: - The first band to explore jazz arranging techniques with authentic Afro-Cuban rhythms on a consistent basis giving it a unique identifiable sound that no other band in the genre of Afro-Cuban based dance music had at the time. Cuban big band arranger Chico O'Farill stated: "This was a new concept in interpreting Cuban music with as much (harmonic) richness as possible. You have to understand how important this was. It made every other band that came after, followers."[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_jazz#cite_note-16) - The first band to explore modal harmony (a concept explored much later by Miles Davis and Gil Evans) from a jazz arranging perspective through their recording of "Tanga." Of note is the sheet of sound effect in the arrangement through the use of multiple layering. - The first big band to explore, from an Afro-Cuban rhythmic perspective, large-scale extended compositional works. e.g. "The Afro-Cuban Jazz Suite" by Chico O'Farill. - The first band to successfully wed jazz big band arranging techniques within an original composition with jazz oriented soloists utilizing an authentic Afro-Cuban based rhythm section in a successful manner. e.g. Gene Johnson - alto, Brew Moore - tenor, composition - "Tanga" (1943). - The first Afro-Cuban based dance band to _overtly_ explore the concept of clave counterpoint from an arranging standpoint. The ability to weave seamlessly from one side of the clave to the other without breaking its rhythmic integrity within the structure of a musical arrangement.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_jazz#cite_note-17) [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cb/Dizzy_Gillespie_playing_horn_1955.jpg/250px-Dizzy_Gillespie_playing_horn_1955.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dizzy_Gillespie_playing_horn_1955.jpg) Dizzy Gillespie, 1955 Bauzá introduced [bebop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bebop "Bebop") innovator [Dizzy Gillespie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie "Dizzy Gillespie") to the Cuban conga drummer [Chano Pozo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chano_Pozo "Chano Pozo"). " [Manteca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manteca_(song) "Manteca (song)")" is the first [jazz standard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_standard "Jazz standard") to be rhythmically based on [clave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clave_(rhythm) "Clave (rhythm)"). "Manteca" was co-written by [Dizzy Gillespie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie "Dizzy Gillespie") and [Chano Pozo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chano_Pozo "Chano Pozo") in 1947. According to Gillespie, Pozo created the layered, [contrapuntal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counterpoint "Counterpoint") [guajeos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guajeo "Guajeo") (Afro-Cuban [ostinatos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ostinato "Ostinato")) of the A section and the introduction, and Gillespie wrote the bridge. The rhythm of the [melody](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melody "Melody") of the A section is identical to a common [mambo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mambo_(music) "Mambo (music)") [bell pattern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bell_pattern "Bell pattern"). [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ee/Manteca_%3D_bell_pattern.tif/lossy-page1-500px-Manteca_%3D_bell_pattern.tif.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Manteca_=_bell_pattern.tif) Top: opening measures of " [Manteca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manteca_(song) "Manteca (song)")" melody. Bottom: common [mambo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mambo_(music) "Mambo (music)") [bell pattern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bell_pattern "Bell pattern") (2-3 [clave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clave_(rhythm) "Clave (rhythm)")). On March 31, 1946, Stan Kenton recorded "Machito," written by his collaborator / arranger [Pete Rugolo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Rugolo "Pete Rugolo"), which is considered by some to be the first Latin jazz recording by American jazz musicians. The Kenton band was augmented by Ivan Lopez on bongos and Eugenio Reyes on maracas. Later, on December 6 the same year, Stan Kenton recorded an arrangement of the Afro-Cuban tune " [The Peanut Vendor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Peanut_Vendor "The Peanut Vendor")" with members of Machito's rhythm section. ### Latin Jazz 1950s - 1960s \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Latin_jazz&action=edit§ion=4 "Edit section: Latin Jazz 1950s - 1960s")\] [Kenny Dorham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenny_Dorham "Kenny Dorham") "Minor's Holiday", "Basheer's Dream",[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_jazz#cite_note-18) Hank Mobley "Recado Bossa Nova" and Sabu Martinez jazz tune developed Afro-Cuban jazz from 50s to 60s.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_jazz#cite_note-19) [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cb/Mongo_Santamaria_1969.JPG/250px-Mongo_Santamaria_1969.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mongo_Santamaria_1969.JPG) Mongo Santamaria, 1969 Cuban percussionist [Mongo Santamaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongo_Santamaria "Mongo Santamaria") recorded album "Afro Blue" in 1959.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_jazz#cite_note-20) "Afro Blue" was the first jazz standard built upon a typical African three-against-two (3:2) [cross-rhythm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross-rhythm "Cross-rhythm"), or [hemiola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hemiola "Hemiola").[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_jazz#cite_note-21) The song begins with the bass repeatedly playing 6 cross-beats per each measure of 12/8, or 6 cross-beats per 4 main beats—6:4 (two cells of 3:2). The following example shows the original [ostinato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ostinato "Ostinato") "Afro Blue" bass line. The slashed noteheads indicate the main [beats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_music "Beat music") (not bass notes), where you would normally tap your foot to "keep time." [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/57/Afro_blue_bass.jpg/500px-Afro_blue_bass.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Afro_blue_bass.jpg)"Afro Blue" bass line, with main beats indicated by slashed noteheads ### Bossa nova \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Latin_jazz&action=edit§ion=5 "Edit section: Bossa nova")\] [Bossa nova](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bossa_nova "Bossa nova") is a hybrid form based on the samba rhythm, but influenced by European and American music from Debussy to US jazz. Bossa nova originated in the 1950s, largely from the efforts of Brazilians [Antonio Carlos Jobim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonio_Carlos_Jobim "Antonio Carlos Jobim") and [João Gilberto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jo%C3%A3o_Gilberto "João Gilberto"). Its most famous song is arguably " [The Girl from Ipanema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Girl_from_Ipanema "The Girl from Ipanema")" sung by Gilberto and his wife, [Astrud Gilberto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astrud_Gilberto "Astrud Gilberto"). While the musical style evolved from [samba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samba_(music) "Samba (music)"), it is more complex harmonically and less percussive. Bossa nova emerged primarily from the upscale beachside neighborhoods of Rio de Janeiro as opposed to samba's origins in the [favelas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Favelas "Favelas") of Rio. Certain similar elements were already evident, even influencing Western classical music like Gershwin's [Cuban Overture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuban_Overture "Cuban Overture") which has the characteristic 'Latin' [clave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clave_(rhythm) "Clave (rhythm)") rhythm. The influence on bossa nova of [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") styles such as [cool jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cool_jazz "Cool jazz") is often debated by historians and fans, but a similar "cool sensibility" is apparent. Bossa nova was developed in Brazil in the mid-1950s, with its creation being credited to artists including [Johnny Alf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnny_Alf "Johnny Alf"), [Antonio Carlos Jobim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonio_Carlos_Jobim "Antonio Carlos Jobim") and [João Gilberto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jo%C3%A3o_Gilberto "João Gilberto"). One of the first songs was " [Bim-Bom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bim-Bom "Bim-Bom")"(Gilberto). Bossa nova was made popular by [Dorival Caymmi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorival_Caymmi "Dorival Caymmi")'s "Saudade da Bahia" and [Elizete Cardoso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizete_Cardoso "Elizete Cardoso")'s recording of " [Chega de Saudade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chega_de_Saudade "Chega de Saudade")" on the _[Canção do Amor Demais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Can%C3%A7%C3%A3o_do_Amor_Demais "Canção do Amor Demais")_ [LP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LP_album "LP album"), composed by [Vinícius de Moraes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vin%C3%ADcius_de_Moraes "Vinícius de Moraes") (lyrics) and Antonio Carlos Jobim (music). The song was soon after released by Gilberto. The initial releases by Gilberto and the internationally popular 1959 film _[Orfeu Negro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orfeu_Negro "Orfeu Negro")_ ("Black Orpheus", with score by [Luiz Bonfá](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luiz_Bonf%C3%A1 "Luiz Bonfá")) brought significant popularity of this musical style in Brazil and elsewhere in Latin America, which spread to North America via visiting American jazz musicians. The resulting recordings by [Charlie Byrd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Byrd "Charlie Byrd") and [Stan Getz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Getz "Stan Getz") cemented its popularity and led to a worldwide boom with 1964's _[Getz/Gilberto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Getz/Gilberto "Getz/Gilberto")_, numerous recordings by famous jazz performers such as [Ella Fitzgerald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ella_Fitzgerald "Ella Fitzgerald") ( _[Ella Abraça Jobim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ella_Abra%C3%A7a_Jobim "Ella Abraça Jobim")_) and [Frank Sinatra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Sinatra "Frank Sinatra") ( _[Francis Albert Sinatra & Antônio Carlos Jobim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Albert_Sinatra_&_Antonio_Carlos_Jobim "Francis Albert Sinatra & Antonio Carlos Jobim")_). Since that time, the bossa nova style maintains a lasting influence in world music for several decades and even up to the present. The first bossa nova single to achieve international popularity was perhaps the most successful of all time, the 1964 Getz/Gilberto recording " [The Girl From Ipanema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Girl_From_Ipanema "The Girl From Ipanema")", edited to include only the singing of [Astrud Gilberto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astrud_Gilberto "Astrud Gilberto"), Gilberto's then wife. The genre would withstand substantial "watering down" by popular artists throughout the next four decades. An early influence on bossa nova was the song " [Dans mon île](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dans_mon_%C3%AEle?action=edit&redlink=1 "Dans mon île (page does not exist)")" by French singer [Henri Salvador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_Salvador "Henri Salvador"), featured in the 1957 Italian movie _[Europa di notte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_films_of_1959 "Italian films of 1959")_ by [Alessandro Blasetti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alessandro_Blasetti "Alessandro Blasetti"); the song was distributed in Brazil and covered later by Brazilian artists [Eumir Deodato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eumir_Deodato "Eumir Deodato") ( _Los Danseros en Bolero_ – 1964) and [Caetano Veloso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caetano_Veloso "Caetano Veloso") ( _Outras Palavras_ – 1981). In 2005, Henri Salvador was awarded the [Brazilian Order of Cultural Merit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazilian_Order_of_Cultural_Merit?action=edit&redlink=1 "Brazilian Order of Cultural Merit (page does not exist)"), which he received from singer and Minister of Culture, [Gilberto Gil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilberto_Gil "Gilberto Gil"), in the presence of President [Lula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luiz_In%C3%A1cio_Lula_da_Silva "Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva") for his influence on Brazilian culture. The so-called "bossa nova clave" (or "Brazilian clave") is played on the snare rim of the [drum kit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drum_kit "Drum kit") in bossa nova. The pattern has a similar rhythm to that of the son [clave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clave_(rhythm) "Clave (rhythm)"), but the second note on the two-side is delayed by one pulse (subdivision). The pattern is shown below in 2/4, as it is written in Brazil. In North American charts it is more likely to be written in cut-time. [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5b/Bossa_nova_pattern.png/330px-Bossa_nova_pattern.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bossa_nova_pattern.png) Bossa nova snare rim pattern ([Play](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/5/5f/Bossa_nova_pattern.mid/Bossa_nova_pattern.mid.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bossa_nova_pattern.mid "File:Bossa nova pattern.mid")) According to drummer [Bobby Sanabria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Sanabria "Bobby Sanabria") the Brazilian composer [Antonio Carlos Jobim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonio_Carlos_Jobim "Antonio Carlos Jobim"), who developed the pattern, considers it to be merely a rhythmic motif and not a [clave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clave_(rhythm) "Clave (rhythm)") ( [guide pattern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bell_pattern "Bell pattern")). Jobim later regretted that Latino musicians misunderstood the role of this bossa nova pattern.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_jazz#cite_note-22) ### Beyond Latin jazz \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Latin_jazz&action=edit§ion=6 "Edit section: Beyond Latin jazz")\] [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/45/Airto_Moreira.jpg/250px-Airto_Moreira.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Airto_Moreira.jpg) Brazilian percussionist Airto Moreira[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a5/Nan%C3%A1_Vasconcelos.jpg/250px-Nan%C3%A1_Vasconcelos.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nan%C3%A1_Vasconcelos.jpg) Naná Vasconcelos playing the Afro-Brazilian [Berimbau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berimbau "Berimbau") Brazilian percussionist [Airto Moreira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airto_Moreira "Airto Moreira") became a professional musician at age 13. He won acclaim as a member of the samba jazz pioneers [Sambalanço Trio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sambalan%C3%A7o_Trio "Sambalanço Trio") and for his landmark recording _Quarteto Novo_ with [Hermeto Pascoal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermeto_Pascoal "Hermeto Pascoal") in 1967. Shortly after, he followed his wife [Flora Purim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flora_Purim "Flora Purim") to the United States. Once in the U.S., Airto introduced Afro-Brazilian folkloric instruments into a wide variety of jazz styles, in ways that had not been done before. However, the terms _jazz samba_ or _Latin jazz_ are too limiting a label for the types of music Airto participated in the U.S. during the 1970s. Airto played in the two most important [avant-garde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde "Avant-garde") electric jazz bands of the day— [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis") and [Weather Report](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report "Weather Report"). He also performed on more mainstream albums, such as those of [CTI Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CTI_Records "CTI Records"). Besides energetic rhythmic textures, Airto added percussion color, using bells, shakers, and whistles to create evocative textures of timbre. Airto paved the way for other [avant garde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant_garde "Avant garde") Brazilian musicians such as [Hermeto Pascoal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermeto_Pascoal "Hermeto Pascoal"), to enter the North American jazz scene. Early 1970s, Deodato released big hit crossover jazz album "Prelude". Another innovative Brazilian percussionist is [Naná Vasconcelos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nan%C3%A1_Vasconcelos "Naná Vasconcelos"). Vasconcelos contributed to four [Jon Hassell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jon_Hassell "Jon Hassell") albums from 1976 to 1980 (including [Possible Musics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourth_World,_Vol._1:_Possible_Musics "Fourth World, Vol. 1: Possible Musics") by [Brian Eno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Eno "Brian Eno") and Hassell), and later to several [Pat Metheny Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pat_Metheny_Group "Pat Metheny Group") works and [Jan Garbarek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Garbarek "Jan Garbarek") concerts from early 1980s to early 1990s. In 1976 joined [Egberto Gismonti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egberto_Gismonti "Egberto Gismonti") to record _[Dança das cabeças](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan%C3%A7a_das_cabe%C3%A7as "Dança das cabeças")_ in [ECM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records "ECM Records") label. In 1984 he appeared on the [Pierre Favre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Favre_(musician) "Pierre Favre (musician)") album _Singing Drums_ along with [Paul Motian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Motian "Paul Motian"). He also appears on [Arild Andersen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arild_Andersen "Arild Andersen")'s album "If You Look Far Enough" with [Ralph Towner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_Towner "Ralph Towner"). Vasconcelos formed a group named [Codona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona "Codona") with [Don Cherry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(jazz) "Don Cherry (jazz)") and [Collin Walcott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collin_Walcott "Collin Walcott"), which released three albums in 1978, 1980 and 1982.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_jazz#cite_note-ALLMUSIC-23)[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_jazz#cite_note-24)[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_jazz#cite_note-25) While Vasconcelos uses Afro-Brazilian rhythms and instruments, he like Airto, transcend the categories of Brazilian jazz and Latin jazz. ## Comparing Latin jazz with straight-ahead jazz \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Latin_jazz&action=edit§ion=7 "Edit section: Comparing Latin jazz with straight-ahead jazz")\] In comparison with straight-ahead jazz, Latin jazz employs [straight rhythm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Straight_rhythm "Straight rhythm") (or "even-eighths"), rather than [swung rhythm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swung_rhythm "Swung rhythm"). Early Latin jazz rarely employed a [backbeat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music) "Beat (music)"), but contemporary forms fuse the backbeat with the [clave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clave_(rhythm) "Clave (rhythm)"). The [conga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conga "Conga"), [timbale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timbales "Timbales"), [güiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G%C3%BCiro "Güiro"), [bongos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bongos "Bongos"), and [claves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claves "Claves") are [percussion instruments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percussion_instrument "Percussion instrument") often used in addition to, or in place of the [drum kit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drum_kit "Drum kit"). ## Formats \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Latin_jazz&action=edit§ion=8 "Edit section: Formats")\] Latin jazz music, like most types of jazz music, can be played in small or large groups. Small groups, or combos, often use the [bebop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bebop "Bebop") format made popular in the 1950s in America, where the musicians play a standard melody, many of the musicians play an improvised solo, and then everyone plays the melody again. Prominent Latin jazz big bands include [Arturo O'Farrill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arturo_O'Farrill "Arturo O'Farrill")'s Afro-Latin Jazz Orchestra, Bobby Sanabria's Multiverse Big Band, Raices Jazz Orchestra, Mambo Legends Orchestra, Pacific Mambo Orchestra, as well as others. In Latin jazz bands, percussion is often featured in solos. Contemporary Latin jazz pieces by musicians such as [Hermeto Pascoal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermeto_Pascoal "Hermeto Pascoal") are mostly composed for these small groups, with percussion solos as well as many wind-instrumentals.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_jazz#cite_note-26) ## Latin jazz as global music \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Latin_jazz&action=edit§ion=9 "Edit section: Latin jazz as global music")\] Most jazz histories emphasize the narrative that jazz is exclusively an American music—a style created by African Americans in the early 20th century, fusing elements of African rhythm and improvisations with European instrumentation, harmonies, and formal structures. The influences of musics from the Caribbean and Latin America—save [Jelly Roll Morton's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jelly_Roll_Morton:_The_Complete_Library_of_Congress_Recordings "Jelly Roll Morton: The Complete Library of Congress Recordings") often quoted comments on the "Spanish tinge" rhythms of early New Orleans jazz, and trumpeter [Dizzy Gillespie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie "Dizzy Gillespie")'s famous Post-War collaborations with Afro-Cuban drummer [Chano Pozo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chano_Pozo "Chano Pozo")—have received little or no mention in standard jazz textbooks used in most American universities.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_jazz#cite_note-27)[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_jazz#cite_note-28) Likewise, the influential 1973 compilation of recordings, the _Smithsonian Collection of Classic Jazz,_ and [Ken Burns'](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ken_Burns'_Jazz "Ken Burns' Jazz") popular documentary film _Jazz,_ make little mention of Latin jazz.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_jazz#cite_note-29) More recent scholarship has challenged this paradigm, arguing that music from the Caribbean and Latin American were essential to the emergence of early [New Orleans jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans_Jazz_&_Heritage_Festival "New Orleans Jazz & Heritage Festival"), to the music's Post-War development in New York City, and to the continued evolution of jazz in twenty-first century urban centers. Proponents of this view advocate for the inclusion of influential Caribbean band leaders including Frank [Machito](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machito "Machito") Grillo, [Mario Bauzá](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mario_Bauz%C3%A1 "Mario Bauzá"), [Chico O'Farrill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chico_O'Farrill "Chico O'Farrill"), [Tito Puente](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tito_Puente "Tito Puente"), [Ray Barretto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_Barretto "Ray Barretto"), and Jerry and Andy Gonzalez in the broader jazz cannon.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_jazz#cite_note-30)[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_jazz#cite_note-31) From this perspective, all jazz, including Latin Jazz, is not viewed as a uniquely American expression, but rather as "a global music" that is "transcultural in its stylistic scope."[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_jazz#cite_note-32) ## See also \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Latin_jazz&action=edit§ion=10 "Edit section: See also")\] - - [nu jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nu_jazz "Nu jazz") | | Other topics | | - [List of musicians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_jazz_fusion_musicians "List of jazz fusion musicians") | **Jazz fusion** (also known as **jazz rock**, **jazz-rock fusion**, or simply **fusion**[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-2)) is a [popular music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popular_music "Popular music") [genre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_genre "Music genre") that developed in the late 1960s when musicians combined [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") harmony and [improvisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_improvisation "Jazz improvisation") with [rock music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music"), [funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funk "Funk"), and [rhythm and blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_and_blues "Rhythm and blues"). [Electric guitars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_guitar "Electric guitar") and [basses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bass_guitar "Bass guitar"), [amplifiers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guitar_amplifier "Guitar amplifier"), and [keyboard instruments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keyboard_instrument "Keyboard instrument") (including [electric pianos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_piano "Electric piano") and [organs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_organ "Electric organ")) that were popular in rock began to be used by jazz musicians, particularly those who had grown up listening to rock and roll. Jazz fusion [arrangements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrangements "Arrangements") vary in complexity. Some employ groove-based vamps fixed to a single key or a single chord with a simple, repeated melody. Others use elaborate [chord progressions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chord_progression "Chord progression"), unconventional time signatures, or melodies with [counter-melodies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hauptstimme "Hauptstimme"), in a similar fashion to [progressive rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock "Progressive rock"). These arrangements, whether simple or complex, typically include improvised sections that can vary in length, much like in other forms of jazz. As with jazz, jazz fusion can employ brass and [woodwind instruments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodwind_instrument "Woodwind instrument") such as trumpet and saxophone, but other instruments often substitute for these. A jazz fusion band is less likely to use acoustic [piano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano "Piano") and [double bass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_bass "Double bass"), and more likely to use electric guitars, electric pianos, organs, [synthesizers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synthesizer "Synthesizer"), and [bass guitar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bass_guitar "Bass guitar"). The term "jazz rock" is sometimes used as a synonym for "jazz fusion" and for music performed by late 1960s- and 1970s-era rock bands that added jazz elements to their music. After a decade of popularity during the 1970s, fusion expanded its improvisatory and experimental approaches through the 1980s in parallel with the development of a radio-friendly style called [smooth jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_jazz "Smooth jazz").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-3) Experimentation continued in the 1990s and 2000s. Fusion albums, even those that are made by the same group or artist, may include a variety of musical styles. Please help update this article to reflect recent events or newly available information._(November 2023)_ | ### Origins \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jazz_fusion&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Origins")\] When [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane") died in 1967, rock was the most popular music in America, and _[DownBeat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DownBeat "DownBeat")_ magazine went so far as to declare in a headline that: "Jazz as We Know It Is Dead".[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-Fusions-4) [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic") states that "until around 1967, the worlds of jazz and rock were nearly completely separate",[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-Fusion_overview-5) although the [Daevid Allen Trio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine "Soft Machine") which later became the Soft Machine formed in 1963,[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-6) while the jazz label [Verve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verve_Records "Verve Records") released the influential debut album, _[Freak Out!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freak_Out! "Freak Out!")_, by artist and composer [Frank Zappa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa "Frank Zappa") in 1966.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-OxMilkowski-7) [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/34/Larry_Coryell_1979.jpg/250px-Larry_Coryell_1979.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Larry_Coryell_1979.jpg) Guitarist [Larry Coryell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Coryell "Larry Coryell") Guitarist [Larry Coryell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Coryell "Larry Coryell"), sometimes called the godfather of fusion, referred to a generation of musicians who had grown up on rock and roll when he said, "We loved Miles but we also loved the [Rolling Stones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stones "Rolling Stones")."[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-OxMilkowski-7) In 1966, he started the band [the Free Spirits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Free_Spirits "The Free Spirits") with [Bob Moses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Moses_(musician) "Bob Moses (musician)") on drums and recorded the band's first album,[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-Fusions-4) _[Out of Sight and Sound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_of_Sight_and_Sound "Out of Sight and Sound")_, released in 1967. That same year, _DownBeat_ began to report on rock music.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-OxMilkowski-7) After the Free Spirits, Coryell was part of a quartet led by vibraphonist [Gary Burton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Burton "Gary Burton"), releasing the album _[Duster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duster_(Gary_Burton_album) "Duster (Gary Burton album)")_ with its rock guitar influence.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-Fusions-4) Burton produced the album _Tomorrow Never Knows_ for Count's Jam Band, which included Coryell, [Mike Nock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Nock "Mike Nock"), and [Steve Marcus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Marcus "Steve Marcus"), all of them former students at Berklee College in Boston.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-Fusions-4) The pioneers of fusion emphasized exploration, energy, electricity, intensity, virtuosity, and volume. [Charles Lloyd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Lloyd_(jazz_musician) "Charles Lloyd (jazz musician)") played a combination of rock and jazz at the [Monterey Jazz Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monterey_Jazz_Festival "Monterey Jazz Festival") in 1966 with a quartet that included [Keith Jarrett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett "Keith Jarrett") and [Jack DeJohnette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_DeJohnette "Jack DeJohnette").[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-OxMilkowski-7) Lloyd adopted the trappings of the California [psychedelic rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychedelic_rock "Psychedelic rock") scene by playing at the rock venue the [Fillmore West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fillmore_West "Fillmore West"), wearing colorful clothes, and giving his albums titles like _Dream Weaver_ and _Forest Flower_, which were bestselling jazz albums in 1967.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-Fusions-4) Flautist [Jeremy Steig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Steig "Jeremy Steig") experimented with jazz in his band Jeremy & the Satyrs with vibraphonist [Mike Mainieri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Mainieri "Mike Mainieri"). [Rahsaan Roland Kirk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rahsaan_Roland_Kirk "Rahsaan Roland Kirk") performed with Jimi Hendrix at [Ronnie Scott's Jazz Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronnie_Scott's_Jazz_Club "Ronnie Scott's Jazz Club") in London.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-OxMilkowski-7) According to music journalist Zaid Mudhaffer, the term "jazz fusion" was coined in a review of _[Song of Innocence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Song_of_Innocence "Song of Innocence")_ by [David Axelrod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Axelrod_(musician) "David Axelrod (musician)") when it was released in 1968.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-8) Axelrod said Davis had played the album before conceiving _[Bitches Brew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew "Bitches Brew")_.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-9) ### Miles Davis \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jazz_fusion&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: Miles Davis")\] [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis") wrote in his autobiography that in 1968 and 1969, he had been listening to [Jimi Hendrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimi_Hendrix "Jimi Hendrix"), [James Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Brown "James Brown"), and [Sly and the Family Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sly_and_the_Family_Stone "Sly and the Family Stone").[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-OxMilkowski-7) As members of Davis' band, [Chick Corea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chick_Corea "Chick Corea") and [Herbie Hancock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock "Herbie Hancock") played electric piano on _[Filles de Kilimanjaro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filles_de_Kilimanjaro "Filles de Kilimanjaro")_. Davis's 1969 album _[In a Silent Way](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way "In a Silent Way")_ is considered his first fusion album.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-Southall-10) Composed of two side-long improvised suites edited heavily by Teo Macero, the album was made by pioneers of jazz fusion: Corea, Hancock, [Tony Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Williams_(drummer) "Tony Williams (drummer)"), [Wayne Shorter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter "Wayne Shorter"), [Joe Zawinul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Zawinul "Joe Zawinul") and [John McLaughlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McLaughlin_(musician) "John McLaughlin (musician)"). When Davis recorded _[Bitches Brew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew "Bitches Brew")_ in 1969, he mostly abandoned the swing beat in favor of a rock and roll backbeat and bass guitar grooves. The album "mixed free jazz blowing by a large ensemble with electronic keyboards and guitar, plus a dense mix of percussion".[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-11) Davis played his trumpet like an electric guitar—plugged in to electronic effects and pedals. By the end of the first year, _Bitches Brew_ sold 400,000 copies, four times the average for a Miles Davis album. [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/81/Miles_Davis_24.jpg/250px-Miles_Davis_24.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Miles_Davis_24.jpg) Trumpet player [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis") was a key figure in the development of fusion. Although _Bitches Brew_ gave him a [gold record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_recording_sales_certification "Music recording sales certification"), the use of electric instruments and rock beats created consternation among some jazz critics, who accused Davis of betraying the essence of jazz.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-considine-12) Music critic Kevin Fellezs commented that some members of the jazz community regarded rock music as less sophisticated and more commercial than jazz.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-Briley-13) Over the next two years, Davis recorded more often, worked with many sidemen, appeared on television, and performed at rock venues, continuing to experiment with rock, [funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funk "Funk"), and electronic treatments. His producer, [Teo Macero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teo_Macero "Teo Macero"), inserted previously recorded material into the [_Jack Johnson_ soundtrack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Johnson_(album) "Jack Johnson (album)"), _[Live-Evil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live-Evil_(Miles_Davis_album) "Live-Evil (Miles Davis album)")_, and _[On the Corner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Corner "On the Corner")_.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-Gioia_history-14) _Jack Johnson_ (1971) has been cited as "the purest electric jazz record ever made" and "one of the most remarkable jazz rock discs of the era".[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-tribute-15)[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-Fordham_tribute-16) ### Other musicians \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jazz_fusion&action=edit§ion=4 "Edit section: Other musicians")\] [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/75/JohnMcLaughlin.jpg/250px-JohnMcLaughlin.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:JohnMcLaughlin.jpg) [John McLaughlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McLaughlin_(musician) "John McLaughlin (musician)") performs during his [Mahavishnu Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahavishnu_Orchestra "Mahavishnu Orchestra") period Herbie Hancock brought elements of funk, disco, and electronic music into commercially successful albums such as _[Head Hunters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head_Hunters "Head Hunters")_ (1973) and _[Feets, Don't Fail Me Now](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feets,_Don't_Fail_Me_Now "Feets, Don't Fail Me Now")_ (1979). Several years after recording _[Miles in the Sky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_in_the_Sky "Miles in the Sky")_ with Davis, guitarist [George Benson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Benson "George Benson") became a vocalist with enough pop hits to overshadow his earlier career in jazz.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-Gioia_history-14) While Davis was sidelined, Chick Corea gained prominence. In the early 1970s Corea combined jazz, rock, pop, and Brazilian music in [Return to Forever](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Return_to_Forever "Return to Forever"), a band that included [Stanley Clarke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_Clarke "Stanley Clarke") on bass guitar and [Al Di Meola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Di_Meola "Al Di Meola") on electric guitar. Corea divided the rest of his career between acoustic and electric music, non-commercial and commercial, jazz and pop rock, with a band for each: the Akoustic Band and the Elektric Band.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-Gioia_history-14) Joe Zawinul and Wayne Shorter started the influential jazz fusion band [Weather Report](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report "Weather Report") in December 1970.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-BKGrove-17) They had a successful career along with major musicians like [Alphonse Mouzon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alphonse_Mouzon "Alphonse Mouzon"), [Jaco Pastorius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaco_Pastorius "Jaco Pastorius"), [Airto Moreira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airto_Moreira "Airto Moreira") and [Miroslav Vitouš](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miroslav_Vitou%C5%A1 "Miroslav Vitouš") until 1986.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-BKGrove-17) Tony Williams was a member of Davis's band since 1963. Williams reflected, "I wanted to create a different atmosphere from the one I had been in...What better way to do it than to go electric?" He left Davis to form [the Tony Williams Lifetime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Tony_Williams_Lifetime "The Tony Williams Lifetime") with English guitarist John McLaughlin and organist [Larry Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Young_(musician) "Larry Young (musician)"). The band combined rock intensity and loudness with jazz spontaneity. The debut album [_Emergency!_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergency!_(album) "Emergency! (album)") was recorded three months before _Bitches Brew_.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-OxMilkowski-7)[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-18)[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-19) Although McLaughlin had worked with Miles Davis, he was influenced more by Jimi Hendrix and had played with English rock musicians [Eric Clapton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Clapton "Eric Clapton") and [Mick Jagger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mick_Jagger "Mick Jagger") before creating the Mahavishnu Orchestra around the same time that Corea started Return to Forever. McLaughlin had been a member of Tony Williams's Lifetime. He brought to his music many of the elements that interested other musicians in the 1960s and early 1970s: counterculture, rock and roll, electronic instruments, solo virtuosity, experimentation, the blending of genres, and an interest in the exotic, such as Indian music.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-Gioia_history-14) He formed the [Mahavishnu Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahavishnu_Orchestra "Mahavishnu Orchestra") with drummer [Billy Cobham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Cobham "Billy Cobham"), violinist [Jerry Goodman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerry_Goodman "Jerry Goodman"), bassist [Rick Laird](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Laird "Rick Laird"), and keyboardist [Jan Hammer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Hammer "Jan Hammer"). The band released its first album, _[The Inner Mounting Flame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Inner_Mounting_Flame "The Inner Mounting Flame")_, in 1971. Hammer pioneered the use of the [Minimoog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimoog "Minimoog") synthesizer with distortion effects. His use of the pitch bend wheel made a keyboard sound like an electric guitar. The Mahavishnu Orchestra was influenced by both psychedelic rock and [Indian classical music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_classical_music "Indian classical music"). The band's first lineup broke up after two studio albums and one live album, but McLaughlin formed another group in 1974 under the same name with jazz violinist [Jean-Luc Ponty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Luc_Ponty "Jean-Luc Ponty"), one of the first electric violinists. After leaving the Mahavishnu Orchestra in 1975 Jean-Luc Ponty signed with [Atlantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Records "Atlantic Records") and released number of successful jazz fusion solo albums that entered top 5 of the [_Billboard_ jazz charts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Top_Jazz_Albums "Top Jazz Albums") in mid '70s — '80s. During the late 1970s, [Lee Ritenour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Ritenour "Lee Ritenour"), [Stuff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuff_(band) "Stuff (band)"), [George Benson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Benson "George Benson"), [Chuck Mangione](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuck_Mangione "Chuck Mangione"), [Spyro Gyra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spyro_Gyra "Spyro Gyra"), [the Crusaders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Crusaders_(jazz_fusion_group) "The Crusaders (jazz fusion group)"), and [Larry Carlton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Carlton "Larry Carlton")[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-20) released fusion albums. [George Duke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Duke "George Duke") and [Aynsley Dunbar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aynsley_Dunbar "Aynsley Dunbar") played on both. 1970s band [Steely Dan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steely_Dan "Steely Dan") has been lauded by music critic [Neil McCormick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_McCormick "Neil McCormick") for their "smooth, smart jazz-rock fusion".[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-30) The jazz artists of the 1960s and 1970s had a large impact on many rock groups of that era such as [Santana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(band) "Santana (band)") and Frank Zappa. They took jazz phrasing and harmony and incorporated it into modern rock music, significantly changing music history and paving the way for artists that would follow in their footsteps. Carlos Santana in particular has given much credit to Miles Davis and the influence he had on his music. While Miles Davis combined jazz with modal and rock influences, [Carlos Santana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Santana "Carlos Santana") combined these along with Latin rhythms and feel, shaping a whole new genre, [Latin rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_rock "Latin rock"). According to AllMusic, the term jazz rock "may refer to the loudest, wildest, most electrified fusion bands from the jazz camp, but most often it describes performers coming from the rock side of the equation...jazz rock first emerged during the late '60s as an attempt to fuse the visceral power of rock with the musical complexity and improvisational fireworks of jazz. Since rock often emphasized directness and simplicity over virtuosity, jazz rock generally grew out of the most artistically ambitious rock subgenres of the late '60s and early '70s: [psychedelia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychedelic_music "Psychedelic music"), [progressive rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock "Progressive rock"), and the singer-songwriter movement."[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-JR_Overview-31) According to jazz writer Stuart Nicholson, jazz rock paralleled [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz") by being "on the verge of creating a whole new musical language in the 1960s". He said the albums _[Emergency!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergency!_(album) "Emergency! (album)")_ (1969) by the [Tony Williams Lifetime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Williams_Lifetime "Tony Williams Lifetime") and _[Agharta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album) "Agharta (album)")_ (1975) by Miles Davis "suggested the potential of evolving into something that might eventually define itself as a wholly independent genre quite apart from the sound and conventions of anything that had gone before". This development was stifled by commercialism, Nicholson said, as the genre "mutated into a peculiar species of jazz-inflected pop music that eventually took up residence on FM radio" at the end of the 1970s.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-32) In the 1970s, American fusion was being combined in the U.K. with progressive rock and psychedelic music. Bands who were part of this movement included Brand X (with [Phil Collins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Collins "Phil Collins") of Genesis), Bruford ( [Bill Bruford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Bruford "Bill Bruford") of Yes), and Nucleus (led by [Ian Carr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Carr "Ian Carr")). Throughout Europe and the world this movement grew due to the efforts of [Magma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magma_(band) "Magma (band)") in France, [Passport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Passport_(band) "Passport (band)") in Germany, guitarist [Jan Akkerman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Akkerman "Jan Akkerman") of the Netherlands, [Terje Rypdal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terje_Rypdal "Terje Rypdal") in Norway, [Jukka Tolonen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jukka_Tolonen "Jukka Tolonen") of Finland, and the Japanese guitarists [Ryo Kawasaki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryo_Kawasaki "Ryo Kawasaki") and [Kazumi Watanabe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kazumi_Watanabe "Kazumi Watanabe").[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-OxMilkowski-7) ## Jazz metal \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jazz_fusion&action=edit§ion=6 "Edit section: Jazz metal")\] | Jazz metal | | --- | | Stylistic origins | - [Heavy metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heavy_metal_music "Heavy metal music")
