Records"), Ayler | Musical artist **Albert Ayler** ([/ˈaɪlər/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); July 13, 1936– November 25, 1970) was an American [avant-garde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde "Avant-garde") [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") saxophonist and composer.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-RCJE-1) After early experience playing [rhythm and blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_and_blues "Rhythm and blues") and [bebop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bebop "Bebop"), Ayler began recording music during the [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz") era of the 1960s. However, some critics argue that while Ayler's style is undeniably original and unorthodox, it does not adhere to the generally accepted critical understanding of free jazz.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-Mandel-2) In fact, Ayler's style is difficult to categorize, and it evoked incredibly strong and disparate reactions from critics and fans alike.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-Claghorn-3) His innovations have inspired many subsequent jazz musicians.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-Mandel-2) His trio and quartet records of 1964, such as _[Spiritual Unity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity "Spiritual Unity")_ and _[The Hilversum Session](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hilversum_Session "The Hilversum Session")_, show him advancing the improvisational notions of [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane") and [Ornette Coleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman "Ornette Coleman") into abstract realms where whole [timbre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timbre "Timbre"), and not just mainly [harmony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmony "Harmony") with [melody](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melody "Melody"), is the music's backbone. His ecstatic music of 1965 and 1966, such as "Spirits Rejoice" and "Truth Is Marching In", has been compared by critics to the sound of a [brass band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brass_band#New_Orleans "Brass band"), and involved simple, march-like themes which alternated with wild group [improvisations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_improvisation "Free improvisation") and were regarded as retrieving jazz's pre- [Louis Armstrong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Armstrong "Louis Armstrong") roots.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-4) ## Biography ### Early life and career Born in [Cleveland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleveland "Cleveland"), Ohio, and raised in [Shaker Heights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shaker_Heights "Shaker Heights"),[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-5) Ayler was first taught alto saxophone by his father Edward, who was a semiprofessional saxophonist and violinist. Edward and Albert played alto saxophone duets in church and often listened to jazz records together, including swing era jazz and then-new bop albums.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-Claghorn-3) Ayler's upbringing in the church had a great impact on his life and music, and much of his music can be understood as an attempt to express his spirituality, including the aptly titled _[Spiritual Unity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity "Spiritual Unity")_, and his album of spirituals, _Goin' Home_, which features "meandering" solos that are meant to be treated as meditations on sacred texts, and at some points as "speaking in tongues" with his saxophone.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-Whitehead-6) Ayler's experience in the church and exposure to swing jazz artists also impacted his sound: his wide vibrato was similar to that of gospel saxophonists, who sought a more vocal-like sound with their instruments, and to that of brass players in New Orleans swing bands.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-Whitehead-6) Ayler attended [John Adams High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Adams_High_School_(Cleveland,_Ohio) "John Adams High School (Cleveland, Ohio)") on Cleveland's East Side, and graduated in 1954 at the age of 18. He later studied at [Academy Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Music_(Cleveland,_Ohio)?action=edit&redlink=1 "Academy Music (Cleveland, Ohio)") in Cleveland with jazz saxophonist [Benny Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benny_Miller?action=edit&redlink=1 "Benny Miller"). Ayler also played the [oboe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oboe "Oboe") in high school. As a teenager, Ayler's understanding of bebop style and mastery of standard repertoire earned him the nickname of "Little Bird", after [Charlie "Bird" Parker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Parker "Charlie Parker"), in the small Cleveland jazz scene.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-7) In 1952, at the age of 16, Ayler began playing bar-walking, honking, [R&B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contemporary_R&B "Contemporary R&B")-style tenor with blues singer and harmonica player [Little Walter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_Walter "Little Walter"), spending two summer vacations with Walter's band.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-Litweiler152-8) In 1958, after graduating from high school, Ayler joined the United States Army, where he switched from alto to tenor sax and jammed with other enlisted musicians, including tenor saxophonist [Stanley Turrentine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_Turrentine "Stanley Turrentine"). Ayler also played in the regiment band, along with future composer [Harold Budd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_Budd "Harold Budd").[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-9) In 1959 he was stationed in France, where he was further exposed to the martial music that would be a core influence on his later work. After his discharge from the army, Ayler tried to find work in Los Angeles and Cleveland, but his increasingly iconoclastic playing, which had moved away from traditional harmony, was not welcomed by traditionalists.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-Litweiler152-8) Ayler relocated to Sweden in 1962, where his recording career began, leading Swedish and Danish groups on radio sessions and jamming as an unpaid member of [Cecil Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor "Cecil Taylor")'s band in the winter of 1962–63. (Long-rumored tapes of Ayler performing with Taylor's group were released by [Revenant Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revenant_Records "Revenant Records") in 2004, as part of a [10-CD set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Ghost:_Rare_&_Unissued_Recordings_(1962%E2%80%9370) "Holy Ghost: Rare & Unissued Recordings (1962–70)").)[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-10) The album _[My Name Is Albert Ayler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My_Name_Is_Albert_Ayler "My Name Is Albert Ayler")_ is a session of standards recorded for a Copenhagen radio station with local musicians including [Niels-Henning Ørsted Pedersen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niels-Henning_%C3%98rsted_Pedersen "Niels-Henning Ørsted Pedersen") and drummer Ronnie Gardiner, with Ayler playing tenor and soprano on tracks such as " [Summertime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summertime_(George_Gershwin_song) "Summertime (George Gershwin song)")". ### Early recording career In 1963, Ayler returned to the US and settled in New York City, where he continued to develop his personal style and occasionally played alongside free jazz pianist Cecil Taylor.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-Claghorn-3) 1964 was the most well-documented year of Ayler's career, during which he recorded many albums, the first of which was _[Spirits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spirits_(Albert_Ayler_album) "Spirits (Albert Ayler album)")_ (re-released later as _Witches and Devils_) in March of that year.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-11) Ayler also began his rich relationship with [ESP-Disk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESP-Disk "ESP-Disk") Records in 1964, recording his breakthrough album (and ESP's very first jazz album) _[Spiritual Unity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity "Spiritual Unity")_ for the then-fledgling record label. ESP-Disk came to play an integral role in recording and disseminating free jazz. _Spiritual Unity_ featured the trio that Ayler had just assembled that summer, including bassist [Gary Peacock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Peacock "Gary Peacock") and drummer [Sunny Murray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunny_Murray "Sunny Murray"). The liner notes of _Spiritual Unity_ include a brief description of the musicians on that day, July 10, 1964, in the Variety Arts Recording Studio:[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-ESP-12) Just before 1 PM, Sunny Murray arrived, a large, genial walrus....Gary Peacock was next, tall, thin, ascetic looking, and soft spoken....Albert Ayler was last, small, wary, and laconic.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-ESP-12) On July 17, 1964, the members of this trio, along with trumpet player [Don Cherry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter) "Don Cherry (trumpeter)"), alto saxophonist [John Tchicai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Tchicai "John Tchicai"), and trombonist [Roswell Rudd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roswell_Rudd "Roswell Rudd"), collaborated in recording _[New York Eye and Ear Control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Eye_and_Ear_Control "New York Eye and Ear Control")_, a freely improvised soundtrack to Canadian artist and filmmaker [Michael Snow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Snow "Michael Snow")'s film of the same name.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-ESP-12) During this time, Ayler began to garner some attention from critics, although he was not able to foster much of a fan following. However, later in 1964, Ayler, Peacock, Murray, and Cherry were invited to travel to Europe for a brief Scandinavian tour, which too yielded some new recordings, including _[The Copenhagen Tapes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Copenhagen_Tapes "The Copenhagen Tapes")_, _[Ghosts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghosts_(Albert_Ayler_album) "Ghosts (Albert Ayler album)")_ (re-released later as _Vibrations_), and _[The Hilversum Session](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hilversum_Session "The Hilversum Session")_. Ayler recorded _[Bells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bells_(album) "Bells (album)")_ on May 1, 1965. It is a ferociously paced 20-minute improvisation featuring his signature military-march influenced melodies. _[Spirits Rejoice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spirits_Rejoice "Spirits Rejoice")_ was recorded on September 23, 1965, at Judson Hall in New York City, and features a much larger band than the sparse trio of his earlier album _Spiritual Unity_. _The Encyclopedia of Popular Music_ describes _Spirits Rejoice_ as a "riotous, hugely emotional and astonishingly creative celebration of the urge to make noise."[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-13) Both albums feature Albert's brother, trumpet player [Donald Ayler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Ayler "Donald Ayler"), who translated his brother's expansive approach to improvisation to the trumpet. Donald played with Albert until he experienced a debilitating nervous breakdown in 1967.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-14) In 1966 Ayler was signed to [Impulse Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impulse_Records "Impulse Records") at the urging of Coltrane, the label's star attraction at that time.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-Jenkins26-15) But even on Impulse, Ayler's radically different music never found a sizable audience. Ayler's first set for Impulse was recorded a few weeks before Christmas in 1966, entitled _[Albert Ayler in Greenwich Village](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler_in_Greenwich_Village "Albert Ayler in Greenwich Village")_. Ayler performed with his brother, Michel Samson, [Beaver Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beaver_Harris "Beaver Harris"), [Henry Grimes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Grimes "Henry Grimes"), and Bill Folwell, while Coltrane was in attendance. For a tune titled "For John Coltrane", Ayler returned to the alto saxophone for the first time in years.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-Jenkins26-15) Ayler first sang on a recording in a version of "Ghosts" performed in Paris in 1966, in which his vocal style was similar to that of his saxophone, with an eerie disregard for pitch.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-16) Ayler continued to experiment with vocals for the rest of his career (see, for example, the wordless vocalising near the end of "Love Cry" from the [album of the same name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love_Cry "Love Cry")); however, his singing on later albums such as _[New Grass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Grass "New Grass")_ and _[Music Is the Healing Force of the Universe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_Is_the_Healing_Force_of_the_Universe "Music Is the Healing Force of the Universe")_ has been the subject of some derision. [Val Wilmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Val_Wilmer "Val Wilmer") referred to his singing as "tortuous",[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-17) and critics have stated that "his words and vocal delivery are truly frightening",[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-18) describing him as having "a bellowing, untrained voice that was wavering at its most controlled,"[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-pitchfork_newgrass-19) and delivering lyrics in "a manic wail".[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-pitchfork_newgrass-19) In 1967, John Coltrane died of liver cancer, and Ayler was asked to perform at his funeral.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-20) (One of Coltrane's last wishes was that Ayler and Ornette Coleman should play at his funeral.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-Wilmer_2018_142-21)) It is said that during his performance, Ayler ripped his saxophone from his mouth at two points: once, to emit a cry of anguish, the other a cry of joy to symbolize his friend and mentor's ascension into heaven.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-Jenkins26-15) Ayler later recalled: "John was like a visitor to this planet. He came in peace and he left in peace; but during his time here, he kept trying to reach new levels of awareness, of peace, of spirituality. That's why I regard the music he played as spiritual music - John's way of getting closer and closer to the Creator."[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-22) In the liner notes for Ayler's album _[Love Cry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love_Cry "Love Cry")_, [Frank Kofsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Kofsky "Frank Kofsky") wrote that Ayler said the following concerning Coltrane's album _[Meditations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meditations_(John_Coltrane_album) "Meditations (John Coltrane album)")_: "The father, son, and holy ghost. What Coltrane was talking about there - maybe it was a biblical term: he was the father, [Pharoah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pharoah_Sanders "Pharoah Sanders") was the son, and I was the holy ghost. And only he could tell me things like that."[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-lovecry-23) ### Final years and death For the next two-and-a-half years Ayler began to move from a mostly improvisatory style to one that focused more closely on compositions.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-Kernfeld-24) Some considered this a result of pressures from Impulse who, unlike ESP-Disk, placed heavier emphasis on accessibility than artistic expression.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-Jenkins27-25) In 1967 and 1968, Ayler recorded three LPs that featured the lyrics and vocals of his girlfriend [Mary Maria Parks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Maria_Parks?action=edit&redlink=1 "Mary Maria Parks") and introduced regular chord changes, funky beats, and electronic instruments.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-Schwartz-26) Ayler himself sang on his album _[New Grass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Grass "New Grass")_, which hearkened back to his roots in R&B as a teenager. However, this album was unsuccessful, scorned by Ayler fans and critics alike.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-Schwartz-26) Ayler staunchly asserted that he wanted to move in this R&B and rock-and-roll direction, and that he was not simply succumbing to the pressures of Impulse and the popular music of that day, and it is true that Ayler heavily emphasizes the spirituality that seems to define the bulk of his work.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-Jenkins27-25) (However, according to [Gary Giddins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Giddins "Gary Giddins"), "In interviews, Ayler left no doubt about who was responsible for _New Grass_: 'They told me to do this. [Bob Thiele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Thiele "Bob Thiele"). You think I would do that? He said, "Look Albert, you gotta get with the young generation now."'"[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-27)) _New Grass_ begins with the track "Message from Albert", in which Ayler speaks directly to his listener, explaining that this album was nothing like his ones before it, that was of "a different dimension in \[his\] life." He claims that, "through meditation, dreams, and visions, \[he has\] been made a Universal Man, through the power of the Creator..." At around this time, there were hints that Ayler was becoming emotionally unstable, blaming himself for his brother's breakdown.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-28) In 1969, he submitted an impassioned, rambling open letter to _[the Cricket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Cricket_(magazine) "The Cricket (magazine)")_ magazine entitled "To Mr. Jones—I Had a Vision", in which he described startling apocalyptic spiritual visions.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-Jenkins27-25) He "saw in a vision the new Earth built by God coming out of Heaven," and implored the readers to share the message of Revelations, insisting that "This is very important. The time is now."[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-29) [Noah Howard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noah_Howard "Noah Howard") recalled seeing Ayler that summer, wearing gloves and a full-length fur coat despite the heat, his face covered in Vaseline, and saying "Got to protect myself."[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-30) His final album, _[Music Is the Healing Force of the Universe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_Is_the_Healing_Force_of_the_Universe "Music Is the Healing Force of the Universe")_, featured rock musicians such as [Henry Vestine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Vestine "Henry Vestine") of [Canned Heat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canned_Heat "Canned Heat") alongside jazz musicians like pianist [Bobby Few](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Few "Bobby Few"). This was a return to his blues-roots with very heavy rock influences, but did feature more of Ayler's signature timbre variations and energetic solos than the unsuccessful _New Grass_. In July 1970, Ayler returned to the free jazz idiom for a group of shows in France (including at the [Fondation Maeght](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fondation_Maeght "Fondation Maeght"), documented on _[Nuits de la Fondation Maeght](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuits_de_la_Fondation_Maeght_(Albert_Ayler_album) "Nuits de la Fondation Maeght (Albert Ayler album)")_), but the band he was able to assemble (Call Cobbs, bassist Steve Tintweiss and drummer [Allen Blairman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allen_Blairman "Allen Blairman")) was not regarded as being of the caliber of his earlier groups.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-31) Ayler disappeared on November 5, 1970, and he was found dead in New York City's [East River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_River "East River") on November 25, a presumed suicide.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-Mandel-2) For some time afterwards rumors circulated that Ayler had been murdered, a long-standing [urban legend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_legend "Urban legend") claiming the Mafia had tied him to a jukebox.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-32) ## Artistry Ayler routinely showcased his highly untraditional personal saxophone style in very conventional musical contexts, including children's songs, march melodies, and gospel hymns.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-Mandel-2) However, Ayler's wild energy and intense improvisations transformed them into something nearly unrecognizable. Ayler took a deconstructive approach to his music, which was characteristic of the free jazz era. Phil Hardy says that Ayler "dismantled" melody and harmony to more deeply explore "the physical properties" of his saxophone.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-33) Ayler wished to free himself and his bandmates to improvise, relate to one another, and relate to their instruments on a more raw, "primal" level.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-Litweiler151-34) The intensely spiritual aspect of Ayler's music was clearly aligned with the beliefs of jazz saxophonist John Coltrane, who was profoundly affected by the "otherworldly" sounds of Ayler's music. This effect is especially evident in Coltrane's albums _[Meditations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meditations_(John_Coltrane_album) "Meditations (John Coltrane album)")_ and _[Stellar Regions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stellar_Regions "Stellar Regions")_.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-Whitehead-6) (Coltrane served as a mentor throughout Ayler's life, providing financial and professional support.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-35)) This intensity, the extremes to which Ayler took his tenor saxophone, is the most defining aspect of his sound. His style is characterized by [timbre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timbre "Timbre") variations, including squeaks, honks, and improvisation in very high and very low registers.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-Shipton-36) He possessed a deep blistering tone—achieved by using the stiff plastic Fibrecane no. 4 reeds[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-37) on his [tenor saxophone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenor_saxophone "Tenor saxophone")—and used a broad, pathos-filled [vibrato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vibrato "Vibrato").[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-Litweiler151-34) Ayler experimented with [microtonality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microtonality "Microtonality") in his improvisations, seeking to explore the sounds that fall between the notes in a traditional scale.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-Shipton-36) This technique was best showcased when he played, as he often did, without a piano, backed only by bass and drums. Ayler also resisted the standard swing beat, and instead built momentum through the frenetic speed of his improvisatory lines, which he forcefully [overblew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overblowing "Overblowing") from his saxophone.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-Litweiler152-8) Jazz historian [Ted Gioia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Gioia "Ted Gioia") describes Ayler as a "virtuoso of the coarse and anomalous", and claims that Ayler aimed to break away from the constraints of playing notes and instead to "enter into a new realm in which the saxophone created " _sound_"."[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-38) ## Influence and legacy At no point in his career was Ayler allowed the comfort of a steady audience. Despite largely positive critical reception, he remained poor for his entire life and often sought financial support from his family and fellow musicians, including Coltrane.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-Kernfeld-24) However, Ayler's influence is still felt, and not only among jazz musicians. His wild sound foreshadowed contemporary hardcore, noise, and experimental rock styles.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-Mandel-2) Albert Ayler is one of the most revered historical figures in the genre of free jazz along with the likes of [Sun Ra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_Ra "Sun Ra"), Cecil Taylor, John Coltrane, Ornette Coleman, and [Milford Graves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milford_Graves "Milford Graves") (who drummed with Ayler). To this day his albums are among the best selling in the narrow genre of "free jazz", along with the aforementioned legends. The so-called "titans" of free jazz in the 21st century who play saxophone, such as [Charles Gayle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Gayle "Charles Gayle"),[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-39) [Ken Vandermark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ken_Vandermark "Ken Vandermark"),[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-40) [Peter Brötzmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Br%C3%B6tzmann "Peter Brötzmann"),[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-41) and the late [David S. Ware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_S._Ware "David S. Ware"),[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-42) were all heavily influenced by Albert Ayler. Ayler was also a crucial influence on some of his renowned contemporaries such as [Frank Lowe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Lowe "Frank Lowe"), Rev. [Frank Wright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Wright_(jazz_musician) "Frank Wright (jazz musician)"), [Charles Tyler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Tyler_(musician) "Charles Tyler (musician)") (on Ayler's album _Bells_), [Marion Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marion_Brown "Marion Brown"), and Frank Smith (on ESP-Disk _Burton Greene Quartet_). Ayler developed a close friendship with John Coltrane, and the two influenced each other's playing. Coltrane said that Ayler "filled an area that it seems I hadn't got to. I think what he's doing, it seems to be moving music into even higher frequencies."[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-43) Ayler stated: "when he \[Coltrane\] started playing, I had to listen just to his tone... To listen to him play was just like he was talking to me, saying, 'Brother, get yourself together _spiritually._ Just one sound - that's how profound this man was..."[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-lovecry-23) According to [Val Wilmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Val_Wilmer "Val Wilmer"), "the relationship between the two men was a very special one. They talked to each other constantly by telephone and by telegram and Coltrane was heavily influenced by the younger man."[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-44) Coltrane first heard Ayler in 1962, after which he told Ayler that "he had heard himself playing like that in a dream once."[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-45) In February of the following year, Ayler sat in with Coltrane's group for the first time during a gig at the [Jazz Temple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Jazz_Temple "The Jazz Temple") in [Cleveland, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleveland "Cleveland").[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-46) Beginning that year, "Coltrane and Ayler, when both in New York, were often in the same room. Various recollections have placed Coltrane watching Ayler and Cecil Taylor at the Take 3 Coffeehouse in the West Village in the fall of 1963; watching Ayler and [Eric Dolphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy "Eric Dolphy") together at the Half Note sometime that year; inviting Ayler onstage at the Half Note in March 1964; hearing Ayler's group with [Rashied Ali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rashied_Ali "Rashied Ali") at a little performance space at 27 Cooper Square in early 1965."[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-47) Following the recording of _[Ascension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album) "Ascension (John Coltrane album)")_ in June 1965 (after Ayler had sent him copies of his albums _[Ghosts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghosts_(Albert_Ayler_album) "Ghosts (Albert Ayler album)")_ and _[Spiritual Unity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity "Spiritual Unity")_), Coltrane "called Ayler and told him, 'I recorded an album and found that I was playing just like you.' Albert's reply: 'No man, don't you see, you were playing like yourself. You were just feeling what I feel and were just crying out for spiritual unity."[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-Wilmer_2018_142-21) While in Antibes a month later, Coltrane "remained... in his hotel room, practicing as usual, playing along to a tape of an Ayler concert."[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-48) The Swedish filmmaker [Kasper Collin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kasper_Collin "Kasper Collin") was so inspired by Ayler's music and life that he produced a documentary, _[My Name Is Albert Ayler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My_Name_Is_Albert_Ayler_(documentary) "My Name Is Albert Ayler (documentary)")_, which includes interviews with ESP-Disk founder [Bernard Stollman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_Stollman "Bernard Stollman"), along with interviews with Ayler's family, girlfriends and bandmates.[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-49) The film includes footage of Albert Ayler (from 1962, 1964, 1966 and 1970) and is built around his music and recordings of his voice (from interviews made between 1963 and 1970). On his 1969 album _[Folkjokeopus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folkjokeopus "Folkjokeopus")_, English guitarist/singer-songwriter [Roy Harper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_Harper_(singer) "Roy Harper (singer)"), dedicated the song "One for All" (" _One for Al_") to Albert Ayler, "who I knew and loved during my time in Copenhagen".[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-50)[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-51) Harper considered Ayler to be "one of the leading jazzmen of the age".[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-52) In the _Folkjokeopus_ [liner notes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liner_notes "Liner notes"), Harper states, "In many ways he \[Ayler\] was the king". - [Miles Davis Quintet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis_Quintet "Miles Davis Quintet") | | | | Website | [milesdavis.com](https://milesdavis.com/) | | Signature | | [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c6/Miles_Davis_Signature.svg/250px-Miles_Davis_Signature.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Miles_Davis_Signature.svg) | **Miles Dewey Davis III** (May 26, 1926–September 28, 1991) was an American trumpeter, bandleader, composer, and painter.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-1) He is among the most influential and acclaimed figures in the history of [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") and [20th-century music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/20th-century_music "20th-century music"). In a career spanning nearly five decades, Davis was at the forefront of several major stylistic developments in jazz, including [bebop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bebop "Bebop"), [cool jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cool_jazz "Cool jazz"), [hard bop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop "Hard bop"), [third stream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_stream "Third stream"), [modal jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz "Modal jazz"), [avant-garde jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde_jazz "Avant-garde jazz") and [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-allmusic-2) His legacy extends into [rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music"), [funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funk "Funk"), [classical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_music "Classical music") and [hip-hop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hip-hop "Hip-hop"). Born into an affluent family in [Alton, Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alton,_Illinois "Alton, Illinois"), and raised in [East St. Louis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_St._Louis "East St. Louis"), Davis started on the trumpet in his early teens. He left to study at the [Juilliard School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juilliard_School "Juilliard School") in New York City, before dropping out and making his professional debut as a member of saxophonist [Charlie Parker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Parker "Charlie Parker")'s bebop quintet from 1944 to 1948. Shortly afterwards, he recorded the _[Birth of the Cool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birth_of_the_Cool "Birth of the Cool")_ sessions for [Capitol Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capitol_Records "Capitol Records"), which were instrumental to the development of cool jazz. In the early 1950s, Davis recorded some of the earliest hard bop music under [Prestige Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prestige_Records "Prestige Records"). After a widely acclaimed comeback performance at the [Newport Jazz Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newport_Jazz_Festival "Newport Jazz Festival"), he signed a long-term contract with [Columbia Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Records "Columbia Records"), and recorded the album _['Round About Midnight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/'Round_About_Midnight "'Round About Midnight")_ in 1955.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEYanow2005176-3) It was his first work with saxophonist [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane") and bassist [Paul Chambers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Chambers "Paul Chambers"), key members of the sextet he led into the early 1960s. During this period, he alternated between orchestral jazz collaborations with arranger [Gil Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gil_Evans "Gil Evans"), such as the [Spanish music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_of_Spain "Music of Spain")–influenced _[Sketches of Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sketches_of_Spain "Sketches of Spain")_ (1960), and band recordings, such as _[Milestones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milestones_(Miles_Davis_album) "Milestones (Miles Davis album)")_ (1958) and _[Kind of Blue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue "Kind of Blue")_ (1959).[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-aar-4) The latter recording remains one of the most popular jazz albums of all time,[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcCurdy200461-5) having sold more than five million copies in the U.S. alone and 6.4 million copies worldwide. Davis made several lineup changes while recording _[Someday My Prince Will Come](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Someday_My_Prince_Will_Come_(Miles_Davis_album) "Someday My Prince Will Come (Miles Davis album)")_ (1961), his [1961 Blackhawk concerts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_Person_Friday_and_Saturday_Nights_at_the_Blackhawk,_Complete "In Person Friday and Saturday Nights at the Blackhawk, Complete"), and _[Seven Steps to Heaven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_Steps_to_Heaven "Seven Steps to Heaven")_ (1963), another commercial success that introduced bassist [Ron Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ron_Carter "Ron Carter"), pianist [Herbie Hancock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock "Herbie Hancock") and drummer [Tony Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Williams_(drummer) "Tony Williams (drummer)").[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-aar-4) After adding saxophonist [Wayne Shorter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter "Wayne Shorter") to his new quintet in 1964,[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-aar-4) Davis led them on a series of more abstract recordings often composed by the band members, helping pioneer the [post-bop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-bop "Post-bop") genre with albums such as _[E.S.P.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E.S.P._(Miles_Davis_album) "E.S.P. (Miles Davis album)")_ (1965) and _[Miles Smiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Smiles "Miles Smiles")_ (1967),[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-6) before transitioning into his electric period. During the 1970s, he experimented with rock, funk, [African rhythms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_rhythms "African rhythms"), emerging [electronic music technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_music_technology "Electronic music technology"), and an ever-changing lineup of musicians, including keyboardist [Joe Zawinul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Zawinul "Joe Zawinul"), drummer [Al Foster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Foster "Al Foster"), bassist [Michael Henderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Henderson "Michael Henderson") and guitarist [John McLaughlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McLaughlin_(musician) "John McLaughlin (musician)").[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFreeman20059%E2%80%9311,_155%E2%80%93156-7) This period, beginning with Davis's 1969 studio album _[In a Silent Way](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way "In a Silent Way")_ and concluding with the 1975 concert recording _[Agharta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album) "Agharta (album)")_, was the most controversial in his career, alienating and challenging many in jazz.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-8) His million-selling 1970 record _[Bitches Brew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew "Bitches Brew")_ helped spark a resurgence in the genre's commercial popularity with jazz fusion as the decade progressed.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-9) After a five-year retirement due to poor health, Davis resumed his career in the 1980s, employing younger musicians and [pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popular_music "Popular music") sounds on albums such as _[The Man with the Horn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Man_with_the_Horn "The Man with the Horn")_ (1981), _[You're Under Arrest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/You're_Under_Arrest_(Miles_Davis_album) "You're Under Arrest (Miles Davis album)")_ (1985) and _[Tutu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tutu_(album) "Tutu (album)")_ (1986). Critics were often unreceptive, but the decade garnered Davis his highest level of commercial recognition. He performed sold-out concerts worldwide, while branching out into visual arts, film and television work, before his death in 1991 from the combined effects of a stroke, [pneumonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pneumonia "Pneumonia") and [respiratory failure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Respiratory_failure "Respiratory failure"), aged 65.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-rsbio-10) In 2006, Davis was inducted into the [Rock and Roll Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_and_Roll_Hall_of_Fame "Rock and Roll Hall of Fame"),[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-Miles_Davis-11) which recognized him as "one of the key figures in the history of jazz".[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-Miles_Davis-11) _[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone "Rolling Stone")_ magazine described him as "the most revered jazz trumpeter of all time, not to mention one of the most important musicians of the 20th century",[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-rsbio-10) while [Gerald Early](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerald_Early "Gerald Early") called him inarguably one of the most influential and innovative musicians of that period.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-12) ## Early life \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Miles_Davis&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Early life")\] Davis was born on May 26, 1926, to an affluent African-American family in [Alton, Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alton,_Illinois "Alton, Illinois"), a suburb of [St. Louis, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Louis,_Missouri "St. Louis, Missouri").[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECook20079-13)[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEarly2001209-14) He had an older sister, Dorothy Mae (1925–1996), and a younger brother, Vernon (1929–1999). His mother, Cleota Mae Henry of [Arkansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arkansas "Arkansas"), was a music teacher and violinist, and his father, [Miles Dewey Davis Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Dewey_Davis_Jr. "Miles Dewey Davis Jr."), also of Arkansas, was a dentist. They owned a 200-acre (81ha) estate near [Pine Bluff, Arkansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pine_Bluff,_Arkansas "Pine Bluff, Arkansas"), with a profitable pig farm. In Pine Bluff, he and his siblings fished, hunted and rode horses.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_Complete_Illustrated_History''200717-15)[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrr201211-16) Davis's grandparents were the owners of an Arkansas farm where he would spend many summers.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWarner2014-17) In 1927, the family moved to [East St. Louis, Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_St._Louis,_Illinois "East St. Louis, Illinois"). They lived on the second floor of a commercial building behind a dental office in a predominantly white neighborhood. Davis's father would soon become distant to his children, as the [Great Depression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Depression "Great Depression") caused him to become increasingly consumed by his job, typically working six days a week.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWarner2014-17) From 1932 to 1934, Davis attended John Robinson Elementary School, an all-black school,[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEarly2001209-14) then Crispus Attucks, where he performed well in mathematics, music and sports.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrr201211-16) Davis had previously attended Catholic school.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWarner2014-17) At an early age he liked music, especially [blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blues "Blues"), [big bands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_band "Big band") and [gospel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gospel_music "Gospel music").[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_Complete_Illustrated_History''200717-15) [![View from the street of Davis's childhood single-family home in East St. Louis](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a8/House_of_Miles%2C_East_St._Louis.jpg/250px-House_of_Miles%2C_East_St._Louis.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:House_of_Miles,_East_St._Louis.jpg) The house at 1701 Kansas Avenue in [East St. Louis, Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_St._Louis,_Illinois "East St. Louis, Illinois"), where Davis lived from 1939 to 1944 In 1935, Davis received his first trumpet as a gift from John Eubanks, a friend of his father.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEarly2001210-18) He then took weekly lessons from "the biggest influence on my \[Davis's\] life", [Elwood Buchanan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elwood_Buchanan "Elwood Buchanan"), a teacher and musician who was a patient of his father's.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECook20079-13)[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-Reader's_Digest-19) His mother wanted him to play the violin instead.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_Complete_Illustrated_History''200719-20) Against the fashion of the time, Buchanan stressed the importance of playing without [vibrato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vibrato "Vibrato") and encouraged him to use a clear, mid-range tone. Davis said that whenever he started playing with heavy vibrato, Buchanan slapped his knuckles.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECook20079-13)[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_Complete_Illustrated_History''200719-20)[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe198932-21) In later years, Davis said, "I prefer a round sound with no attitude in it, like a round voice with not too much tremolo and not too much bass. Just right in the middle. If I can't get that sound I can't play anything."[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKahn2001a-22) The family soon moved to 1701 Kansas Avenue in East St. Louis.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWarner2014-17) In his autobiography, Davis stated, "By the age of 12, music had become the most important thing in my life."[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-Reader's_Digest-19) On his 13th birthday, his father bought him a new trumpet,[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEarly2001210-18) and Davis began to play in local bands. He took additional trumpet lessons from Joseph Gustat, principal trumpeter of the [St. Louis Symphony Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Louis_Symphony_Orchestra "St. Louis Symphony Orchestra").[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEarly2001210-18) Davis would also play the trumpet in talent shows he and his siblings would put on.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWarner2014-17) In 1941, the 15-year-old attended [East St. Louis Lincoln High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_St._Louis_Lincoln_High_School "East St. Louis Lincoln High School"), where he joined the marching band directed by Buchanan and entered music competitions. Years later, Davis said that he was discriminated against in these competitions due to his race, but he added that these experiences made him a better musician.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrr201211-16) When a drummer asked him to play a certain passage of music, and he could not do it, he began to learn [music theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_theory "Music theory"): "I went and got everything, every book I could get to learn about theory."[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_Complete_Illustrated_History''200723-23) At Lincoln, Davis met his first girlfriend, Irene Birth (later Cawthon).[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorton200510-24) He had a band that performed at the Elks Club.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-Arons-25) Part of his earnings paid for his sister's education at [Fisk University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fisk_University "Fisk University").[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEarly2001211-26) Davis befriended trumpeter [Clark Terry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clark_Terry "Clark Terry"), who suggested he play without vibrato, and performed with him for several years.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEarly2001210-18)[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEarly2001211-26) With encouragement from his teacher and girlfriend, Davis filled a vacant spot in the [Rhumboogie Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhumboogie_Caf%C3%A9 "Rhumboogie Café"), also known as the Blue Devils, led by Eddie Randle. He became the band's musical director, which involved hiring musicians and scheduling rehearsal.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEarly2001211-26)[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrr201212-27) Years later, Davis considered this job one of the most important of his career.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_Complete_Illustrated_History''200723-23) [Sonny Stitt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonny_Stitt "Sonny Stitt") tried to persuade him to join the [Tiny Bradshaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiny_Bradshaw "Tiny Bradshaw") band, which was passing through town, but his mother insisted he finish high school before going on tour. He said later, "I didn't talk to her for two weeks. And I didn't go with the band either."[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrr201213-28) In January 1944, Davis finished high school and graduated in absentia in June; the next month, his girlfriend gave birth to a daughter, Cheryl.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEarly2001211-26) In July 1944, [Billy Eckstine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Eckstine "Billy Eckstine") visited St. Louis with a band that included [Art Blakey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Blakey "Art Blakey"), [Dizzy Gillespie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie "Dizzy Gillespie") and [Charlie Parker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Parker "Charlie Parker"). Trumpeter Buddy Anderson was too sick to perform,[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECook20079-13) so Davis was invited to join. He played with the band for two weeks at [Club Riviera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Club_Riviera "Club Riviera").[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEarly2001211-26)[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECook200710-29) After playing with these musicians, he was certain he should move to New York City, "where the action was".[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_Complete_Illustrated_History''200729-30) His mother wanted him to go to Fisk University, like his sister, and study piano or violin. Davis had other interests.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrr201213-28) ## Career \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Miles_Davis&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Career")\] ### 1944–1948: New York City and the bebop years \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Miles_Davis&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: 1944–1948: New York City and the bebop years")\] [![Davis playing trumpet in a jazz club beside Tommy Potter on bass, Charlie Parker playing alto saxophone, Max Roach on drums and Duke Jordan playing the piano](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/99/Charlie_Parker%2C_Tommy_Potter%2C_Miles_Davis%2C_Duke_Jordan%2C_Max_Roach_%28Gottlieb_06851%29.jpg/250px-Charlie_Parker%2C_Tommy_Potter%2C_Miles_Davis%2C_Duke_Jordan%2C_Max_Roach_%28Gottlieb_06851%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Charlie_Parker,_Tommy_Potter,_Miles_Davis,_Duke_Jordan,_Max_Roach_(Gottlieb_06851).jpg) _From left_: [Tommy Potter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tommy_Potter "Tommy Potter"), [Charlie Parker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Parker "Charlie Parker"), [Max Roach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Roach "Max Roach") \[occluded\], Miles Davis and [Duke Jordan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_Jordan "Duke Jordan") at the [Three Deuces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_Deuces "Three Deuces") in August 1947 In September 1944, Davis accepted his father's idea of studying at the [Juilliard School of Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juilliard_School_of_Music "Juilliard School of Music") in New York City.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEarly2001211-26) After passing the audition, he attended classes in music theory, piano and dictation.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_Complete_Illustrated_History''200732-31) Davis often skipped his classes.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-Encyclop%C3%A6dia_Britannica-2020-32) Much of Davis's time was spent in clubs seeking his idol, Charlie Parker. According to Davis, [Coleman Hawkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coleman_Hawkins "Coleman Hawkins") told him "finish your studies at Juilliard and forget Bird \[Parker\]".[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECook200710-29)[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe198956-33) After finding Parker, he joined a cadre of regulars at [Minton's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minton's "Minton's") and [Monroe's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monroe's "Monroe's") in Harlem who held [jam sessions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jam_session "Jam session") every night. The other regulars included [J. J. Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._J._Johnson "J. J. Johnson"), [Kenny Clarke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenny_Clarke "Kenny Clarke"), [Thelonious Monk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thelonious_Monk "Thelonious Monk"), [Fats Navarro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fats_Navarro "Fats Navarro") and [Freddie Webster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freddie_Webster "Freddie Webster"). Davis reunited with Irene and their daughter Cheryl when they moved to New York City. Parker became a roommate.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEarly2001211-26)[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECook200710-29) Around this time Davis was paid an allowance of $40 (equivalent to $730in 2025[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-inflation-US-34)).[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-Cook-1985-35) In mid-1945, Davis failed to register for the year's autumn term at Juilliard and dropped out after three semesters[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_Complete_Illustrated_History''200717-15)[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEarly2001211-26)[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEarly200138-36) because he wanted to perform full-time.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEarly200168-37) Davis began performing at clubs on [52nd Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/52nd_Street_(Manhattan) "52nd Street (Manhattan)") with Coleman Hawkins and [Eddie "Lockjaw" Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddie_%22Lockjaw%22_Davis "Eddie \"Lockjaw\" Davis"). Davis recorded for the first time on April 24, 1945, when he entered the studio as a [sideman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sideman "Sideman") for [Herbie Fields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Fields "Herbie Fields")'s band.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEarly2001211-26)[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECook200710-29) During the next year, he recorded as a leader for the first time with the Miles Davis Sextet plus [Earl Coleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_Coleman_(singer) "Earl Coleman (singer)") and [Ann Baker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ann_Baker_(singer) "Ann Baker (singer)"), one of the few times he accompanied a singer.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-38) [![Davis seated playing piano; behind him stands Howard McGhee playing trumpet and Joe Albany, with Brick Fleagle, seated](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/92/Howard_McGhee%2C_Brick_Fleagle_and_Miles_Davis%2C_ca_September_1947_%28Gottlieb%29.jpg/250px-Howard_McGhee%2C_Brick_Fleagle_and_Miles_Davis%2C_ca_September_1947_%28Gottlieb%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Howard_McGhee,_Brick_Fleagle_and_Miles_Davis,_ca_September_1947_(Gottlieb).jpg) Davis on piano with [Howard McGhee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howard_McGhee "Howard McGhee") (trumpet), [Joe Albany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Albany "Joe Albany") (piano, standing) and [Brick Fleagle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brick_Fleagle "Brick Fleagle") (guitar, smoking), September 1947 In 1945, Davis replaced Dizzy Gillespie in Charlie Parker's quintet. On November 26, he participated in several recording sessions as part of Parker's group Reboppers that also involved Gillespie and [Max Roach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Roach "Max Roach"),[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEarly2001211-26) displaying hints of the style he would become known for. On Parker's tune " [Now's the Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Now's_the_Time_(composition) "Now's the Time (composition)")", Davis played a solo that anticipated [cool jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cool_jazz "Cool jazz"). He next joined a big band led by [Benny Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benny_Carter "Benny Carter"), performing in St. Louis and remaining with the band in California. He again played with Parker and Gillespie.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEarly2001212-39) In Los Angeles, Parker had a [nervous breakdown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nervous_breakdown "Nervous breakdown") that put him in the hospital for several months.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEarly2001212-39)[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-40) In March 1946, Davis played in studio sessions with Parker and began a collaboration with [Charles Mingus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus "Charles Mingus") that summer. Cawthon gave birth to Davis's second child, Gregory, in East St. Louis before reuniting with Davis in New York City the following year.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEarly2001212-39) Davis noted that by this time, "I was still so much into the music that I was even ignoring Irene." He had also turned to alcohol and cocaine.[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1989105-41) Davis was a member of [Billy Eckstine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Eckstine "Billy Eckstine")'s big band in 1946 and Gillespie's in 1947.[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-New_Grove-42) He joined a quintet led by Parker that also included Max Roach. Together they performed live with [Duke Jordan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_Jordan "Duke Jordan") and [Tommy Potter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tommy_Potter "Tommy Potter") for much of the year, including several studio sessions.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEarly2001212-39) In one session that May, Davis wrote the tune "Cheryl", for his daughter. Davis's first session as a leader followed in August 1947, playing as the Miles Davis All Stars that included Parker, pianist [John Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Lewis_(pianist) "John Lewis (pianist)") and bassist [Nelson Boyd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson_Boyd "Nelson Boyd"); they recorded " [Milestones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milestones_(instrumental_composition) "Milestones (instrumental composition)")", " [Half Nelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_Nelson_(composition) "Half Nelson (composition)")" and "Sippin' at Bells".[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEarly2001212-39)[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECook200712-43) After touring Chicago and Detroit with Parker's quintet, Davis returned to New York City in March 1948 and joined the [Jazz at the Philharmonic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_at_the_Philharmonic "Jazz at the Philharmonic") tour, which included a stop in St. Louis on April 30.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEarly2001212-39) ### 1948–1950: Miles Davis Nonet and _Birth of the Cool_ \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Miles_Davis&action=edit§ion=4 "Edit section: 1948–1950: Miles Davis Nonet and Birth of the Cool")\] In August 1948, Davis declined an offer to join [Duke Ellington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_Ellington "Duke Ellington")'s orchestra, as he had entered rehearsals with a nine-piece band featuring baritone saxophonist [Gerry Mulligan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerry_Mulligan "Gerry Mulligan") and arrangements by [Gil Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gil_Evans "Gil Evans"), taking an active role on what soon became his own project.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-44)[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEarly2001212-39) Evans's Manhattan apartment had become the meeting place for several young musicians and composers such as Davis, Roach, Lewis and Mulligan who were unhappy with the increasingly virtuoso instrumental techniques that dominated bebop.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECook200714-45) These gatherings led to the formation of the Miles Davis [Nonet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonet_(music) "Nonet (music)"), which included atypical modern jazz instruments such as the [French horn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_horn_in_jazz "French horn in jazz") and tuba, leading to a thickly textured, almost orchestral sound.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-Encyclop%C3%A6dia_Britannica-2020-32) The intent was to imitate the human voice through carefully arranged compositions and a relaxed, melodic approach to improvisation. In September, the band completed their sole engagement as the opening band for [Count Basie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count_Basie "Count Basie") at the [Royal Roost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Roost "Royal Roost") for two weeks. Davis had to persuade the venue's manager to write the sign "Miles Davis Nonet. Arrangements by Gil Evans, John Lewis and Gerry Mulligan". Davis returned to Parker's quintet, but relationships within the quintet were growing tense mainly due to Parker's erratic behavior caused by his drug addiction.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEarly2001212-39) Early in his time with Parker, Davis abstained from drugs, chose a vegetarian diet, and spoke of the benefits of water and juice.[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECook20072-46) In December 1948, Davis quit, saying he was not being paid.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEarly2001212-39) His departure began a period when he worked mainly as a freelancer and sideman. His nonet remained active until the end of 1949. After signing a contract with [Capitol Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capitol_Records "Capitol Records"), they recorded sessions in January and April 1949, which sold little but influenced the " [cool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cool_jazz "Cool jazz")" or " [West Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Coast_jazz "West Coast jazz")" style of jazz.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEarly2001212-39) The lineup changed throughout the year and included tuba player [Bill Barber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Barber_(musician) "Bill Barber (musician)"), alto saxophonist [Lee Konitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Konitz "Lee Konitz"), pianist [Al Haig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Haig "Al Haig"), trombone players [Mike Zwerin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Zwerin "Mike Zwerin") with [Kai Winding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kai_Winding "Kai Winding"), French horn players [Junior Collins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Junior_Collins "Junior Collins") with Sandy Siegelstein and [Gunther Schuller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunther_Schuller "Gunther Schuller"), and bassists [Al McKibbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_McKibbon "Al McKibbon") and [Joe Shulman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Shulman "Joe Shulman"). One track featured singer [Kenny Hagood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenny_Hagood "Kenny Hagood"). The presence of white musicians in the group angered some black players, many of whom were unemployed at the time, yet Davis rebuffed their criticisms.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1989117-47) Recording sessions with the nonet for Capitol continued until April 1950. The Nonet recorded a dozen tracks which were released as singles and subsequently compiled on the 1957 album _[Birth of the Cool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birth_of_the_Cool "Birth of the Cool")_.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-Encyclop%C3%A6dia_Britannica-2020-32) In May 1949, Davis performed with the [Tadd Dameron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tadd_Dameron "Tadd Dameron") Quintet with [Kenny Clarke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenny_Clarke "Kenny Clarke") and [James Moody](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Moody_(saxophonist) "James Moody (saxophonist)") at the [Paris International Jazz Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_Jazz_Festival "Paris Jazz Festival"). On his first trip abroad, Davis took a strong liking to Paris and its cultural environment, where he felt black jazz musicians and people of color in general were better respected than in the U.S. The trip, he said, "changed the way I looked at things forever".[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1989126-48) He began an affair with singer and actress [Juliette Gréco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juliette_Gr%C3%A9co "Juliette Gréco").[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1989126-48) ### 1949–1955: Signing with Prestige, heroin addiction and hard bop \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Miles_Davis&action=edit§ion=5 "Edit section: 1949–1955: Signing with Prestige, heroin addiction and hard bop")\] After returning from Paris in mid-1949, Davis became depressed and found little work except a short engagement with [Bud Powell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bud_Powell "Bud Powell") in October and guest spots in New York City, Chicago and Detroit until January 1950.[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTESzwed200491-49) He was falling behind in hotel rent and attempts were made to repossess his car. His heroin use became an expensive addiction, and Davis, not yet 24 years old, "lost my \[his\] sense of discipline, lost my sense of control over my life, and started to drift".[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEarly2001212-39)[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1989129-50) In August 1950, Cawthon gave birth to Davis's second son, Miles IV. Davis befriended boxer [Johnny Bratton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnny_Bratton "Johnny Bratton") which began his interest in the sport. Davis left Cawthon and his three children in New York City in the hands of one his friends, jazz singer [Betty Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betty_Carter "Betty Carter").[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTESzwed200491-49) He toured with Eckstine and [Billie Holiday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billie_Holiday "Billie Holiday") and was arrested for heroin possession in Los Angeles. The story was reported in _[DownBeat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DownBeat "DownBeat")_ magazine, which led to a further reduction in work, though he was acquitted weeks later.[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECook200725-51) By the 1950s, Davis had become more skilled and was experimenting with the middle register of the trumpet alongside harmonies and rhythms.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-Encyclop%C3%A6dia_Britannica-2020-32) In January 1951, Davis's fortunes improved when he signed a one-year contract with [Prestige](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prestige_Records "Prestige Records") after owner [Bob Weinstock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Weinstock "Bob Weinstock") became a fan of the nonet.[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1989175%E2%80%93176-52) Davis chose Lewis, trombonist [Bennie Green](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bennie_Green "Bennie Green"), bassist [Percy Heath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percy_Heath "Percy Heath"), saxophonist [Sonny Rollins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonny_Rollins "Sonny Rollins") and drummer [Roy Haynes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_Haynes "Roy Haynes"); they recorded what became part of _[Miles Davis and Horns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis_and_Horns "Miles Davis and Horns")_ (1956). Davis was hired for other studio dates in 1951[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECook200725-51) and began to transcribe scores for record labels to fund his heroin addiction. His second session for Prestige was released on _[The New Sounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_Sounds "The New Sounds")_ (1951), _[Dig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dig_(Miles_Davis_album) "Dig (Miles Davis album)")_ (1956) and _[Conception](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conception_(album) "Conception (album)")_ (1956).[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECook200726-53) Davis supported his heroin habit by playing music and by living the life of a hustler, exploiting prostitutes and receiving money from friends. By 1953, his addiction began to impair his playing. His drug habit became public in a _DownBeat_ interview with [Cab Calloway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cab_Calloway "Cab Calloway"), whom he never forgave, as it brought him "all pain and suffering".[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1989164-54) He returned to St. Louis and stayed with his father for several months.[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1989164-54) After a brief period with Roach and Mingus in September 1953,[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1989164%E2%80%93165-55) he returned to his father's home, where he concentrated on addressing his addiction.[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1989169%E2%80%93170-56) Davis lived in Detroit for about six months, avoiding New York City where it was easy to get drugs. Though he used heroin, he was still able to perform locally with [Elvin Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elvin_Jones "Elvin Jones") and [Tommy Flanagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tommy_Flanagan_(musician) "Tommy Flanagan (musician)") as part of [Billy Mitchell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Mitchell_(saxophonist) "Billy Mitchell (saxophonist)")'s house band at the [Blue Bird](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Bird_Inn "Blue Bird Inn") club. He was also "pimping a little".[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1989171-57) However, he was able to end his addiction, and, in February 1954, Davis returned to New York City, feeling good "for the first time in a long time", mentally and physically stronger, and joined a gym.[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1989174,_175,_184-58) He informed Weinstock and [Blue Note](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note "Blue Note") that he was ready to record with a quintet, which he was granted. He considered the albums that resulted from these and earlier sessions— _[Miles Davis Quartet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis_Quartet "Miles Davis Quartet")_ and _[Miles Davis, Vol. 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis_Volume_2 "Miles Davis Volume 2")_—"very important" because he felt his performances were particularly strong.[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1989175-59) He was paid roughly $750 (equivalent to $9,000in 2025[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-inflation-US-34)) for each album and refused to give away his publishing rights.[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1989176-60) [![An aluminum Harmon trumpet mute with the stem inserted](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/26/Trumpet_WahWahMute.jpg/250px-Trumpet_WahWahMute.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Trumpet_WahWahMute.jpg) During the 1950s, Davis began using a [Harmon mute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmon_mute "Harmon mute") on his trumpet. It became part of his signature sound for the rest of his career. Davis abandoned the bebop style and turned to the music of pianist [Ahmad Jamal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmad_Jamal "Ahmad Jamal"), whose approach and use of space influenced him.[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1989190-61) When he returned to the studio in June 1955 to record _[The Musings of Miles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Musings_of_Miles "The Musings of Miles")_, he wanted a pianist like Jamal and chose [Red Garland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Garland "Red Garland").[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1989190-61) _[Blue Haze](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Haze "Blue Haze")_ (1956), _[Bags' Groove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bags'_Groove "Bags' Groove")_ (1957), _[Walkin'](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walkin' "Walkin'")_ (1957) and _[Miles Davis and the Modern Jazz Giants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis_and_the_Modern_Jazz_Giants "Miles Davis and the Modern Jazz Giants")_ (1959) documented the evolution of his sound with the [Harmon mute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmon_mute "Harmon mute") placed close to the microphone and the use of more spacious and relaxed phrasing. He assumed a central role in [hard bop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop "Hard bop"), less radical in harmony and melody, and used popular songs and [American standards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_American_Songbook "Great American Songbook") as starting points for improvisation. Hard bop distanced itself from cool jazz with a harder beat and music inspired by the blues.[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-62) A few critics consider _Walkin'_(April 1954) the album that created the hard bop genre.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKahn2001a-22) Davis gained a reputation for being cold, distant and easily angered. He wrote that in 1954, [Sugar Ray Robinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sugar_Ray_Robinson "Sugar Ray Robinson") "was the most important thing in my life besides music", and he adopted Robinson's "arrogant attitude".[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1989183-63) He showed contempt for critics and the press.\[ _[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] Davis had an operation to remove [polyps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polyp_(medicine) "Polyp (medicine)") from his larynx in October 1955.[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTESzwed2004-64) The doctors told him to remain silent after the operation, but he got into an argument that permanently damaged his vocal cords and gave him a raspy voice for the rest of his life.[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-65) He was called "the Prince of Darkness", adding a patina of mystery to his public persona.[\[a\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-69) ### 1955–1959: Signing with Columbia, first quintet and modal jazz \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Miles_Davis&action=edit§ion=6 "Edit section: 1955–1959: Signing with Columbia, first quintet and modal jazz")\] In July 1955, Davis's fortunes improved considerably when he played at the [Newport Jazz Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newport_Jazz_Festival "Newport Jazz Festival"), with a lineup of Monk, Heath, drummer [Connie Kay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connie_Kay "Connie Kay"), and horn players [Zoot Sims](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zoot_Sims "Zoot Sims") and [Gerry Mulligan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerry_Mulligan "Gerry Mulligan").[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_Complete_Illustrated_History''200773-70)[\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-Natambu-2014-71) The performance was praised by critics and audiences alike, who considered it to be a highlight of the festival, as well as helping Davis, the least well known musician in the group, to increase his popularity among affluent white audiences.[\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-Natambu-2014-71)[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorton200527-72) He tied with Dizzy Gillespie for best trumpeter in the 1955 _DownBeat_ magazine Readers' Poll.[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECook200743%E2%80%9344-73) [George Avakian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Avakian "George Avakian") of [Columbia Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Records "Columbia Records") heard Davis perform at Newport and wanted to sign him to the label. Davis had one year left on his contract with Prestige, which required him to release four more albums. He signed a contract with Columbia that included a $4,000 advance (equivalent to $48,000in 2025[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-inflation-US-34)) and required that his recordings for Columbia remain unreleased until his agreement with Prestige expired.[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarr199896-74)[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1989192-75) At the request of Avakian, he formed the [Miles Davis Quintet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis_Quintet "Miles Davis Quintet") for a performance at [Café Bohemia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caf%C3%A9_Bohemia "Café Bohemia"). The quintet contained [Sonny Rollins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonny_Rollins "Sonny Rollins") on tenor saxophone, [Red Garland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Garland "Red Garland") on piano, [Paul Chambers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Chambers "Paul Chambers") on double bass and [Philly Joe Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philly_Joe_Jones "Philly Joe Jones") on drums.
