## Personal life \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Miles_Davis&action=edit§ion=13 "Edit section: Personal life")\] In 1957,[\[178\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-179) Davis began a relationship with [Frances Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frances_Taylor_Davis "Frances Taylor Davis"), a dancer he had met in 1953 at [Ciro's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ciro's "Ciro's") in Los Angeles.[\[179\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-180)[\[180\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1989227-181) They married in December 1959 in [Toledo, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toledo,_Ohio "Toledo, Ohio").[\[181\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-182) Due to Miles Davis's physical abuse of Frances Taylor, their relationship suffered. He later wrote, "Every time I hit her, I felt bad because a lot of it really wasn't her fault but had to do with me being temperamental and jealous."[\[182\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1989228-183)[\[183\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1989290-184)[\[184\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-185) One theory about his behavior was that in 1963 he had increased his use of alcohol and cocaine to alleviate joint pain caused by [sickle cell anemia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sickle_cell_anemia "Sickle cell anemia").[\[185\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1989267-186)[\[186\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEThe_Complete_Illustrated_History2007109-187) He hallucinated, "looking for this imaginary person" in his house while wielding a kitchen knife. Soon after the photograph for the album _[E.S.P.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E.S.P._(Miles_Davis_album) "E.S.P. (Miles Davis album)")_ (1965) was taken, Taylor left him for the final time.[\[187\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1989281%E2%80%93282-188) She filed for divorce in 1966; it was finalized in February 1968.[\[188\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-189)[\[189\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTESzwed2004268-190) In September 1968, Davis married 23-year-old model and songwriter [Betty Mabry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betty_Mabry "Betty Mabry").[\[190\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-191) In his autobiography, Davis described her as a "high-class groupie, who was very talented but who didn't believe in her own talent".[\[191\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1989-192) Mabry, a familiar face in the New York City counterculture, introduced Davis to popular rock, soul and funk musicians.[\[192\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_Complete_Illustrated_History''2007143-193) Jazz critic [Leonard Feather](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Feather "Leonard Feather") visited Davis's apartment and was shocked to find him listening to albums by [the Byrds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Byrds "The Byrds"), [Aretha Franklin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aretha_Franklin "Aretha Franklin") and [Dionne Warwick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dionne_Warwick "Dionne Warwick"). He also liked [James Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Brown "James Brown"), [Sly and the Family Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sly_and_the_Family_Stone "Sly and the Family Stone"), and [Jimi Hendrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimi_Hendrix "Jimi Hendrix"),[\[193\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_Complete_Illustrated_History''2007145-194) whose group [Band of Gypsys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Band_of_Gypsys "Band of Gypsys") particularly impressed Davis.[\[194\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-195) Davis filed for divorce from Mabry in 1969, after accusing her of having an affair with Hendrix.[\[191\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1989-192) [![Davis, wearing sunglasses, a fedora and a trench coat, to the left of Cicely Tyson, who is wearing sunglasses and a fur coat and is holding a rolled-up poster. They are seated in a waiting area at Amsterdam Airport Schiphol.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/48/Miles_Davis_and_Cicely_Tyson_1982.jpg/250px-Miles_Davis_and_Cicely_Tyson_1982.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Miles_Davis_and_Cicely_Tyson_1982.jpg) Davis and [Cicely Tyson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cicely_Tyson "Cicely Tyson") in 1982 On October 10, 1969, Davis was shot at five times while in his Ferrari with Marguerite Eskridge, one of his lovers. One bullet grazed his hip; Eskridge was unharmed.[\[122\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_Complete_Illustrated_History''2007150-123) Davis later wrote that the incident arose from a dispute among nightclub promoters.[\[195\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-196) In 1970, Marguerite gave birth to their son Erin. By 1979, Davis rekindled his relationship with actress [Cicely Tyson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cicely_Tyson "Cicely Tyson"), who helped him to overcome his cocaine addiction and regain his enthusiasm for music. The two married in November 1981,[\[196\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1989348-197)[\[197\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEThe_Complete_Illustrated_History2007180-198) but their tumultuous marriage ended with Tyson filing for divorce in 1988, which was finalized in 1989.[\[198\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1989390%E2%80%93391-199) In 1984, Davis met 34-year-old sculptor Jo Gelbard.[\[199\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-The_Last_Miles-200) She taught Davis how to paint; the two were frequent collaborators and were soon romantically involved, eventually leaving their respective partners and living together.[\[165\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-Broeske-2006-166)[\[199\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-The_Last_Miles-200)[\[200\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-201) By 1985, Davis was [diabetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Type_2_diabetes "Type 2 diabetes") and required daily injections of insulin.[\[201\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1989363%E2%80%9364-202) Davis became increasingly aggressive in his final year due in part to the medication he was taking,[\[199\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-The_Last_Miles-200) and his aggression manifested as violence towards Gelbard.[\[199\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-The_Last_Miles-200) ## Death \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Miles_Davis&action=edit§ion=14 "Edit section: Death")\] [![Davis's grave headstone, inscribed: "In Memory Of / Sir Miles Davis / 1926–1991". Engraved on the right side is a trumpet, and across the bottom is a musical staff with the first two measures of his composition "Solar". Around the base of the headstone are pine branches with red flowers and a bow.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e7/Sir_Miles_Davis_Gravesite.JPG/250px-Sir_Miles_Davis_Gravesite.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sir_Miles_Davis_Gravesite.JPG) Davis's grave in [Woodlawn Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodlawn_Cemetery_(Bronx) "Woodlawn Cemetery (Bronx)"), Bronx; the headstone is inscribed with the beginning notes of his composition " [Solar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_(composition) "Solar (composition)")".[\[202\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-203) In early September 1991, Davis checked into [St. John's Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_John's_Health_Center "Saint John's Health Center") near his home in [Santa Monica, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Monica,_California "Santa Monica, California"), for routine tests.[\[203\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorton2005149-204) Doctors suggested he have a [tracheal tube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tracheal_tube "Tracheal tube") implanted to relieve his breathing after repeated bouts of [bronchial pneumonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bronchial_pneumonia "Bronchial pneumonia"). A tracheal tube would have made playing the trumpet nearly impossible. The suggestion provoked an outburst from Davis that led to an [intracerebral hemorrhage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intracerebral_hemorrhage "Intracerebral hemorrhage") followed by a coma. According to Jo Gelbard, on September 26, Davis painted his final painting—and that painting, composed of dark, ghostly figures dripping blood, "was full of his imminent demise".[\[141\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-Byrnes-2005-142) After several days on life support, his machine was turned off and he died on September 28, 1991, in the arms of Gelbard.[\[165\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-Broeske-2006-166)[\[204\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorton2005150-205) He was 65 years old. Davis's death was attributed to the combined effects of a stroke, pneumonia and respiratory failure.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-Miles_Davis-11) According to Troupe, Davis was taking [azidothymidine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azidothymidine "Azidothymidine") (AZT), a type of [antiretroviral drug](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antiretroviral_drug "Antiretroviral drug") used for the treatment of [HIV and AIDS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HIV_and_AIDS "HIV and AIDS"), during his treatments in the hospital.[\[205\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTESzwed2004393-206) A funeral service was held on October 5, 1991, at [St. Peter's Lutheran Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citigroup_Center#St._Peter's_Lutheran_Church "Citigroup Center") on [Lexington Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lexington_Avenue "Lexington Avenue") in New York City[\[206\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-207)[\[207\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-208) which was attended by around 500 friends, family members and musical acquaintances, with many fans standing in the rain.[\[208\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-209)[\[209\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-210)[\[210\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECole2005409-211) He was buried in [Woodlawn Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodlawn_Cemetery_(Bronx) "Woodlawn Cemetery (Bronx)") in [the Bronx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bronx "The Bronx"), New York City, with one of his trumpets, near the site of [Duke Ellington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_Ellington "Duke Ellington")'s grave.[\[210\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECole2005409-211)[\[211\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisSussman2006-212) At the time of his death, Davis's estate was valued at more than $1 million (equivalent to roughly $2.4 million in 2025[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-inflation-US-34)). In his will, Davis left 20 percent to his daughter Cheryl Davis, 40 percent to his son Erin Davis, 10 percent to his nephew Vincent Wilburn Jr. and 15 percent each to his brother Vernon Davis and his sister Dorothy Wilburn. He excluded his two sons Gregory and Miles IV.[\[212\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-213) ## Views on his earlier work \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Miles_Davis&action=edit§ion=15 "Edit section: Views on his earlier work")\] Late in his life, from the "electric period" onwards, Davis repeatedly explained his reasons for not wishing to perform his earlier works, such as _[Birth of the Cool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birth_of_the_Cool "Birth of the Cool")_ or _[Kind of Blue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue "Kind of Blue")_. In his view, remaining stylistically static was the wrong option.[\[213\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisSultanof20022%E2%80%933-214) He commented, "' [So What](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/So_What_(Miles_Davis_composition) "So What (Miles Davis composition)")' or _Kind of Blue_, they were done in that era, the right hour, the right day, and it happened. It's over... What I used to play with [Bill Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans "Bill Evans"), all those different modes, and substitute chords, we had the energy then and we liked it. But I have no feel for it anymore, it's more like warmed-over turkey."[\[214\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKahn2001b-215) When [Shirley Horn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shirley_Horn "Shirley Horn") insisted in 1990 that Miles reconsider playing the ballads and modal tunes of his _Kind of Blue_ period, he said, "Nah, it hurts my lip."[\[214\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKahn2001b-215) Bill Evans, who played piano on _Kind of Blue_, said, "I would like to hear more of the consummate melodic master, but I feel that big business and his record company have had a corrupting influence on his material. The rock and pop thing certainly draws a wider audience."[\[214\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKahn2001b-215) Throughout his later career, Davis declined offers to reinstate his 1960s quintet.[\[141\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-Byrnes-2005-142) Many books and documentaries focus on his work before 1975.[\[141\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-Byrnes-2005-142) According to an article by _[The Independent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Independent "The Independent")_, from 1975 onwards a decline in critical praise for Davis's output began to form, with many viewing the era as "worthless": "There is a surprisingly widespread view that, in terms of the merits of his musical output, Davis might as well have died in 1975."[\[141\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-Byrnes-2005-142) In a 1982 interview in _[DownBeat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DownBeat "DownBeat")_, [Wynton Marsalis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wynton_Marsalis "Wynton Marsalis") said, "They call Miles's stuff jazz. That stuff is not jazz, man. Just because somebody played jazz at one time, that doesn't mean they're still playing it."[\[141\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-Byrnes-2005-142) Despite his contempt for Davis's later work, Marsalis's work is "laden with ironic references to Davis' music of the '60s".[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-Cook-1985-35) Davis did not necessarily disagree; lambasting what he saw as Marsalis's stylistic conservatism, Davis said, "Jazz is dead... it's finito! It's over and there's no point apeing the shit."[\[215\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-gilroy1993-216) Writer [Stanley Crouch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_Crouch "Stanley Crouch") criticized Davis's work from _[In a Silent Way](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way "In a Silent Way")_ onwards.[\[141\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-Byrnes-2005-142) ## Legacy and influence \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Miles_Davis&action=edit§ion=16 "Edit section: Legacy and influence")\] [![A larger-than-lifesize bronze statue of Davis playing trumpet wearing sunglasses and a trench coat. Behind it is the Kielce Cultural Centre.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/81/Pomnik_Milesa_Davisa_Kielce_01_ssj_20060304.jpg/250px-Pomnik_Milesa_Davisa_Kielce_01_ssj_20060304.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pomnik_Milesa_Davisa_Kielce_01_ssj_20060304.jpg) The [Statue of Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statue_of_Miles_Davis "Statue of Miles Davis") by Grzegorz Łagowski, unveiled in 2001, in [Kielce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kielce "Kielce"), Poland Miles Davis is considered one of the most innovative, influential and respected figures in the history of music. _[The Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Guardian "The Guardian")_ described him as "a pioneer of 20th-century music, leading many of the key developments in the world of jazz."[\[216\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-guardian-217) He has been called "one of the great innovators in jazz",[\[217\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-218) and had the titles Prince of Darkness and the Picasso of Jazz bestowed upon him.[\[218\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_Complete_Illustrated_History''20078-219) _[The Rolling Stone Encyclopedia of Rock & Roll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone "Rolling Stone")_ said, "Miles Davis played a crucial and inevitably controversial role in every major development in jazz since the mid-'40s, and no other jazz musician has had so profound an effect on rock. Miles Davis was the most widely recognized jazz musician of his era, an outspoken social critic and an arbiter of style—in attitude and fashion—as well as music."[\[219\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-220) William Ruhlmann of [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic") wrote, "To examine his career is to examine the history of jazz from the mid-1940s to the early 1990s, since he was in the thick of almost every important innovation and stylistic development in the music during that period... It can even be argued that jazz stopped evolving when Davis wasn't there to push it forward."[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-allmusic-2) Francis Davis of _[The Atlantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Atlantic "The Atlantic")_ noted that Davis's career can be seen as "an ongoing critique of bebop: the origins of 'cool' jazz..., hard bop, or 'funky'..., modal improvisation..., and jazz–rock fusion... can be traced to his efforts to tear bebop down to its essentials."[\[220\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-Davis-2016-221) His approach, owing largely to the African-American performance tradition that focused on individual expression, emphatic interaction, and creative response to shifting contents, had a profound impact on generations of jazz musicians.[\[221\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-possible-222) In 2016, the digital publication _[The Pudding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pudding "The Pudding")_, in an article examining Davis's legacy, found that 2,452 Wikipedia pages mention Davis, with over 286 citing him as an influence.[\[222\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-223) [![A close-up of a brown and green street-name sign reading: "W 77 St / Miles Davis Way"](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/30/Miles_Davis_Way%2C_NYC_IMG_5819.JPG/250px-Miles_Davis_Way%2C_NYC_IMG_5819.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Miles_Davis_Way,_NYC_IMG_5819.JPG) The westernmost part of 77th Street in New York City has been named Miles Davis Way. He once lived on the block. On November 5, 2009, U.S. Representative [John Conyers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Conyers "John Conyers") of Michigan sponsored a measure in the United States House of Representatives to commemorate _Kind of Blue_ on its 50th anniversary. The measure also affirms jazz as a national treasure and "encourages the United States government to preserve and advance the art form of jazz music".[\[223\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-224) It passed with a vote of 409–0 on December 15, 2009.[\[224\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-225) The trumpet Davis used on the recording is displayed on the campus of the [University of North Carolina at Greensboro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_North_Carolina_at_Greensboro "University of North Carolina at Greensboro") ( UNCG). It was donated to the school by Arthur "Buddy" Gist, who met Davis in 1949 and became a close friend. That gift was the reason why the jazz program at UNCG is named the Miles Davis Jazz Studies Program.[\[225\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-226) In 1986, the [New England Conservatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_England_Conservatory "New England Conservatory") awarded Davis an honorary doctorate for his contributions to music.[\[226\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-227) Since 1960, the [National Academy of Recording Arts and Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Academy_of_Recording_Arts_and_Sciences "National Academy of Recording Arts and Sciences") (NARAS) honored him with eight [Grammy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Awards "Grammy Awards"), a [Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Lifetime_Achievement_Award "Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award") and three [Grammy Hall of Fame Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Hall_of_Fame "Grammy Hall of Fame").\[ _[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] In 2001, _The Miles Davis Story_, a two-hour documentary film by [Mike Dibb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Dibb "Mike Dibb"), won an [International Emmy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Emmy_Award "International Emmy Award") for arts documentary of the year.[\[227\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-Deans-228) Since 2005, the Miles Davis Jazz Committee has held an annual Miles Davis Jazz Festival.[\[228\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-Moon-2016-229) Also in 2005, the Davis biography _[The Last Miles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Miles "The Last Miles")_ was published;[\[229\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-230) a London exhibition was held of his paintings; _The Last Miles: The Music of Miles Davis, 1980–1991_ was released, detailing his final years; and eight of his albums from the 1960s and 1970s were reissued in celebration of the 50th anniversary of his signing to Columbia Records.[\[141\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-Byrnes-2005-142) In 2006, Davis was inducted into the [Rock and Roll Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_and_Roll_Hall_of_Fame "Rock and Roll Hall of Fame").[\[230\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-Rolling_Stone_Stamp-231) In 2012, the [U.S. Postal Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Postal_Service "U.S. Postal Service") issued commemorative stamps featuring Davis.[\[230\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-Rolling_Stone_Stamp-231) _[Miles Ahead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Ahead_(film) "Miles Ahead (film)")_ was a 2015 American music film directed by [Don Cheadle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cheadle "Don Cheadle"), co-written by Cheadle with [Steven Baigelman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Baigelman "Steven Baigelman"), Stephen J. Rivele and [Christopher Wilkinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Wilkinson "Christopher Wilkinson"), which interprets the life and compositions of Davis. It premiered at the [New York Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Film_Festival "New York Film Festival") in October 2015. The film stars Cheadle, [Emayatzy Corinealdi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emayatzy_Corinealdi "Emayatzy Corinealdi") as Frances Taylor, [Ewan McGregor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ewan_McGregor "Ewan McGregor"), [Michael Stuhlbarg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Stuhlbarg "Michael Stuhlbarg") and [LaKeith Stanfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LaKeith_Stanfield "LaKeith Stanfield").[\[231\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-232) That same year, a statue of Davis was erected in his home city, [Alton, Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alton,_Illinois "Alton, Illinois"), and listeners of [BBC Radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_Radio "BBC Radio") and [Jazz FM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_FM_(UK) "Jazz FM (UK)") voted Davis the greatest jazz "Miles Davis: Birth of the Cool")_, directed by [Stanley Nelson Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_Nelson_Jr. "Stanley Nelson Jr."), premiered at the [Sundance Film series.[\[236\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-Rolling_Stone_2020-237) Davis is the subject of the upcoming period romance film _[Miles & In a statement to accompany the film's announcement, English musician and co-producer [Mick Jagger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mick_Jagger "Mick Jagger") regarded Davis as "inarguably one of the most influential and important musicians of the 20th Century."[\[237\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-238) Davis has, however, been subject to criticism. In 1990, writer [Stanley Crouch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_Crouch "Stanley Crouch"), a prominent critic of jazz fusion, labeled Davis "the most brilliant sellout in the history of jazz."[\[141\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-Byrnes-2005-142) A 1993 essay by [Robert Walser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Walser "Robert Walser") in _[The Musical Quarterly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Musical_Quarterly "The Musical Quarterly")_ claims that "Davis has long been infamous for missing more notes than any other major trumpet player."[\[238\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-Walser-1993-239) Also in the essay is a quote by music critic [James Lincoln Collier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Lincoln_Collier "James Lincoln Collier"), who states that "if his influence was profound, the ultimate value of his work is another matter", and calls Davis an "adequate instrumentalist" but "not a great one".[\[238\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-Walser-1993-239) In 2013, _[The A.V. Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_A.V._Club "The A.V. Club")_ published an article titled "Miles Davis beat his wives _and_ made beautiful music".
